Grammar Module
20 chapters · 190 grammar points · 10 recaps
N5 Study Guide

This is a route through the N5 material, not the order the chapters happen to be in. Chapters group grammar by function so you can find things; a syllabus has to introduce them in the order they become useful, and that is a different order entirely. Work down the stages in sequence.

Every card is listed by its coordinate, so CH.2·CR.2 means chapter 2, second card. Tap one and you land on it; the back button will bring you here again.

Verb conjugation itself is not taught in this module. The plain and polite forms, past, and negative are drill material rather than something to reason about, and they live in the main app under Study Conjugation. Get ます・ました・ません・ませんでした comfortable before Stage 3, and the plain た・ない forms before Stage 5 — nearly every pattern below attaches to one of them.

Stage 1Naming things

Start where every Japanese sentence starts: saying that one thing is another thing. です comes first because it is polite and safe with anyone, and だ second so you can recognise it in casual speech and buried inside longer sentences. Add the two particles that decide what a sentence is about — は and が — then the question marker か, and you can already ask and answer what is this?

Stage 2Where things are

Existence comes next because it is the first thing you actually need in a room, a shop or a station. Japanese splits it in two — あります for things, います for anything alive — and that split never goes away. The position words and the two place particles finish the job: に marks where something sits or where you are heading, で marks where something happens.

Stage 3Doing things to things

Now put a verb in. を marks what the action lands on, and that is very nearly the whole of basic transitivity. に + 行く gives you a purpose for going somewhere, which is the first time you join two verbs in one sentence. と・や and も are listing and addition — small cards, but they turn bare single-object sentences into real ones.

Stage 4Putting two events in order

Everything so far has been one clause. This is how you get to two. The て-form chain is the workhorse — did this, then this — and the rest are time boundaries: 前に before, てから after, から from, まで until. Learn them together, because they are constantly mistaken for one another, and finish on the recap that sets all of them side by side.

Stage 5What is happening right now

ている is the most useful thing in N5 and the most mistranslated. It is not simply the present continuous: it covers an action in progress, a state left behind by a finished action, and a permanent condition, which is exactly why there are three cards rather than one. もう and まだ pair with it naturally — already done, not yet done.

Stage 6Saying what you want

Three ways of talking about yourself that you will reach for on day one and keep using forever. Note that 好き and 上手 take が, not を. That が is a recurring trap across the whole language, and it is far cheaper to build the habit correctly now than to unlearn it at N4.

Stage 7Asking for things, suggesting things

The first properly social stage. てください is the request you will use most, and ましょう / ませんか are how you propose doing something together. Dwell on ませんか — using a negative question as an invitation feels backwards in English and is completely ordinary here.

Stage 8May I, must I, must I not

These belong together and should be learned together, because the opposite of must is not must not. てもいい grants permission, なければいけない imposes a duty, てはいけない forbids — and the recap spells out the three-way distinction that learners routinely collapse into two.

Stage 9Giving and receiving

Japanese makes you say which way a thing moved. あげる is away from you, くれる is toward you, もらう is you receiving — and picking the wrong one is one of the most audible beginner errors, because it makes you sound like you are narrating somebody else's life. The recap's mirror table is the fastest way to fix it.

Stage 10Talking about the past

Both patterns here are built on the plain past た, so this is the point at which the た-form drills in the main app stop being optional. たり lists sample activities without claiming the list is complete; たことがある is how you say you have done something at least once in your life.

Stage 11How much, how many, which is more

Quantity and comparison sit together because they answer the same kind of question. より and のなかで are the two comparison frames you will need constantly; だけ, たくさん and くらい handle amount. Structurally none of this is hard — it behaves more like vocabulary than grammar, so move through it briskly.

Stage 12Things becoming other things

なる is become, and the only real difficulty is remembering that adjectives change shape in front of it: 大きくなる, 静かになる. The recap ties this back to the copula and existence cards from Stages 1 and 2, which makes it a natural checkpoint before the final stage.

Stage 13Sounding like a person, not a textbook

Last, the layer that makes speech sound human: よ and ね for aiming information at a listener, んです for explaining rather than merely stating, でしょう for hedging a claim you are not certain of. Add the remaining question words and N5 is complete. The conjecture recap will look thin at this point — it fills out the moment N4 is switched on.

That is all 59 N5 grammar points and all nine N5 recaps. When they feel solid, switch N4 on with the cog on the menu screen and start the N4 guide.

N4 Study Guide

This guide assumes N5 is solid. Every stage below either extends something you already know or attaches to a form you can already produce, and where a stage builds directly on an N5 card the text says so.

Sort one thing out before you begin: almost all of N4 attaches to plain forms rather than polite ones. If 書く・書いた・書かない・書いている do not come out automatically, spend a week in the main app's conjugation drills first. Everything downstream depends on it.

Stages are ordered by what they unlock, not by difficulty alone — the て-form extensions come early because so much of N4 is built from them, and voice comes last because nothing else needs it.

Stage 1More particles, more precision

Start with the cheapest wins. These extend particles you already use and can be dropped straight into sentences you can already build, which makes them a gentle way back in. ので is the one to note: it does the same job as N5's から but sounds objective rather than personal, and that difference matters in writing and at work.

Stage 2The て-form stops meaning and then

In N5 the て-form only chained events in sequence. Here it becomes the joint the language turns on: cause, means, concession, apology. Do this stage before anything else in N4 — a dozen later structures are nothing more than a て-form plus one word, and none of them will hold if the base is shaky.

Stage 3Verbs bolted onto the て-form

Now the auxiliaries. Each is a real verb doing double duty — みる see, おく put, しまう finish — and the literal meaning is a reliable guide to the grammatical one. Slow down on てある: it looks like ている but says that somebody did this deliberately and left it in that state.

Stage 4Where an action sits in time

N5 gave you is doing and has done. This stage gives you the rest of the timeline: about to, in the middle of, only just finished, started, kept going, ended. ところだ and たばかり are close enough that they are worth learning back to back, so the difference actually lands.

Stage 5Being able to

The potential form is the first N4 conjugation you have to produce rather than merely recognise, so give it real drilling time in the main app. The particle shift is what people forget: what was を becomes が. 見える and 聞こえる are kept separate on purpose — they are about what reaches you, not about what you are capable of.

Stage 6Wanting and intending

N5 let you say what you want to do. This stage lets you say what you want somebody else to do, what you intend, and what has been arranged — three different degrees of commitment, which the つもり card lays out explicitly. がる is the rule that stops you claiming to know how other people feel.

Stage 7Asking, ordering, advising

This is a politeness ladder, not a list. It runs from the blunt imperative through casual favours up to the humble request you would use with a stranger or a superior, and the ていただけませんか card carries the table showing every rung at once. Learn where each one sits before using any of them — the cost of getting this wrong is social, not grammatical.

Stage 8Doing things for people

The benefactive layer sitting on top of N5's giving verbs: what changes hands is no longer a thing but an action. The direction rules are identical to the ones you already know, so if あげる・くれる・もらう are solid this is a short stage. Mind the caution on てあげる — announcing your own kindness lands badly.

Stage 9Duty, in N4 shades

Three refinements of the N5 obligation set: permission not to do something, a contracted have to you will hear constantly in speech, and a formal it is necessary. The chapter recap gains its N4 rows once you reach this point, so re-read it here rather than at N5.

Stage 10If

The hardest stage in N4 and the one worth slowing right down for. Japanese has four conditionals where English has one, and they are not interchangeable: と for automatic consequences, たら for a completed trigger, ば for a hypothetical, なら for picking up something the other person has just said. Learn 時 first — it is the gentlest of the family and it establishes the clause-before-noun pattern the rest depend on.

Stage 11Joining clauses properly

The connectors that let you build paragraphs instead of sentences. のに is the emotional one — it carries a complaint that けど does not. For real conversation んですが is the most valuable thing in this stage: it is how you open a request without ever stating it outright.

Stage 12Reporting what was said

All five hang off the quotation particle と, so take them as one block. The governing rule is that everything before と stays plain, no matter how polite the rest of the sentence is. そうだ here is hearsay — it is not the そう of Stage 14, and the only visible difference is whether the verb keeps its final る.

Stage 13Turning clauses into things

The structural leap of N4: a whole clause can act as a noun, or sit in front of one to describe it. こと and の do the first job; a bare clause in front of a noun does the second. Because there are no relative pronouns the clause simply stands there — English speakers under-use it for months. Get this and your sentences stop being short.

Stage 14How certain are you

Another ladder, this time of confidence, running from かもしれない at the bottom up to はずだ. Learn them against each other rather than one at a time — the recap in this chapter orders the whole set and is the single most useful table in the module. そう here is appearance judged by looking; hold it against the hearsay そうだ from Stage 12.

Stage 15Voice

The hardest conjugations in N4, left late on purpose. Begin with the 他動詞・自動詞 pairs — they are not voice at all, but they train the same instinct about whether an action is done to something or simply happens to it. Then passive れる・られる, then causative せる・させる, then the fused させられる, which is how you say you were made to do something you did not want to do.

Stage 16Making things change

The deliberate counterpart to N5's なる: なる is what happens, する is what somebody does. The 〜く・〜に card is small but load-bearing — it is the adverb rule both of them depend on, and it is also why 上手に and 静かに look the way they do.

Stage 17Counting and limiting

A big stage but an easy one — mostly fixed expressions rather than new structure, which makes it good material for a slow week or for filling gaps between harder stages. 以上・以下・以外 pay for themselves immediately in anything written, and すぎる you will use daily.

Stage 18Adverbs and discourse glue

The largest stage and the least structural: these are words, not patterns. Do not sit down and learn eighteen adverbs. Take two or three a week and force them into whatever you are already saying. だんだん, ほとんど and ぜんぜん earn their keep fastest, and the それ-connectors are what make spoken paragraphs hang together instead of stopping dead at every full stop.

Stage 19Ending a sentence with attitude

Last, the finals — how you wonder aloud, fish for agreement, or press a point. These are heavily register-marked: かしら reads as feminine, かい as distinctly masculine and old-fashioned, and both are more useful to recognise than to produce. The chapter recap sorts them by who actually says them.

1 Core Particles
  1. は · がTopic marker · Subject marker
  2. をDirect object marker
  3. に · へDestination · Location · Time · Direction

  5. でPlace of action · Means · Method
  6. と · やAnd (exhaustive) · With · And (non-exhaustive)
  7. もAlso · Too · Either · Both
  8. のPossession · Description · Nominalizer
  9. けど · けれども · がBut · However — contrast & concession
  10. などSuch as · And so on
  11. とか〜とかThings like · For example — casual listing
  12. でもOr something · Whether A or B

N5CH.1 · CR.1
は · が
(wa · ga)
Topic marker · Subject marker
subject
Subject + が + Predicate
topic
Topic + は + Comment
About は

は is a particle that marks the topic of the sentence — what the whole sentence is "about." The topic is always something the speaker assumes is already present in the listener's mind. The emphasis falls on what comes after は — the new information or comment. The particle is written は but pronounced わ (wa).

Once a topic is established, it can be dropped in subsequent sentences — Japanese avoids unnecessary repetition.

Contrast use: は has a secondary function of signalling comparison when it appears mid-sentence on something other than the main topic.

About が

が is a particle that marks the grammatical subject. It surfaces when the subject is new, unknown, or being specifically identified or contrasted. Because が identifies the subject as the specific answer to "who" or "what," it emphasizes what comes before it — the core contrast with は. What follows can be a verb, an い-adjective, or a な-adjective or noun rounded off with だ／です — all four count as predicates.

New subject · identification: when answering a だれ or なに question, が must be used. Once established, subsequent sentences naturally shift to は.

は vs が

は emphasizes what comes after it — the comment. が emphasizes what comes before it — the subject being identified. The two particles can coexist in the same sentence doing different jobs.

Words that always require が

Certain verbs and adjectives require が to mark what they relate to:

いる,
ある,
わかる,
できる,
見える,
聞こえる,
好き,
きらい,
上手,
下手,
欲しい,
必要,
大切.

は — topic
東京は大きいです。
Tokyo is big.
は marks topic; neutral general statement about Tokyo
い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
魚は好きです。肉は嫌いです。
I like fish. I dislike meat. (contrastive は)
contrastive は; each は draws contrast with the other preference
な-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
カレーは辛い。
Curry is spicy.
plain casual general truth; は used for a known fact about curry
い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
が — subject
海が見えます。
The sea can be seen.
が marks the visible subject; perceptual verbs like 見える take が
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
公園に猫がいます。
There is a cat in the park.
が marks the existent subject; 猫 is new information introduced into the scene
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
近所の子供たちが走る。
The neighbourhood kids are running.
が marks the specific subjects doing the action; observed scene
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
は vs が — contrast
田中さんはコーヒーを飲みます。
Tanaka drinks coffee. (は = Tanaka is the topic)
は makes Tanaka the topic; could contrast with other people
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
田中さんがコーヒーを飲みます。
It's Tanaka who drinks coffee. (が = specific identification)
が identifies Tanaka specifically; answers the question 'who?'
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
猫が好き。
I like cats. (が = emphatic, strong feeling)
strong emotional preference; が often used with feelings and abilities
な-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
猫は好きだけど、犬は苦手。
I like cats, but dogs not so much. (contrastive は)

な-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N5CH.1 · CR.2
を
(wo)
Direct object marker
Noun + を + Verb
About

を is a particle that marks the direct object of a verb — the thing being acted upon. The particle is written を but pronounced お (o). を is never dropped and cannot be replaced by any other particle in this role.

Movement through a place: を also marks a place that an action passes through or moves along: 公園を歩く — walk through a park. This is distinct from に (destination) or で (location of action).

Examplesshow ▶
Direct object
パンを食べます。
I eat bread.
basic transitive object marker; を marks the direct object
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
肉を食べません。
I don't eat meat.
negative; を is retained even in negation
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE
映画を見ました。
I watched a movie.
polite past transitive action
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
毎日音楽を聞く。
I listen to music every day.
聴く specifically for intentional listening, unlike 聞こえる for passive hearing
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
テレビをあまり見ない。
I don't watch TV much.
あまり + negative = 'not very much'; を retained in negation
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
Movement through space
公園を歩きます。
I walk through the park.
を marks the space traversed; に would mark the destination
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
公園を歩く。
I walk through the park.
を marks the path or space moved through, not a destination
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
道を走った。
I ran down the road.
を used for movement through or along a space; common with 走る、飛ぶ、歩く
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N5CH.1 · CR.3
に · へ
(ni · e)
Destination · Location · Time · Direction
destination / direction
Place + に / へ + Motion Verb
specific time
Time + に + Verb
indirect object / recipient
Person + に + Verb
existence location
Place + に + がある / がいる
About に

に is a particle that always marks a fixed endpoint or target — a specific point in space, time, or relation that the action reaches or is anchored to.

Destination: with motion verbs (行く, 来る, 帰る, 入る, 乗る), に marks the arrival point: 学校に行く.

Existence location: いる and ある always use に to mark where something exists. に marks where something is (fixed point); で marks where an action takes place.

Indirect object · recipient: を marks the direct object; に marks the receiver or direction of the verb's effect: 母にプレゼントをあげた, 先生に質問をしました.

に with time — required, forbidden, optional

Required: exact numbered time references — clock times, specific dates, days of the week, years.

Forbidden: relative time expressions (きのう、あした、今日、まいにち、いま、とき) reject に entirely.

Optional: parts of the day and seasons allow but often omit に.

About へ

へ is a particle that marks direction or goal of movement with motion verbs. に specifies the arrival point precisely; へ is more abstract — toward. に is more common in everyday speech.

About に — frequency (per)N4

Timeframe + に + count expresses frequency: 一週間に三回 — three times a (= per) week. に keeps its usual sense of marking a target space — here the period of time inside which the count happens.

Don't swap in で: で with time expresses how long something takes to complete (2年間で50万円貯めた — saved 500,000 yen in two years), not how often it happens.

Destination

に with 向かう; marks the target direction

Time

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

に marks recipient of giving; に + あげる/もらう/くれる is a fixed pairing
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

I ask the teacher a question.
に marks the person directed at; 質問する is always paired with に
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
友達にメッセージを送る。
I send a message to my friend.
に marks the recipient; 送る takes に for the person receiving
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
Location of existence
部屋に猫がいます。
There is a cat in the room.
に marks location of existence; います and あります always take に
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
テーブルの上に本がある。
There's a book on the table.
に marks location of existence; ある/います always take に for location
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
へ — direction
家へ帰ります。
I'm going home.
へ sounds more directional and homeward; に also works but へ feels natural here
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
東京へ行く。
I'm going to Tokyo.
へ for casual direction statement; interchangeable with に but slightly softer
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
Frequency — perN4
一週間に三回、ジムに行っています。
I go to the gym three times a week.
period first, count after に
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
母は一日に二回、犬と散歩します。
My mother walks the dog twice a day.
daily routine — 一日に = per day
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
一年に一回、家族で旅行します。
Once a year, we take a family trip.
annual events are the textbook case
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
彼は一ヶ月に一回だけ部屋を掃除するよ。
He only cleans his room once a month.
frequency + だけ to underline how little
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
一日に何回、歯を磨きますか？
How many times a day do you brush your teeth?
asking about frequency — 何回 slots into the count position
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
N5CH.1 · CR.4
に + 行く · 来る · 帰る
(ni+iku · kuru · kaeru)
To go · come · return in order to ~
to go
Place + に + Verb stem + に + 行く
to come
Place + に + Verb stem + に + 来る
to return
Place + に + Verb stem + に + 帰る
About

This grammar structure is used to express going, coming, or returning somewhere for the purpose of doing something — equivalent to go/come/return in order to [verb] in English. It describes the intention behind the movement, not just the movement itself.

There are two に particles in this structure. The first に marks the destination (place you are heading to). The second に marks the purpose (the action you intend to do there). The verb before the second に must be in its stem form: う-verbs shift the final kana to the い-row (買う → 買い), and る-verbs drop る (食べる → 食べ). Neither the dictionary form nor the polite form is used here.

The destination particle に can be replaced by へ with a slight nuance shift: に emphasises the destination as an endpoint, while へ emphasises the direction of travel or the journey itself.

Examplesshow ▶
行く — to go
山へ花を見に行きます。
I'm going to the mountain to see the flowers.
verb stem + に + motion verb; purpose expressed as a noun-like stem
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
どこに食べに行きますか？
Where are you going to eat?
asking about the destination of a purpose trip
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
今日は映画を見に行きません。
I'm not going to see a movie today.
not going for that purpose today; polite negative
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE
スーパーに肉を買いに行きました。
I went to the supermarket to buy meat.
went specifically to buy; に marks both destination and purpose
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
公園に走りに行く。
I'm going to the park for a run.
going to run; the park is both destination and context
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
何しに行く？
What are you going there for?
casual; what are you going there for?
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
海に泳ぎに行った。
I went to the beach to swim.
casual past; went to swim; に marks purpose and destination
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
今日は買い物に行かない。
I'm not going shopping today.
買い物 is already a noun so に行かない works directly without a stem
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
来る — to come
先生が説明しに来ます。
The teacher is coming to explain.
someone coming to you with a purpose; 来る used when motion is toward speaker
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
何時に会いに来ますか？
What time are you coming to see me?
迎えに来る is a fixed expression meaning 'to come and pick someone up'
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
今日は手伝いに来ません。
I'm not coming to help today.
not coming for that purpose today; 手伝い is noun form
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE
ともだちがあそびに来ました。
My friend came to hang out.
friend visiting for leisure; あそびに来る is a common phrase
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
弟が本を借りに来る。
My younger brother is coming to borrow a book.
expected near-future visit from a sibling
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
何しに来るの？
What are you coming here for?
slightly suspicious or curious; の adds a seeking-explanation nuance
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
彼が謝りに来た。
He came to apologize.
came to apologize; purpose of coming is the key information
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
今日は食べに来ない。
He's not coming over to eat today.
negation of a recurring visit; 'not coming to hang out today'
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
帰る — to return
荷物を取りに帰ります。
I'm going back to get my luggage.
帰る = return home; purpose is retrieval of an item left behind
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
昼に家に食べに帰りますか？
Are you going home for lunch?
going home midday for lunch; common practice in Japan
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
今日は食事に帰りません。
I'm not going home to eat today.

N5CH.1 · CR.5
で
(de)
Place of action · Means · Method
place of action
Place + で + Action Verb
tool / means / method
Tool / Means + で + Verb
About

で is a particle that marks the context of an action — where it happens, how it is done, or with what it is done. It always marks something required for the action to take place.

Place of action: で marks the location where an action verb takes place — a verb describing something the subject actively does, such as 食べる, 勉強する or 働く. The place is not a destination — it is the context the action requires. Verbs of existence and state (いる, ある) are not action verbs and take に instead: 学校で勉強する, レストランで食べた.

Tool · instrument · method: で marks what the action is carried out with — the instrument in the hand, the material worked with, or the method chosen. The tool is never the doer; it is what the doer employs: はしで食べます, ペンで書きます.

Transportation · communication: で marks vehicles and languages as means in exactly the same sense — the vehicle is how the movement is achieved, the language is how the speaking is achieved: バスで行きます — by bus, 日本語で話しましょう — in Japanese.

で vs に: に marks where something goes or exists. で marks where an action happens. Existence verbs いる and ある always use に, never で.

N5CH.1 · CR.6
と · や
(to · ya)
And (exhaustive) · With · And (non-exhaustive)
with — accompaniment
Person + と + Verb
and — exhaustive list
Noun A + と + Noun B
and — non-exhaustive list
Noun A + や + Noun B
(や)optional
About と

と is a particle that joins nouns together, and also marks the person an action is performed together with.

Exhaustive list: と connects nouns into a complete group — implying nothing has been left out. と appears after each noun; the final と is often dropped in conversation.

Accompaniment: と marks who someone does an action together with. Both parties are mutually involved — distinguishing it from に: 先生と話す — talk with the teacher — mutual vs 先生に話す — talk to the teacher — one-directional.

About や

や is a particle that connects nouns in a non-exhaustive list — the items are examples from a larger set. It may also follow the final item (ビールやワインや), but that closing や is usually dropped.

と vs や: と = complete list. や = representative sample. ビールとワインを飲んだ — only those two. ビールやワインを飲んだ — among other drinks.

About と — quotationN4

Beyond and/with, と marks a quotation: what was said, thought, heard or written, followed by a verb like 言う, 思う, 聞く. Direct quotes take brackets — 「行きます」と言いました; indirect quotes use the plain form — 行くと思います.

After nouns and な-adjectives, だ is required before と: 猫だと思う, 無理だと思う. In casual speech と becomes って — covered in card CH.16 · CR.4.

N5CH.1 · CR.7
も
(mo)
Also · Too · Either · Both
also / too / either
Noun + も + Predicate
both A and B
Noun A + も + Noun B + も + Predicate
About

も is a particle that signals inclusion — whatever is true for A is also true for B. も replaces は, が, or を entirely — the original particle is dropped. も always builds on prior context. It attaches to a noun; the predicate that follows may be a verb, an い-adjective, or a な-adjective or noun with だ／です.

Negative sentences: in a negative sentence, も shifts meaning from also to either or neither: 私も行きません.

Double も — both A and B: も can appear twice when two items share the same verb and grammatical role: パンもたまごも食べました.

About Number + も — emphasisN4

After a number + counter, も flags the amount itself as surprising. With an affirmative predicate it reads as many/much as — 12時間も寝た — slept a whole 12 hours. It's the same も as too/also: the amount is being included in a group where you wouldn't expect it.

With a negative predicate it flips to not even, and 一 + counter + も + negative is the fixed not even one: 一回も見ていない — haven't seen it even once.

N5CH.1 · CR.8
の
(no)
Possession · Description · Nominalizer
nominalizer
Verb plain form
+ の + は / が
possession / description
Noun A + の + Noun B
About の — possession / description

の is a particle that links two nouns, where the first noun modifies or describes the second. The second noun is always the main idea. This covers possession (わたしの本), origin (日本の車), category (日本語の本), and description (白いシャツの人).

の as pronoun substitute

When the noun is clear from context, の can stand in for it: これはわたしのです — This is mine, 赤いのを買います — I'll buy the red one.

のは / のが — nominalizer

の can follow a verb phrase in plain form to turn it into a noun. The nominalized phrase then functions as topic (のは) or subject (のが): 日本語を話すのが好きです. のが is the natural partner for 好き, 嫌い, 上手, 下手.

N5CH.1 · CR.9
けど · けれども · が
(kedo · keredomo · ga)
But · However — contrast & concession
Casual
Verb / い-adjective
Verb / い-adj + けど + Clause B
な-adjective / Noun
な-adj / Noun + だけど + Clause B
Formal
Verb / い-adjective
Verb / い-adj + けれども + Clause B
な-adjective / Noun
な-adj / Noun + だけれども + Clause B
Most formal
Verb / い-adjective
Verb / い-adj + が、 + Clause B
な-adjective / Noun
な-adj / Noun + だ + が、 + Clause B
About

This grammar structure connects two clauses with a contrasting or softening relationship — A, but B or A; however, B. Clause A states something, and Clause B introduces a point that qualifies, contrasts, or adds to it. The contrast can be strong or soft — all three forms can also soften a statement rather than express direct opposition.

All three forms follow the same attachment rules: verbs and い-adjectives attach directly. な-adjectives and nouns require だ before the conjunction.

Register scale: the same conjunction runs across a full formality range. Least formal first:

けど — casual; natural with friends and family
けども — casual, a shade softer than けど
けれど — neutral; safe in most conversation
けれども — polite speech and careful writing
が — most formal and direct; written Japanese and formal statements

Trailing が: a sentence can simply stop on が, with Clause B never said. The listener is left to supply the objection themselves. まあ、綺麗ですが。 — Well, it is pretty, but… — the speaker flags a reservation without naming it, which lands far more softly than stating it outright.

N4CH.1 · CR.10
など
(~nado)
Such as · And so on
Listing
Noun + など
Category
Noun + などの + Noun
About

など is a particle that presents a noun (or a list of nouns) as representative examples of a larger category — such as, and so on. It signals that the list is not complete: other members of the same category exist. It very often closes a list built with や: パンや卵など — bread, eggs and the like.

などの + Noun names the category explicitly after the examples: 寺や神社などの古い建物 — old buildings such as temples and shrines. In writing, など frequently appears as the kanji 等.

Attached to people — especially 私など — it lowers the noun: someone like me. This humble use is polite about oneself but dismissive about others, so handle with care.

N4CH.1 · CR.11
とか〜とか
(~to ka ~to ka)
Things like · For example — casual listing
Noun
Noun A + とか + Noun B +
(とか)optional
Verb
Verb A + とか + Verb B +
(とか)optional
About

とか is a particle that strings together examples while making clear the list is non-exhaustive — the listener assumes there is more where that came from. Unlike や, which only joins nouns, とか also attaches to verbs and adjectives in their plain form. The final とか of a list can be (and often is) dropped.

とか is a conversational particle. In writing or formal speech it sounds careless; the combination of や closed with など is used instead.

A single とか hedges one item — or something (like that). It softens the mention, as if the speaker were only half-committing to the example: お土産とか — souvenirs or anything like that.

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.1 · CR.12
でも
(~demo)
Or something · Whether A or B
Suggestion
Noun + でも + Suggestion
Whether / or
A + でも + B + でも
About

でも is an adverbial particle that presents its noun as one example out of several possibilities. お茶でも means tea, or something like it — the speaker names tea, but signals that other options would be just as welcome. In Japanese this use is called 例示 — presenting examples.

Because it leaves the choice open, でも softens suggestions, invitations and offers — naming the thing directly (お茶を飲みませんか) sounds more insistent. It pairs naturally with ませんか, ましょう(か) and てください. When attached, でも replaces を and が — never をでも.

Don't confuse this with でも at the start of a sentence (but, a conjunction), or with question word + でも (だれでも — anyone) — that pattern is covered in card CH.3 · CR.5.

About でも〜でも

When でも is used twice in a sequence, it presents two examples and marks them as interchangeable: 肉でも魚でも — whether it is meat or fish (either way). With an affirmative predicate the pattern reads whether A or B; with a negative one, neither A nor B. This is the same example-presenting でも described above — two samples are given instead of one, and the rest of the category remains included.

い-adjectives and verbs enter this pattern through their て-forms (高くても安くても); that version is covered in card CH.7 · CR.8.

週末は映画でも見に行きましょう。
Let's go see a movie or something this weekend.
a movie is one idea among many; でも keeps the plan flexible

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.1 · CR.13
までに
(~made ni)
By · No later than — deadlines
Noun
Time noun + までに
Verb
Verbdictionary form
+ までに
About

までに is a compound particle: まで plus the case particle に. The two look alike but differ clearly: まで means until — a state or action continues all the way up to the limit — while までに means by — a one-time action happens at some point before the limit. Compare 5時まで働きます — I work until 5 with 5時までに帰ります — I'll go home by 5.

The に is doing its usual job of marking a target point: までに literally sets the deadline as the target. Before までに a verb always appears in its dictionary form — the plain non-past, and this holds for every verb type, not just る-verbs. It stays that way even when the sentence itself is about the past: 家を出るまでに食べた — I ate before leaving the house. In formal writing you may occasionally see the kanji 迄.

Examplesshow ▶
レポートは金曜日までに出してください。
Please hand in the report by Friday.
deadline — any point before friday is fine

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.1 · CR.14
ので
(~node)
Because · Since — polite, objective reason
Verb
Verbplain form
+ ので
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ ので
な-adjective
な-adj + なので
Noun
Noun + なので
About

ので is a conjunctive particle that joins a reason (A) to its result (B): 雨が降っているので、出かけません. It attaches to the plain form; nouns and な-adjectives insert な before it — 日曜日なので, 静かなので.

The contrast with から is register and tone. ので presents the reason as objective — a fact that naturally leads to B — which makes it softer, more explanatory, and the default choice in polite requests and formal situations. から is more direct and subjective, at home in casual speech, opinions and commands. Both are correct; the choice signals how you frame the reason.

In very polite speech, ます-forms also appear before ので (ありますので). In casual speech you'll often hear the contraction んで.

Examplesshow ▶
雨が降っているので、今日は出かけません。
Since it's raining, I'm not going out today.
the rain is presented as plain fact — ので keeps it objective

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.1 · CR.15
でできる・からできる
(~de dekiru · ~kara dekiru)
Made of · Made from
Visible material
Noun [material]recognisable in the product
+ でできている
Raw material
Noun [material]transformed beyond recognition
+ からできている
About

Both grammar patterns state what something is made of. The material takes で or から, and できている describes the resulting state of a specific thing: このテーブルは木でできている — this table is made of wood. For general statements about a kind of thing, plain できる also appears.

The standard distinction: で — made of is used when the material is still recognisable in the product — wood in a table, paper in a bag; から — made from is used when the raw material has been transformed — soybeans in tofu, milk in cheese. から keeps the focus on the ingredients as they were before the change.

In modern spoken Japanese the distinction has blurred and で is used in most situations — but it remains relevant in reading and in JLPT questions.

This table is made of wood.
the wood is right there to see — で

N5CH.2 · CR.1
だ
(da)
Am · Is · Are — plain copula
な-adjective
な-adj + だ
Noun
Noun + だ
About

This grammar structure is used to identify or describe something in plain speech — the casual equivalent of です, translating as am, is, or are in English.

だ follows nouns and な-adjectives directly. It cannot be used with い-adjectives — this is one of the most important rules about だ. The plain form of an い-adjective already carries the meaning of is on its own: 大きい means it is big without any copula attached. Never add だ after an い-adjective.

だ is used exclusively in casual speech. In polite speech, です takes its place. While the two are often treated as direct equivalents, they are not interchangeable — だ will never appear in formal or polite sentences.

Questions: だ does not have a dedicated question form — to ask a question in casual speech, either add か directly after it or drop it and use rising intonation instead. Adding か sounds blunt and is typically associated with masculine speech; rising intonation is softer and more common in everyday conversation. In polite speech, ですか takes over this role entirely and is the standard way to ask questions.

N5CH.2 · CR.2
です
(desu)
Am · Is · Are — polite copula
い-adjective
い-adj spoken / daily use
+ です
な-adjective
な-adj + です
Noun
Noun + です
About

This grammar structure is used to identify or describe something in polite speech — the polite equivalent of だ, translating as am, is, or are in English.

です attaches to nouns and な-adjectives in the same way as だ. Unlike だ, it also attaches to い-adjectives to form polite predicates — this is the standard way to make an い-adjective polite in everyday speech. In strictly formal writing, い-adjective + です is sometimes considered incorrect, but in daily spoken Japanese and texting it is completely normal and you will use it constantly.

です and だ are often described as polite and casual versions of each other, but they are standalone structures — not simply interchangeable forms of the same word.

Questions: Append か to any of the four forms to turn a statement into a question: ですか · じゃないですか · でしたか · じゃなかったですか. Intonation rises naturally on the final か.

N5CH.2 · CR.3
がある
(ga aru)
There is, Have — existence of inanimate things
Casual
Affirmative
Noun + がある
Negative
Noun + がない
Formal
Affirmative
Noun + があります
Negative
Noun + がありません
About

This grammar structure is used to express that something exists, is present, or is possessed — equivalent to there is or to have in English. ある is used exclusively for inanimate · non-living things: objects, events, places, time, abstract concepts. For living things, いる is used instead.

Location is expressed with the に particle before が: テーブルの上にケーキがある — there is a cake on the table. In casual speech, が is often dropped entirely, leaving just the noun + ある.

ある is an う-verb, but its negative form is irregular: ない, not あらない. The polite negative is ありません. The kanji form 有る carries no difference in meaning and is common in written Japanese.

N5CH.2 · CR.4
がいる
(ga iru)
There is, Have — existence of living things
Casual
Affirmative
Noun + がいる
Negative
Noun + がいない
Formal
Affirmative
Noun + がいます
Negative
Noun + がいません
About

This grammar structure is used to express that a living thing exists, is present, or is possessed — equivalent to there is or to have in English. いる is used for living · animate things: people, animals, and by extension things operated or controlled by living beings (a police car with officers inside, for example). For inanimate objects and abstract things, ある is used instead.

Location is expressed with the に particle before が: 部屋に猫がいる — there is a cat in the room. In casual speech, が is often dropped, leaving just the noun + いる.

いる is a る-verb (Ichidan verb): polite form います, negative いない, polite negative いません. The kanji form 居る is common in written Japanese and carries no difference in meaning.

N5CH.2 · CR.5
になる · くなる
(~ni naru · ~ku naru)
To become — change of state
Casual
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + く + なる
な-adjective
な-adj (no な) + になる
Noun
Noun + になる
Formal
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + く + なります
な-adjective
な-adj (no な) + になります
Noun
Noun + になります
About

This grammar structure is used to express a change of state — that something or someone is becoming, has become, or will become something. It applies to all three word types, each with a different connector before なる.

For い-adjectives, drop the final い and add く before なる: 寒い → 寒くなる. For な-adjectives, attach に directly to the stem — do not add な: 静か → 静かになる. For nouns, attach に directly: 先生 → 先生になる.

Exception: いい — good does not follow the regular rule — it conjugates as よくなる, not いくなる.

なる conjugates normally for tense and polarity.

Examplesshow ▶
六月になると、日が長くなります。
When June comes, the days get longer.
natural cycle change; になる marks transition into a new state

N4CH.2 · CR.6
〜く・〜に
(~ku · ~ni)
Turning adjectives into adverbs
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + く + Verb
な-adjective
な-adj + に + Verb
About

This grammar structure turns adjectives into adverbs — the role English assigns to "-ly". Adjectives describe nouns; to describe a verb — to state how an action is done — they take an adverbial form.

い-adjectives replace the final い with く (the conjunctive form): 早い → 早く,
な-adjectives take に directly on the stem: 静か → 静かに.

The adverb normally stands immediately before the verb it modifies: 大きく書く — write big, きれいに掃除する — clean thoroughly. These are the same forms used in くなる・になる — but they apply to every verb, not only なる.

One exception must be memorized: いい uses its older stem よ, giving よく — well, and by extension often.

字をもっと大きく書いてください。
Please write the characters bigger.
大きい → 大きく — the い is gone, the action is modified
い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
服をきれいに洗いました。
I washed the clothes clean.
な-adjective + に — きれい describing the cleaning, not the room
な-ADJ PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

This morning I got up early and ran in the park.
早く — the workhorse く-adverb of daily life
い-ADJ PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

い-ADJ PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

な-ADJ PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.2 · CR.7
にする・くする
(~ni suru · ~ku suru)
To make ~ · deliberate change of state
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + くする
な-adjective
な-adj + にする
Noun
Noun + にする
About

This grammar structure is used to express deliberately changing the state or condition of something — to make (something) ~ or to make (something) more ~. The adjective is converted to the same adverbial form introduced in card CH.2 · CR.6 and combined with する.

い-adjectives drop the final い and add く: 冷たい → 冷たくする — to make (something) cold; the irregular いい becomes よくする,
な-adjectives take に: 簡単な → 簡単にする — to make (something) simple,
Nouns also attach にする.

The thing that undergoes the change is marked with を: 部屋をきれいにする — to make the room clean.

The heart of the pattern is deliberate control — someone acts on the object to bring the change about. This sets にする・くする against なる: 部屋をきれいにする means someone cleans the room, while 部屋がきれいになる merely reports that the room became clean, with no agent in view. The pair mirrors the transitive–intransitive divide covered in card CH.19 · CR.1 — する acts on things, なる happens to them. It also differs from ようにする: this pattern changes a property of a thing, while ようにする directs sustained effort at one's own behaviour.

Negative forms are natural, above all as requests: 問題をこれ以上難しくしないでください — please don't make the questions any harder. 静かにする is a set phrase meaning to keep quiet, most often heard as the request 静かにしてください — the thing being quietened is left unsaid. With nouns the pattern means turning one thing into another — 倉庫を事務所にする, to turn the warehouse into an office — and covers choices of style or appearance, often borrowing みたいに from the resemblance family: 髪をボブみたいにする — to style one's hair like a bob.

N4CH.2 · CR.8
ようになる・ようにする
(~you ni naru · ~you ni suru)
To reach the point · To make an effort
Change arrives
Verbdictionary / potential
+ ようになる
Effort is made
Verbdictionary / negative
+ ようにする
About

This pair of grammar structures combines よう — a state or manner treated as a goal — with the particle に and the two fundamental verbs of change: なる — to become and する — to do. The split mirrors the verbs themselves: with なる the change arrives on its own, while with する the speaker pushes the change into being through deliberate effort.

Usage 1 — ようになる: attaches to the plain non-past form and expresses that an action has reached the point of happening or being possible — to come to, to reach the point that. It is most often paired with the potential form, describing an ability that arrived gradually: 漢字が書けるようになりました — I got to where I can write kanji. With a plain dictionary form it marks a new habit or state that came about: 弟は野菜を食べるようになった. For changes in the negative direction, ないようになる exists but everyday Japanese strongly prefers the compact なくなる.

Usage 2 — ようにする: attaches to the dictionary or ない form and expresses a conscious effort or standing policy — to try to, to make sure to. The action is something the speaker goes out of their way to do, and effort is implied. In the form ようにしている it describes a maintained routine: 毎日走るようにしています — I make a point of running every day. With ない it means making sure something is avoided: 遅れないようにする — make sure not to be late.

N4CH.2 · CR.9
をしている
(~o shite iru)
Has a feature · Wearing
Feature / accessory
Noun + をしている
About

This grammar structure is a use of する beyond to do: it describes that someone has a certain physical feature, or is wearing an accessory. The feature is marked with を as in any active sentence, and because having a feature is a state rather than an event, the verb almost always appears as している — the ている form from cards CH.8 · CR.1 to CH.8 · CR.3: 母は大きい目をしています — my mother has big eyes.

The range of features is limited by convention. Most common are faces and expressions (困った顔をしている — has a troubled look), followed by eyes, build, and voices (きれいな声をしている). For worn items, the pattern covers accessories that are added or fastened — watches, earrings, masks, ties — while garments covering large areas take their own verbs (着る for tops, 履く for things worn on the legs and feet). The appearance family from card CH.18 · CR.4 combines naturally here: 悲しそうな目をしている — has sad-looking eyes.

Quick RecapCH.2 · CR.10
Copula, existence & change of state
だ · です · がある · がいる · になる · にする · ようになる · をしている
Comparison
Form Group Function Feels like
だ Copula State what something is — plain "Is / Am / Are"
です Copula State what something is — polite "Is / Am / Are"
がある Existence Say that a thing exists or is possessed "There is / I have"
がいる Existence Say that a living thing exists or is present "There is / I have"
〜になる · 〜くなる Change of state Something becomes so on its own "Becomes / Gets"
〜にする · 〜くするN4 Change of state Somebody deliberately makes it so "Makes it / Turns it into"
ようになる · ようにするN4 Change of state Reach a point over time · make a standing effort "Came to / Make sure to"
をしているN4 State Describe a feature somebody or something has "Has / Is wearing"
〜く · 〜にN4 Formation Adverbial form that both なる and する attach to "Quietly / Bigger"
When to use what
Saying what something is, among friends and family → だ
Saying what something is, in polite conversation → です
Saying an object, plant or abstract thing is there → がある
Saying a person or animal is there → がいる
The change happens by itself, nobody caused it → 〜になる · 〜くなる
Somebody chooses to bring the change about → 〜にする · 〜くするN4
The change builds up over time, or you resolve to keep it up → ようになる · ようにするN4
Describing a permanent feature — eyes, build, a voice, or something worn → をしているN4
Key pairing: なる is what happens, する is what someone does — both take the same 〜く · 〜に form in frontN4
3 Demonstratives & Question Words
  1. こそあどDemonstrative reference system
  2. Noun の [location word]Relative position expressions
  3. Question WordsOpen-ended question words
  4. なんで · どうして · なぜWhy — casual → neutral → formal
  5. WH-word + か · もSomeone · Somewhere · No one · Nowhere
  6. そういうThis kind of · That kind of — こういう family
  7. そんなSuch a · That kind of — そんな family
  8. そんなにSo much · That much — degree adverb
N5CH.3 · CR.1
こそあど
(ko-so-a-do)
Demonstrative reference system
こ
near speaker
そ
near listener
あ
far from both
ど
question
Reference
Type こ そ あ ど
Thing (pronoun) これ それ あれ どれ
Modifier (pre-noun) この その あの どの
Place ここ そこ あそこ どこ
About

This grammar structure is used to point to things, modify nouns, and refer to places relative to where the speaker and listener are. The four stems — こ, そ, あ, ど — represent distance: near the speaker, near the listener, far from both, and unknown (question).

Critical rule — standalone vs noun-required: この · その · あの · どの must always be followed directly by a noun. They cannot stand alone under any circumstances, not even in casual speech. これ · それ · あれ · どれ and ここ · そこ · あそこ · どこ stand alone as complete words. If you want to say this book, use この本. If you want to say this one without naming the noun, use これ.

これ · それ · あれ · どれ — thing pronouns: These refer to things and ideas, not people. For people use この人 · あの人 etc. どれ is used when choosing from three or more options — for two options, どちら is used instead. In casual speech these can appear alone if context is clear (これ？、それ。), but in full sentences they need a verb, です, or a particle.

この · その · あの · どの — noun modifiers: These work for both objects and people. あの人 — that person over there is the standard way to refer to someone at a distance.

この and これ serve different grammatical roles and cannot replace each other. この modifies a noun that follows it; これ stands in place of the noun entirely. Mixing them up is one of the most common early mistakes.

ここ · そこ · あそこ · どこ — place words: These refer only to places — never to things or people. They function like location nouns and combine with place particles depending on purpose:

〜にある · いる existence at a location — where something/someone is
〜に行く · 来る arrival at a location — used with motion verbs
〜へ行く · 来る direction toward a location — emphasis on movement
〜で〜する place where an action occurs

N5CH.3 · CR.2
Noun の [location word]
(Noun no [location])
Relative position expressions

location

Noun + の + location word + に + ある / いる
Reference
Kanji Hiragana Meaning
右 みぎ right
左 ひだり left
前 まえ in front of
後ろ うしろ behind
中 なか inside
上 うえ on · above
下 した under · beneath

About

This grammar structure is used to describe where something is positioned relative to another object. Unlike ここ · そこ · あそこ which are complete location words on their own, these words are relative — they cannot stand alone. They always require a reference noun connected by の: テーブルの下 — under the table, 駅の前 — in front of the station.

The particle after the location phrase depends on what follows. Use です to identify where something is. Use に with ある or いる to say something exists at that location. Use で to mark where an action takes place.

あいだ — between requires two reference nouns joined by と: デパートと病院のあいだ — between the department store and the hospital.

なに vs なん — pronunciation shift

Use なん instead of なに when the following word begins with a d-line sound (だ、で、ど) or an n-line sound (な、に、ぬ、ね、の). This is purely for ease of pronunciation — both mean what. Examples:

Question word Common particles Function

About

Question words follow normal Japanese word order — the rest of the sentence stays the same. What marks a sentence as a question is the final particle か in polite speech, or rising intonation in casual speech where か is dropped.

なぜ · どうして · なんで — why are covered in card CH.3 · CR.4.

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
N5CH.3 · CR.4
なんで · どうして · なぜ
(nande · doushite · naze)
Why — casual → neutral → formal
Casual
なんで + Question
Neutral
どうして + Question
Formal
なぜ + Question
About

All three words ask why and are structurally identical — they sit at the start of a question or embed mid-sentence. The only meaningful difference is register.

なんで is the most casual. It is frequent in everyday conversation with friends, family, and close acquaintances. It can come across as direct, demanding, or even accusatory depending on tone, so it is best avoided with strangers or people of higher status. Literally it is 何 — what + で (particle for means) — by what means — which is why in some contexts なんで can also mean how. The clearer form for that meaning is なにで.

どうして is the neutral default. It works in both polite and casual speech without sounding odd in either. Literally it breaks down as どう — how + して (te-form of する) — how did it come to be that way? — so it can carry a nuance of curiosity or mild surprise rather than a hard demand for logic. When in doubt, どうして is the safest choice.

なぜ is the most formal. It is common in writing, formal speeches, news, and serious situations where a logical reason or cause is being demanded. In everyday casual conversation it can sound stiff or even confrontational.

One word to keep separate: どうした looks similar to どうして but means what's wrong? or what happened? — it expresses concern, not a why-question. It is often followed by の in casual speech (どうしたの？).

N5CH.3 · CR.5
WH-word + か · も
(~ka · ~mo)
Someone · Somewhere · No one · Nowhere
positive
WH-word + か + affirmative sentence
negative
WH-word + も +
Verbnegative form
Reference
Base word + か (positive) + も (negative)
だれ だれか — someone · anyone だれも — no one
どこ どこか — somewhere · anywhere どこも — nowhere
なに なにか — something · anything なにも — nothing
About

This grammar structure is used to turn question words into indefinite pronouns. Adding か to a question word makes it mean some- or any- in positive sentences. Adding も paired with a negative verb makes it mean no- or not any-.

English "anyone" covers both uses — Japanese keeps them separate: だれか for the positive (is anyone here?) and だれも〜ない for the negative (no one came). Mixing them up is a common mistake.

When another particle is also present — such as に or へ — か slots in before the particle and も slots in after it. The verb must be negative when using も.

だれかに話した Talked to someone — か before に
どこかへ行った Went somewhere — か before へ
だれかと食べた Ate with someone — か before と
どこかで見た Saw it somewhere — か before で
だれにも話さなかった Didn't talk to anyone — も after に
どこへも行かなかった Didn't go anywhere — も after へ
だれとも食べなかった Didn't eat with anyone — も after と
どこでも見なかった Didn't see it anywhere — も after で
About WH-word + でも — "any"N4

でも completes the paradigm you know from か and も: だれか — someone · だれも — no one (+ negative) · だれでも — anyone. Likewise なんでも — anything, どこでも — anywhere, いつでも — anytime.

The key contrast with も: でも takes an affirmative predicate — だれでも知っている — everyone/anyone knows, versus だれも知らない — no one knows. No matter who/what/where is often the most natural English.

N4CH.3 · CR.6
そういう
(~sou iu)
This kind of · That kind of — こういう family
こういう / そういう / ああいう / どういう + Noun
About

This grammar structure combines the こそあど prefixes with いう (from 言う) to form kind of words — literally (A) said in that way. Four members, following the usual distance logic: こういう — like this (near the speaker), そういう — like that (near the listener, or just mentioned), ああいう — like that (distant, known to both), どういう — what kind of (questions). Each sits directly before a noun.

In conversation そういう usually points back at what was just said: そういう人 — people like that (like you just described). And どういう意味ですか — what do you mean? — is a set phrase that should be learned as a unit.

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.3 · CR.7
そんな
(~sonna)
Such a · That kind of — そんな family
Casual
そんな / こんな / あんな / どんな + Noun
Formal
そのような / このような / あのような / どのような + Noun
About

そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな sit directly before a noun and mean this/that kind of. They are contractions of そのような etc., and follow the usual こそあど distance logic: こんな near me, そんな near you or just mentioned, あんな distant and known to both, どんな in questions.

The uncontracted forms — このような・そのような・あのような・どのような — carry the same meaning but belong to a polite, formal register. They are the appropriate choice in formal settings such as customer service, job interviews, and formal writing, where the contracted そんな family would sound too casual.

Compared with そういう, そんな is more casual and often more emotional — そんなこと frequently carries protest or dismissal (そんなことは言わないでください). どんな, on the other hand, is the completely neutral what kind of question word.

NOUN PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.3 · CR.8
そんなに
(~sonna ni)
So much · That much — degree adverb
そんなに / こんなに / あんなに / どんなに + Predicate
About

Adding に to the そんな family produces degree adverbs: そんなに means to that extent and modifies verbs, い-adjectives and な-adjectives — so much, that much. Same distance logic as always: こんなに — this much (right here), あんなに — that much (as we both remember), どんなに — how much.

そんなに is used most frequently with negative predicates, where it rejects an assumed extent: そんなに高くない — it's not that expensive. どんなに almost always pairs with 〜ても — no matter how... — that combination is covered in card CH.7 · CR.8.

(takusan)

About

This grammar structure is used to express a large quantity or degree — a lot, many, or plenty. Unlike English, Japanese does not use adjective forms like "many" or "much" in the same way. たくさん is technically classified as a noun used adverbially, meaning it does not conjugate at all — it works the same in casual and polite speech, past or present.

When たくさん comes before a verb or predicate, it modifies the action directly — no connector needed. When it comes before a noun, の is inserted between them (たくさんの猫 — a lot of cats). Dropping の is possible but shifts the nuance: without の, たくさん feels like it is describing the whole scene rather than the specific noun.

Word order is flexible when an object is involved. Both 水をたくさん飲む and たくさん水を飲む are natural — たくさん can sit before or after the を-marked object without changing the meaning.

The kanji form 沢山 exists but in everyday writing たくさん in hiragana is standard.

N5CH.4 · CR.2
〜くらい · 〜ぐらい
(~kurai · ~gurai)
About ~, approximately ~
quantity
Number / Counter + くらい
question
どの + くらい
About

This grammar structure is used to express an approximate quantity, amount, or duration — equivalent to about or approximately in English. It attaches directly after a number or counter word. The speaker is not stating an exact figure, just a rough estimate.

くらい and ぐらい are completely interchangeable in meaning. ぐらい is more common in casual spoken Japanese; くらい is slightly more formal and more frequent in writing. Either is acceptable at N5 level.

どのくらい is the standard way to ask about how much or about how long. It can be followed by a particle depending on what is being asked — どのくらいで — how long until, どのくらい alone as an adverb, and so on.

One limit to know: くらい works best with specific or countable extents. For vague, broad time periods (around spring, around that era) ごろ is used instead. However, when a specific time point is involved, くらい and ごろ can overlap — 3時くらい and 3時ごろ both mean around 3 o'clock.

N5CH.4 · CR.3
けっこう
(kekkou)
Quite, fairly, rather, a good deal
adverb
けっこう + Predicate
set phrase
けっこうです
About

This grammar structure is used as a degree adverb meaning quite, fairly, or rather — expressing that something is more than expected or more than average, but short of extreme. It modifies verbs, い-adjectives and な-adjectives directly, with no connector such as な or だ — けっこう歩いた, けっこう高い, けっこう静かだ — and can take a whole phrase in its scope. It does not attach straight to a noun: modifying one requires な (けっこうな量), which is the rare adjectival use. Although technically classified as a な-adjective, it almost never appears with な — its natural role is adverbial.

けっこう often carries a nuance of mild surprise — that something turned out to be more than the speaker assumed. けっこう難しい implies it's harder than I expected. This sets it apart from neutral degree words and gives it a slightly evaluative feel.

けっこうです is a completely separate set expression used to politely decline an offer. When someone offers you something and you say けっこうです, it means No thank you or I'm fine, thanks. Context is everything — the same words either praise the degree of something or politely refuse it.

N5CH.4 · CR.4
AよりBのほうが〜
(A yori B no hou ga ~)
B is more ~ than A
Casual
い-adjective
B + のほうが + A + より +
い-adjplain form
な-adjective
B + のほうが + A + より + な-adj + だ
Question — which is more?
Noun A + と + Noun B + と　どっちのほうが + ？
Formal
い-adjective
B + のほうが + A + より +
い-adjplain form
+ です
な-adjective
B + のほうが + A + より + な-adj + です
Question — which is more?
Noun A + と + Noun B + と　どちらのほうが + ですか
About

This grammar structure is used to directly compare two things and state that one has more of a quality than the other. のほうが marks the winner — the side with more of the quality. より marks the baseline — the thing being compared against, roughly equivalent to than in English.

A key difference from English: adjectives do not change form. There is no Japanese equivalent of faster or cheaper. A い-adjective stays in its plain form; a な-adjective also stays in its plain stem form. Register and tense are expressed by what follows — だ vs です, or past でした — not by modifying the adjective itself.

The より clause can be dropped when the comparison baseline is obvious from context. この店のほうがいいです — this store is better — works without stating what it is better than.

For questions, どちら is the standard polite form meaning which of the two. どっち is its casual contraction. Both take the listing pattern A と B と — と here is not a case particle but a conjunction linking the two options being compared.

Tense and polarity: the predicate conjugates like any normal い-adjective or な-adjective — four forms for each.

い-adjective: 安い → 安くない → 安かった → 安くなかった,
な-adjective: 便利 → 便利じゃない → 便利だった → 便利じゃなかった.

Adding です to any form makes it polite.

About より — standaloneN4

より also works without のほうが: 今年は去年より寒い — this year is colder than last year. The word より attaches to is always the lesser side of the comparison — a common trap, since English "more than" points the other way. Verbs work too: 歩くより — than walking.

思ったより — than I expected is worth memorising as a set pattern, as is bare より + adjective with no comparison target at all — より良い方法 — a better method, a formal, written flavour meaning simply more.

(~no naka de ~ga ichiban ~)

い-adjective
Group + の中で + Winner + が　いちばん +
い-adjplain form

Question — which is the most?

い-adjplain form
/ な-adj + ？
Formal
い-adjective
Group + の中で + Winner + が　いちばん +
い-adjplain form
+ です
な-adjective
Group + の中で + Winner + が　いちばん + な-adj + です
Question — which is the most?
Group + の中で + Q-word + が　いちばん +
い-adjplain form
/ な-adj + ですか
About

This grammar structure is used to express a superlative — picking the one thing out of a group that has the highest degree of a quality. の中で sets the group being compared (among ~), が marks the winner as the subject, and いちばん (literally number one) works as a degree word meaning most. Like with より comparisons, the adjective stays in its plain form unchanged.

The group can be a single noun (食べ物の中で), a demonstrative (この中で、その中で), or a list of items joined with と (ロシアとフランスと日本の中で). When context is clear, の中で can also be dropped entirely — 秋がいちばん好きです works without stating the group.

For questions, the subject slot is replaced with a question word. Which word to use depends on what you are asking about:

なに what — asking about a thing in general
どれ which one — selecting from a specific visible set
どこ which place — asking about location
だれ who — asking about a person
いつ when — asking about a time or period

Tense and polarity: the predicate conjugates like any normal い-adjective or な-adjective — four forms for each.

い-adjective: いちばん高い → 高くない → 高かった → 高くなかった,
な-adjective: いちばん有名 → 有名じゃない → 有名だった → 有名じゃなかった.

Adding です to any form makes it polite.

About の中で — "among" without いちばんN4

の中で was introduced bound to いちばん, but it is also used on its own. Noun + の中で marks off a group and locates something among it, with no superlative required: ラーメンの中では味噌が好き — among ramen, miso is the one I like. それ・これ take it directly: その中で.

Since 中 is literally inside, the same structure also covers plain location: 車の中で夕食を食べた — ate dinner in the car — the で here is the ordinary place-of-action で from card CH.1 · CR.5.

N4CH.4 · CR.6
と〜と、どちらが
(~to ~to, dochira ga)
Between A and B, which one?
Noun
Noun A + と + Noun B + と、どちらが
Casual
Verb
Verb Aplain form
+ の + と +
Verb Bplain form
+ の + と、どちらが
Formal
Verb
Verb Aplain form
+ こと + と +
Verb Bplain form
+ こと + と、どちらが
About

This grammar structure is used to ask which of exactly two options is preferred, better, or more so — between A and B, which one? The two choices are joined by the particle と in its listing sense, and the question word どちら — which of the two — follows with が: 紅茶とコーヒーと、どちらが好きですか — between tea and coffee, which do you like? The second と is frequently omitted, since どちら already implies that both items belong to the same comparison. どちら is the polite member of its pair — casual speech uses どっち — and both can take のほう (どちらのほう, どっちのほう) to spell out the side being chosen.

To compare two actions rather than two things, the verbs are turned into noun phrases first, using こと or the lighter の on the plain form: 走ることと泳ぐことと、どちらが好きですか — running or swimming, which do you like? In casual speech の is the usual choice and the second と drops away.

This pattern is restricted to exactly two choices. For three or more options, Japanese switches to the superlative frame のなかで〜がいちばん covered in card CH.4 · CR.5. The natural answer to a どちらが question uses のほうが from card CH.4 · CR.4: コーヒーのほうが好きです — I like coffee more.

N4CH.4 · CR.7
すぎる
(~sugiru)
Too much · excessively
Verb
Verb stem + すぎる
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + すぎる
な-adjective
な-adj + すぎる
About

This grammar structure is used to say that something is too much or goes beyond normal limits — too ~, excessively. It does not mean very: 高すぎる is not emphatic praise of a price but a complaint that it exceeds what is acceptable, and the tone is negative or unwelcome by default. The suffix comes from the verb 過ぎる — to exceed, to pass — and is usually written in kana when attached to other words.

Verbs take it on the stem: 食べすぎる — to eat too much,
い-adjectives drop the final い: 難しすぎる — too difficult,
な-adjectives attach the bare stem: 静かすぎる — too quiet.

The irregular いい uses its stem よ: よすぎる, never いすぎる.

Because すぎる is itself a regular る-verb, the whole expression conjugates normally:

すぎます,
すぎました,
すぎない,
すぎなかった.

Its て-form すぎて very often links the excess to its consequence: 食べすぎて、おなかが痛い — I ate too much, so my stomach hurts. In casual speech the final る is regularly clipped off, leaving bare すぎ as an exclamation: 可愛すぎ！ — way too cute! — and in this use the excess can flip into praise.

すぎる and ない

Attached to a negative, すぎる means too much not — that is, not enough. When ない behaves as an い-adjective — the independent ない of お金がない — the connector さ is required: お金がなさすぎる — to have far too little money. After a verb's negative ない, the さ is standardly omitted — 食べなすぎる — although なさすぎる is often heard there in casual speech. This is the same さ split that governs the appearance form そう (なさそう with さ for adjectives, なそう without it for verbs). Negative な-adjectives keep their では/じゃ: 元気じゃなさすぎる.

Keep the position of ない straight, because it decides the meaning: ない before すぎる states an excessive shortage (野菜を食べなすぎる — eats far too few vegetables), while ない after すぎる negates the excess itself (食べすぎない — not overeat, as in 食べすぎないでください — please don't overeat).

5 Counting, Quantity & Limits
  1. だけOnly, Just
  2. しか〜ないOnly · Nothing but — exclusive negative
  3. ほかに・ほかにはBesides · Other than — another thing
  4. 以上・以下・以外At least · At most · Except — the 以 family
  5. Amount + はAt least · Or so — the contrastive floor
  6. 何 + Counter + かSome · Several — uncertain amounts
  7. ごとに・各Each · Every — intervals and members
  8. の次にNext after · Second to — relative order
  9. は〜の一つだOne of many — membership in a category
  10. 〜代Decades — of age and of history
  11. かかる・するTakes time · Costs money
  12. 〜らPluralizing suffix — we · they · these
  13. ない〜はない・少なくないDouble negatives — emphatic affirmatives
N5CH.5 · CR.1
だけ
(dake)
Only, Just
Verb
Verb plain form
+ だけ
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ だけ
な-adjective
な-adj + な + だけ
Noun
Noun + だけ
About

This grammar structure is used to limit or restrict scope to only one thing, person, or action — equivalent to only or just in English. The implication is that other possibilities exist but are excluded.

Attachment is straightforward for verbs (plain form), い-adjectives, and nouns — だけ attaches directly. For な-adjectives, な is required before だけ when the adjective is used as a quality. If the な is dropped, the な-adjective is treated as a noun instead, which slightly shifts the nuance: 綺麗なだけ = just beautiful (as a quality); 綺麗だけ = just beauty (as a concept/thing).

About だけで — just byN4

だけ + the means-particle で gives with only (A) → just by A: (B) is achieved and nothing beyond A was needed. It follows a plain-form verb or a noun: 話すだけで楽しい — just talking is fun, 野菜だけで作った — made with only vegetables.

The negative counterpart is だけでは〜ない: A alone is not enough — 練習だけでは上手になりません.

About だけでなく — not onlyN4

だけでなく — だけ plus the abbreviated negative ではなく — builds not only (A), but also (B): 安いだけでなく、おいしい. It attaches wherever だけ attaches: nouns, plain-form verbs and adjectives.

The (B) clause usually carries も — B too: 英語だけでなく、中国語も話す. The fuller variants ではなく(て) and じゃなく(て) express the same meaning at higher and lower formality respectively.

N4CH.5 · CR.2
しか〜ない
(shika ~ nai)
Only · Nothing but — exclusive negative
Number
Amount + しか +
Verb [ない]negative form
Noun
Noun + しか +
Verb [ない]negative form
About

しか is an adverbial particle meaning only. Unlike だけ, it requires a negative predicate: 千円しか持っていない is literally apart from 1,000 yen, I hold nothing. The negation does not negate the sentence as a whole — it expresses that nothing exists apart from (A).

This structure is also what gives しか its nuance. だけ states a quantity neutrally (just this); しか〜ない presents it as insufficient — no more than this. The same fact carries opposite attitudes: 千円だけある is neutral, 千円しかない emphasizes the shortfall.

It works identically on amounts and on nouns (コーヒーしか飲まない — drinks nothing but coffee), and like でも, it replaces を and が — never をしか or がしか.

N4CH.5 · CR.3
ほかに・ほかには
(hoka ni · hoka ni wa)
Besides · Other than — another thing
Another one
他の + Noun
Besides
Noun + の +
他に(も)(も) optional
Other than
他には +
Phrase [ない]usually negative
About

他 (ほか, sometimes written 外, usually kana) is a noun meaning another thing, other. Its most basic use is 他の + noun: 他の店 — a different shop. The attached particles adjust the meaning from there.

他に asks or adds anything else, in addition: 他に質問はありますか. 他にも emphasizes the addition — even more besides, implying confidence that more exists. 他には is contrastive and typically pairs with negatives: 彼の他にはいない — other than him, there is no one.

One restriction: because 他にも asserts addition, it cannot appear in a plain negative statement — その他にもない is ungrammatical (in addition there is also nothing). Questions are the exception, as in English: その他にも何かありませんか — is there nothing else besides? is natural.

他の + noun — another specific thing
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

には + negative — the set outside him is empty

N4CH.5 · CR.4
以上・以下・以外
(ijou · ika · igai)
At least · At most · Except — the 以 family
≥ at least
Amount + 以上
≤ at most
Amount + 以下
Except
Noun/
Verbplain present
+ 以外
About

以上, 以下 and 以外 share one mechanism: 以 means taking (A) as the reference point, and the second kanji states the position relative to it — 上 above, 下 below, 外 outside. With numbers, the reference point is included: 20歳以上 is 20 and up (≥), 17歳以下 is 17 and under (≤) — unlike English "more/less than", which excludes the number named.

以上 after an amount sets it as the minimum: 百人以上 — a hundred people or more; それ以上 — any more than that. It is also used as a closing formula — 以上です — that is all — literally the above (list) is everything, standard when finishing an order or a report.

以下 is the mirror image: the amount becomes the maximum — 五万円以下 — 50,000 yen or less. It also refers forward to what follows: 以下のページ — the following pages, the standard way documents reference upcoming content.

以外 — outside the reference point — means except (A), other than (A): 和食以外 — anything but Japanese food. It follows nouns or plain-form verbs, and names the set everything else stands outside of.

以上 — at least
説明会に百人以上の学生が来ました。
A hundred or more students came to the information session.
the named amount is the floor — and it counts
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
私からの報告は以上です。
That's all from me.
以上です — "the above is everything"; standard closer
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
以下 — at most
詳しいスケジュールは以下のページを見てください。
For the detailed schedule, see the following pages.
以下 pointing forward — "the following"
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
この店の服は五万円以下だった。
The clothes at this shop were under fifty thousand yen.
ceiling set at the amount — the amount itself qualifies
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
以外 — except
私は魚以外は何でも食べる。

以外 + 何でも — the exception carved out of "anything"
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
たまには仕事以外の話もしない？

NOUN PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.5 · CR.5
Amount + は
(~wa)
At least · Or so — the contrastive floor
Amount + Counter +
はoptional くらい before
About

This grammar structure uses the contrastive function of は. Besides marking the topic, は marks contrast; placed after an amount, the contrastive reading applies: 年に五回は行く means I go five times a year — as opposed to fewer. English renders this as at least or or so. The reading is わ, as always.

The contrast implies an unstated alternative: (A), as opposed to (B), where (B) — some lesser amount — is left unsaid. The named amount is therefore a subjective minimum rather than a precise bound. This is the difference from 以上: 以上 sets an exact mathematical boundary (≥), while は expresses the speaker's sense of no less than this.

Adding くらい before it — 二キロくらいは — softens the statement further, toward or so, at least roughly.

Examplesshow ▶
一日に水を二リットルは飲んでください。
Please drink at least two liters of water a day.
the floor — two liters, as opposed to anything less

京都には年に三回は行っている。
I go to Kyoto at least three times a year.
felt minimum — the real count may be higher
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.5 · CR.6
何 + Counter + か
(nan + counter + ka)
Some · Several — uncertain amounts
Counting
何 + Counter + か
Set word
いくつか
About

This grammar structure applies the question word + か pattern (だれか — someone) to numbers. 何回か is literally how many times, I wonder → several times, some number of times. Any counter fits: 何人か — a few people, 何枚か — some sheets.

The stem いく (from 幾) forms the set words: いくつか — several, a few (things), alongside the already familiar いくら — how much and いくつ — how many / how old. なん is the standard choice for counting concrete things; いく〜 appears mostly in those fixed forms.

One reading caution applies, carried over from card CH.3 · CR.3: the kanji is the same 何, but なん counts, なに identifies — 何冊か is なんさつか.

Examplesshow ▶
いくつか質問があります。
I have a few questions.
いくつか — the all-purpose "several"
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

counter 人 — some uncertain number of them
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

the speaker hasn't counted — that's the whole point of か

vague request — any small number will do
NOUN PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.5 · CR.7
ごとに・各
(~goto ni · kaku~)
Each · Every — intervals and members
Intervals
Noun/
Verbplain present
+ ごとに
Each member
各 +
Nounkanji / katakana word
About ごとに

ごとに is the noun ごと plus the particle に, used adverbially for every (A) or at intervals of (A): 三時間ごとに — every three hours. Its kanji is 毎 — the same one as 毎日 — though it is usually written in kana.

It follows nouns (most commonly amounts of time or distance) or non-past verbs: 会うごとに — each time we meet. With a verb, the interval is not on the clock but between repetitions of the event.

About 各

各 (かく) is a prefix — a slightly formal each · every · respective that attaches almost exclusively to kanji compounds and katakana words: 各階 — each floor, 各地 — every region. It is used mainly for the members of a sequence — floors, pages, rooms, stations — and rarely for units of time.

The distinction from ごとに: ごとに expresses the pace of recurring events (every three hours, every time A happens); 各 refers to the members of a set one by one (each floor, each branch office).

Examplesshow ▶
ごとに — intervals
この薬は六時間ごとに飲んでください。
Please take this medicine every six hours.
interval on the clock — the most common ごとに
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
このバスは十分ごとに来る。
This bus comes every ten minutes.
regular beat — at ten-minute intervals
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

Every time we meet, her Japanese has gotten better.
verb + ごとに — the interval is between repetitions of the event
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.5 · CR.8
の次に
(~no tsugi ni)
Next after · Second to — relative order
Noun + の次に
About

This grammar structure is used to place something immediately after another in an order. It is composed of の + the noun 次 — next + に: テストの次に面接があります — after the test comes the interview. A noun must stand before の. The most basic use is literal sequence — what comes next in time.

The same structure also expresses relative ranking: second (only) to (A). The scale can be numerical — 東京の次に人口が多い — the largest population after Tokyo — or based on preference and importance: 健康の次に大切なのは… — after health, what matters most is.... Whatever the scale, (A) holds first place and the subject of the sentence stands directly behind it.

Examplesshow ▶
会議の次に昼休みがあります。
After the meeting comes the lunch break.
literal sequence — the next slot in the schedule
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
日本で東京の次に有名な町は京都です。
After Tokyo, the most famous town in Japan is Kyoto.
ranking — second place, measured in numbers
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
私にとって、家族の次に友達が大切だ。
For me, friends matter most after family.
ranking by importance — preference, not figures
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

asking for second place on someone's list
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.5 · CR.9
は〜の一つだ
(~wa ~ no hitotsu da)
One of many — membership in a category
Noun (A) + は + Category (B) + の一つだ
About

This grammar structure presents something as one member of a larger category — (A) is one of the (B)s: AはBの一つだ. For example, 柔道は日本のスポーツの一つです — judo is one of Japan's sports. (A) takes は; the category follows; の一つ states single membership without claiming uniqueness.

一つ is just the default counter — swap it to fit the noun: の一人 for people, の一種 for kinds and species, の一本 for long things. The frame stays the same; the counter agrees with what is being counted.

〜代
(~dai)

About

The suffix 代 marks a decade of someone's age — exactly what English does with "teens, twenties, thirties". Attach it to the age in tens:

10代 — teens,
20代 — twenties,
60代 — sixties.

Historical decades take 年代 instead: 70年代 — the seventies, 90年代の音楽 — nineties music.

The same kanji appears throughout the wider era vocabulary — 時代 — era, period, or ordinal generations like 第5代将軍 — the fifth shogun. Wherever 代 appears in time-related vocabulary, it marks a span of years or a position in a succession.

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
