N4CH.5 · CR.11
かかる・する
(kakaru · suru)
Takes time · Costs money
Takes / costs
Noun + がかかる
Amount
Amountno particle
+ かかる
Costs — する
Priceno particle
+ する
About かかる

かかる is a verb whose core meaning is to hang, to weigh upon. Applied to time or money, it means takes or costs: 時間がかかる — it takes time, お金がかかる — it costs money — the expense weighs on the task as a burden or requirement. It is intransitive, so a general noun for time or money is marked with が.

With a specific counted amount, the が is dropped entirely and the amount functions adverbially, describing the verb directly: 駅まで三十分かかる — it takes thirty minutes to the station, 手続きに二週間かかった. Counted amounts standing directly before verbs without a particle is the general pattern for counters.

About する

する, although most often translated as to do, is also used to state a price: このバッグは五万円する — this bag costs 50,000 yen. The item takes は or が; the price stands bare, functioning adverbially, with する directly after it.

The nuance comes from する being an active verb: the item actively holds its price, comparable to English "it will run you...". A neutral statement of fact uses です — この時計は十万円です; using 十万円する instead marks the amount itself as noteworthy, usually because it is high.

It takes an hour to the airport by taxi.
counted amount, bare — no が before かかる

N4CH.5 · CR.12
〜ら
(~ra)
Pluralizing suffix — we · they · these
Pronoun + ら
About

ら is a suffix that adds more than one to pronouns:

彼ら — they,
私ら — we,
これら — these.

It is written with the same kanji as 等, and its literal sense is closer to (A) and the rest, (A) etc. — that "and the rest" is exactly where the plurality comes from.

The こそあど series takes it as well: これら・それら — these · those carry a written, somewhat formal flavour and are the natural use for things. 彼ら・彼女ら are the standard they for people.

The same "etc." origin has a side effect with people: including someone in "and the rest" can sound dismissive, so ら on person words (お前ら, あいつら) ranges from rough-casual to rude. When a polite plural for people is needed, 達 (たち) — the suffix in 友達 — is almost always the better choice.

Examplesshow ▶
彼らは同じ大学の学生です。
They are students at the same university.
彼ら — the standard neutral "they"
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
これらの本は図書館のものです。
These books belong to the library.
これら — written, formal flavour; safest on things
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
私らは先に帰るよ。
We're heading home first.
私ら — rough casual "we"; 私たち is the safe default
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.5 · CR.13
ない〜はない・少なくない
(nai ~ wa nai · sukunakunai)
Double negatives — emphatic affirmatives
No ~ that isn't
Clause [ない]negative modifier
+ Noun + はない
Not a few
Noun + は / が / も + 少なくない
About ない〜はない

Japanese uses double negation for emphatic affirmation, and this is the standard pattern: a negative modifier on a noun, followed by はない negating the whole. この歌を知らない人はいない — there is no one who doesn't know this song — an emphatic way of saying that everyone knows it. The two negations cancel, and the cancellation carries the emphasis.

The modifier can be a verb in ない-form, an い-adjective in くない-form, or a な-adjective with じゃない. These sentences require careful reading — the surface is negative, the meaning is universal.

About 少なくない

少なくない is the same principle in a single word: 少ない — few negated — not a few, yielding an understated quite a lot. It follows a noun with は, が or も; the polite form is 少なくありません.

The understatement defines its register: where 多い states many directly, 少なくない is more measured and slightly formal in flavour, and is very common in observations about society and habits.

ない〜はない

N5CH.6 · CR.1
もう
(mou)
Already · Anymore · One more
already
もう +
Phrase past tense
anymore
もう +
Phrase negative
one more
もう + Number / Counter
About

This grammar structure is used to express that something has already happened or is no longer the case. The literal meaning is something has unexpectedly ended — which is why it maps to already in past sentences and anymore in negative ones.

In positive-past sentences, もう indicates the action was completed sooner than expected. In negative sentences, it indicates a state that was ongoing has now ended. In questions, the speaker suspects something may have ended and wants to confirm.

もう also has a completely separate usage with numbers and counters, meaning one more or a little more — もう一度 — one more time, もう少し — a little more, もう一枚 — one more sheet. Context always makes clear which meaning is intended.

もう is the opposite of まだ. もう signals something has ended; まだ signals it is still ongoing.

Already
もう宿題をしました。

もう + past = 'already done'; often said to reassure or preempt the question

N5CH.6 · CR.2
まだ
(mada)
Still · Not yet
ている
まだ +
Verb [て] て-form
+ いる
いる
まだ + Noun + が + いる
ある
まだ + Noun + が + ある
About

This grammar structure is used to describe a state that is still ongoing — equivalent to still in English. まだ itself simply flags that the state is continuing; the verb tense controls whether it reads as still (positive) or not yet (negative).

With ている it describes an action or condition that is actively continuing. With が + いる or が + ある it describes a person, animal, or thing that is still present or still exists. まだ with a negative verb (not yet) is covered in card CH.6 · CR.3.

まだ can also be used in questions when the speaker thinks something might still be ongoing and wants to confirm — まだ日本語の勉強しているの？ — Are you still studying Japanese?

まだ is the opposite of もう. When emphasising that something is nowhere near finished or ready, まだ is often doubled — まだまだ — meaning still a long way to go or not nearly there yet.

Rare kanji form: 未だ.

I'm still working.
ongoing activity that hasn't ended; implies the expected end hasn't come yet

まだまだ is a fixed expression; used as honest or playful feedback on progress
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N5CH.6 · CR.3
まだ〜ていません
(mada ~te imasen)
Still haven't done ~
Casual
まだ +
Verb [て] て-form
+ いない
Formal
まだ +
Verb [て] て-form
+ いません
About

This grammar structure is used to say something is still not done — the action has not occurred yet as of now, but may still happen. It focuses on the current state of incompletion rather than the past. This is close to the English present perfect negative (haven't done X yet).

It combines まだ — not yet with the ている construction in its negative form. まだ sets the expectation that the action is pending; ていない · ていません describes the state of it not having happened.

Critical distinction — まだ〜ていません vs 〜ませんでした: まだ〜ていません is strictly for things that are still incomplete at the present moment. It cannot be used for completed past events. If something did not happen at a specific point in the past and that moment is now over, use the simple past negative 〜ませんでした instead.

私はまだ宿題をしていません。 I haven't done my homework yet. Present incomplete — may still do it
私はきのう宿題をしませんでした。 I didn't do my homework yesterday. Past negative — event is finished

VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
Quick RecapCH.6 · CR.4
もう vs まだ
もう · まだ · まだ〜ていません
Comparison
Form With affirmative With negative Feels like
もう Already — the change has happened (もう食べた) Anymore — the state has ended (もう食べない) "Already" / "Not anymore"
まだ Still — the situation continues (まだ食べている) Not yet — it hasn't happened (まだ食べていない) "Still" / "Not yet"
まだ〜ていません — The standard polite way to say an action hasn't happened yet "Still haven't ~"
When to use what
It has happened or the change is complete → もう + affirmative
It used to be the case but no longer is → もう + negative
The situation is still going on → まだ + affirmative
It hasn't happened yet, but is expected to → まだ〜ていません
Mirror logic: もう marks a change, まだ marks no change — polarity decides the English: already / not anymore / still / not yet
N4CH.6 · CR.5
だんだん・どんどん
(~dandan · ~dondon)
Gradually · Rapidly — pace of change
Gradual
だんだん(と)(と) optional
+ Phrase
Rapid
どんどん(と)(と) optional
+ Phrase
About

だんだん is an adverb expressing slow but constant progression — gradually, little by little. It comes from 段々 — step by step and modifies a whole phrase, most often one describing change: だんだん寒くなる — it gradually gets colder.

どんどん is onomatopoeia — the pounding of a drum or feet — and expresses the opposite pace: rapid, vigorous progression, more and more. In requests it adds a don't hold back nuance: どんどん食べてください.

Both may take the particle と, but it is very often omitted, as with most sound-symbolic adverbs. The contrast between the two is the essential point: in the same sentence, だんだん減る describes a slow, year-by-year decrease, while どんどん減る describes a rapid, visible one.

春になって、だんだん明るくなってきましたね。
Spring has come and it's gradually getting brighter, isn't it?
seasonal change — the most typical context for だんだん
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
日本語の勉強がだんだん楽しくなりました。
Studying Japanese has gradually become fun.
slow, steady shift over months
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

My mother's illness is gradually getting better.

N4CH.6 · CR.6
ずっと
(zutto)
Continuously · Ever since — unbroken span
The whole time
ずっと + Phrase

About

ずっと is an adverb expressing that an action or state continues over an unbroken span: the whole time, all along, continuously. It stands before the phrase it prolongs, and because the state persists, it frequently appears with ている: ずっと待っている — I've been waiting this whole time.

Anchored to a starting point — point in time + から + ずっと — it reads ever since: 昨日からずっと — ever since yesterday. It also conveys the emotional weight of long duration: ずっと会いたかった is I wanted to see you for so long, not merely continuously.

I was in the meeting room all afternoon.

ずっと + ている — the natural pair for ongoing states

VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.6 · CR.7
とうとう
(toutou)
Finally · At last — after long effort
とうとう + Phrase
About

とうとう is an adverb used to express that something finally happened after a long period of time or effort. The kanji form 到頭 — 到 — arrive at plus 頭 — head, crux — reflects this meaning: reaching the point everything was heading toward. In practice it is almost always written in kana, and like many adverbs it usually opens the phrase or sentence.

The outcome itself can be positive or negative — とうとう concerns the time and effort invested, not the quality of the result. It is equally natural for a dream finally realized and for a shop finally closing down. With a negative predicate it means in the end, never did: とうとう謝らなかった — the awaited action never happened.

It is not used for events that arrive on their own, with no waiting or effort involved. For the change of seasons or a scheduled event drawing near, いよいよ (finally, at last in the sense of natural arrival) is used instead: いよいよ夏が来た, not とうとう.

五年かかりましたが、とうとう自分の店を開きました。
It took five years, but I finally opened my own shop.
long effort reaching its arrival point — the classic とうとう

とうとう新しい家が決まったんですか？
So the new house is finally settled?
asking about a long-awaited outcome; んです adds the "so it's true?" flavour

三年かかったが、とうとう論文が完成した。
It took three years, but the thesis is finally done.
time invested is the point — とうとう measures the wait

(daitai)
Mostly · Roughly · In the first place
Mostly
だいたい + Phrase
Roughly

Rough ~
だいたいの + Noun
About

だいたい (大体, literally the general body) is an adverb meaning mostly, generally, for the most part: the statement holds for the main part of the matter, details aside. Kanji and kana are both common.

Before a number it approximates: だいたい十五分 — roughly fifteen minutes. With の it modifies a noun directly: だいたいの内容 — the rough content, the gist.

It has a second use: opening an exasperated question, it means in the first place — だいたい、なんで… — and anyway, why.... Both uses share the same core: pointing at the essential part of the matter.

The distinction from ほとんど: ほとんど expresses the near-totality of a group (nearly all of them), while だいたい expresses generality (broadly speaking).

The report is mostly written.
the main body is done — polish remains

N4CH.6 · CR.9
ほとんど
(hotondo)
Almost all · Hardly any — near-totality
Most
ほとんど + Phrase
Most of
ほとんどの + Noun
Hardly any
ほとんど +
Negative phraseない / ません
About

ほとんど (kanji 殆ど, though it is almost always written in kana) is an adverbial noun whose core is almost the whole of it. With an affirmative predicate it reads most or almost all: 宿題はほとんど終わった — the finished part is nearly the full set.

Before a noun it connects with の — ほとんどの学生 — most students — and being a noun itself, it can also carry particles directly: クラスのほとんどが同じ答えを書いた.

With a negative predicate the same near-totality flips to near-zero: hardly any, hardly ever. ほとんど降らなかった means the rain barely existed — the group that should have been almost complete is almost absent instead. One word covers both ends of the scale; the polarity of the sentence determines which reading applies.

The travel preparations are almost finished.
nearly the full set — a few boxes left at most

Most of the class wrote the same answer.
ほとんど as a noun — carrying が directly
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

I've hardly talked with my father lately.
negative flips it — the talking barely exists

N4CH.6 · CR.10
ぜんぜん・あまり・少しも
(zenzen · amari · sukoshi mo)
Not at all · Not very · Not even a little
Not at all
ぜんぜん +
Negative phraseない / ません
Not very
あまり +
Negative phraseない / ません
Not even a little
少しも +
Negative phraseない / ません
About

This card covers the three adverbs that traditionally appear only in negative sentences. Each precedes a predicate ending in ない or ません and specifies how completely it negates; the adverb itself signals that a negative is coming.

全然 makes the negation total — not (A) at all. Kanji and kana are equally common in writing. Its formal counterpart is 全く, which expresses the same total negation with a stiffer, more formal tone; ぜんぜん is the standard conversational choice.

あまり limits the negation to not very or not much — a partial denial where ぜんぜん is absolute. In casual speech it becomes あんまり. With nouns and な-adjectives the negative is ではない, contracted to じゃない in conversation.

少しも — 少し — a little plus も — is the emphatic extreme: not even a little, not in the least. Where ぜんぜん states total absence, 少しも emphasizes that not even a trace exists. It stands at the head of the sentence or directly before the word it negates. Attachment follows the same rules: verbs and い-adjectives take plain ない, な-adjectives take ではない.

None of these adverbs marks a grammatical role, so no particle is attached to them. Their position is flexible; the most natural placement is directly after the topic, before the element being negated.

ぜんぜん with positives

In traditional grammar, ぜんぜん in an affirmative sentence is ungrammatical, and this remains the textbook rule. Modern casual speech, however, increasingly uses it as an intensifier meaning totally: 全然大丈夫 — totally fine. This use should be understood when heard, but produced only in casual settings — it is not accepted in polite or written Japanese.

ぜんぜん — not at all

I've been busy this week and haven't watched TV at all.

"not much" — some exercise happened, just not enough

あんまり + じゃない — the fully casual kit

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.6 · CR.11
なるべく
(narubeku)
As much as possible · Whenever possible
なるべく + Phrase
About

なるべく is an adverb meaning as ~ as possible or whenever possible. It combines the verb 成る — to become with the classical auxiliary 可く — ought to · can — literally as far as circumstances allow. It is written in kana in all but the most formal texts, and stands before the whole phrase it modifies.

It is used most often in requests and descriptions of habits: なるべく早く — as soon as possible, なるべく毎日 — every day if possible. Because it concedes from the start that circumstances might not allow it, it sounds considerate rather than demanding.

The related expression できるだけ — to the full extent possible is stronger: it asks for the limit of someone's ability, while なるべく states a preference. なるべく早く来てください is a polite wish; できるだけ早く来てください demands maximum effort.

なるべく早く返事をください。
Please reply as soon as you can.
the standard soft deadline — firm request, considerate framing
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
体のために、なるべく自転車を使っています。
For my health, I use my bicycle whenever I can.

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
夜はなるべく食べない。
I avoid eating at night as much as I can.
なるべく + negative — minimizing rather than maximizing
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN

softened casual request — なるべく leaves room for real life

casual favour-asking; the wish is stated, the limit is theirs

N4CH.6 · CR.12
まず
(~mazu)
First of all · To start with
まず + Phrase
About

まず is a sentence adverb meaning first, to start with — it marks the first thing to do, and usually opens the statement. It is associated with the kanji 先 (as 先ず), ahead / first. It is used mainly in procedures, instructions and plans, often paired with それから — and then.

Note that まず orders actions, not rank — for finished first or came first use 一番 or 最初 instead. And since it often frames advice (the first thing you should do...), it can come across as pushy; polite forms or a softening と思う are used to moderate the tone.

N4CH.6 · CR.13
また
(~mata)

About

また is an adverb whose core meaning is repetition of an action or pattern. When the same action repeats, it reads again: また会いましょう — let's meet again. The parting phrase じゃあ、また/またね — see you is this use with the verb dropped.

As a conjunction — typically sentence-initial, with a comma — また adds a further point of the same kind: also, moreover. This use has a written, slightly formal flavour: この店は安いです。また、駅から近いです。 The kanji form 又 exists, but また is almost always written in kana.

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.6 · CR.14
あとで
(~ta ato de · ato de)
After · Later — following in time
After doing
Verb [た]plain past
+ あとで
After a thing
Noun + のあとで
Later
あとで + Phrase
About

あとで is the noun 後 — after · behind plus the particle で, forming an adverbial phrase: after (A), (B). A verb before it always stands in the た-form, whatever the tense of the sentence — the mirror image of 前に, which locks the dictionary form. 食べたあとで is after eating even when the eating is tomorrow's.

A noun connects with の: 仕事のあとで — after work. Standing alone at the head of a sentence, あとで simply means later: あとで電話する.

The difference from てから (card CH.15 · CR.2) is the strength of the connection. てから ties (B) directly to the completion of (A), with the sequence itself as the point; あとで simply places (B) somewhere after (A), making no claim about what happens in between.

Examplesshow ▶
映画を見たあとで、レストランで食事をしました。
After watching the movie, we had dinner at a restaurant.

I go to the gym after work.
noun + のあとで — a standing routine
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
会議のあとで、少し話しませんか？
Shall we talk for a bit after the meeting?
softened invitation anchored to "after" — no exact time promised
NOUN PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.6 · CR.15
ごろ
(~goro · koro)
Around · About — approximate points in time
Clock time / date
Time + ごろ
Life period
Noun + のころ
About

ころ (kanji 頃) is a noun meaning an approximate point in time. Suffixed directly to a clock time or date it voices to ごろ: 11時ごろ — around 11. The result behaves like the time word itself and takes the same particles: 6時ごろに起きる.

After a noun it connects with の and names a period of life or history: 子供のころ — when I was a child, 大学生のころ — in my university days. Plain-form clauses attach directly: 日本にいたころ — back when I was in Japan.

The distinction from くらい (card CH.4 · CR.2) lies in domain and precision. ころ is used only for broad points in time; くらい covers amounts and more specific timeframes. Distances and lengths never take ごろ: a mark two meters away is 二メートルぐらい, never ごろ. Conversely, a life period is 子供のころ — くらい cannot express it.

I get up around six every morning.

NOUN PAST NEGATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.6 · CR.16
毎〜のように
(mai ~ no you ni)

毎 + Time unit + のように
About

This grammar structure is used to express that something happens in the manner of every (day, week, year). 毎 supplies the every; よう (様) supplies manner, appearance — so the pattern claims not literal totality but the appearance of it: almost every day, on a near-daily basis.

It attaches to the usual time words:

毎日,
毎週,
毎年,
毎晩.

Exactly how close "almost every" runs to "every" is left to the listener's interpretation — that margin of imprecision is the reason the pattern exists.

In most contexts のように and みたいに are interchangeable, but not in this pattern — 毎日みたいに is unnatural. みたい derives from を見たよう (looking as if) and is used for things that can be observed directly, which a frequency cannot.

Examplesshow ▶
大学のころは毎週のように映画館へ行きました。
In my university days I went to the movies almost every week.
near-weekly habit — のころ setting the period
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
母は毎年のように海に行っています。
My mother goes to the sea almost every year.
most years, not provably all — のように holds the door open
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
兄は毎日のようにラーメンを食べている。
My brother eats ramen practically every day.
the look of "every day" — a rest day may exist, barely
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
最近、毎晩のように残業してるの？

worried casual check — near-nightly is the alarming part
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.6 · CR.17
真っ
(ma~ · man~)
Completely · Exactly — intensifying prefix
Default
真っ + Word
ま / な row
真ん + Word
は row
真っ +
Wordh → p sound
About

真っ is a prefix built on 真 — true, and it intensifies what follows to completely, exactly, right (at): 真っ白 — pure white, 真ん中 — dead center, 真っ直ぐ — straight ahead. It fuses onto colour words, position words and a handful of others — and the fusion itself changes shape depending on the first kana of the host word.

Default — small っ: 真っ白 (まっしろ), 真っ暗 (まっくら), 真っ先 (まっさき)
Before ま- and な-row sounds — 真ん: 真ん中 (まんなか), 真ん丸 (まんまる)
Before は-row sounds — the h hardens into p: 裸 → 真っ裸 (まっぱだか)

Two colour words are irregular: 青い → 真っ青 reads まっさお, and 赤い → 真っ赤 reads まっか — the host word itself changes sound. Each 真っ word is therefore best learned as a vocabulary item: the prefix is productive, but not freely so.

Examplesshow ▶
雪で山が真っ白になりました。
The mountains turned pure white with snow.
default fusion — 真っ + 白 (まっしろ)
な-ADJ PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
ケーキはテーブルの真ん中に置いてください。
Put the cake right in the middle of the table.
真ん before a ま/な-row sound — 真ん中 (まんなか)
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

真っ暗 — total darkness, no light survives the prefix
な-ADJ PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

な-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.6 · CR.18
たとえば
(tatoeba)
For example — presenting instances
たとえば + Phrase
About

たとえば (例えば) is an adverb used to introduce an example — a direct equivalent of for example. It is literally the ば-conditional of the verb 例える — to liken, to compare: if we were to liken it.... It opens the sentence or the individual statement whose example follows.

It combines naturally with the example-marking structures covered earlier: たとえば、寿司や天ぷらなど — たとえば announces the example, や・など・とか mark the items as a non-exhaustive sample. In conversation it also introduces tentative suggestions: たとえば、来月は？ — for example, how about next month?.

Examplesshow ▶
日本料理が好きです。たとえば、うどんや天ぷらをよく食べます。
I like Japanese food. For example, I often eat udon and tempura.
general claim first, たとえば opens the evidence

たとえば、来月の第一週はどうですか？
How about, say, the first week of next month?
floating a trial option — one example among possible dates
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
安い物、たとえばチョコレートとかをよく買う。

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.6 · CR.19
もし
(moshi)
If — flagging a conditional early
もし +
Phrase [たら]also ば / と / ても
About

もし is an adverb used to emphasize and announce a conditional before the conditional form itself appears. English "if" stands at the front of its clause; Japanese conditionals attach to the verb at the end — もし therefore signals the conditional in advance, and the ending (たら, ば, と or ても) completes it.

It also adds hypothetical distance — if by any chance, supposing — which makes conditions feel less presumptuous and softens requests and offers: もしよかったら — if you like is a standard politeness formula built on exactly this effect.

The conditional endings themselves are each covered in cards CH.15 · CR.8 to CH.15 · CR.11. もし only announces the condition — it cannot make a sentence conditional on its own.

Examplesshow ▶
もし時間があったら、電話してください。
If you happen to have time, please call me.
もし…たら — the announcement and the condition, working as a pair
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
もし雨が降っても、試合はあります。
Even if it rains, the match is on.
もし…ても — early warning for an "even if"
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
もし分からなければ、いつでも聞いてね。
If you don't understand, ask me anytime.
もし…ば — softened standing offer
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
もし宝くじが当たったら、何を買う？
If you won the lottery, what would you buy?
pure hypothetical — もし stretches the distance from reality
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.6 · CR.20
それに・それで・それでも
(sore ni · sore de · sore demo)
Moreover · Therefore · Even so — それ + particle
Adding
Phrase (A)。 + それに + Phrase (B)
Result
Phrase (A)。 + それで + Phrase (B)
Contrast
Phrase (A)。 + それでも + Phrase (B)
About

それに, それで and それでも are conjunctions built on the same mechanism: the pronoun それ refers to the whole preceding sentence, and the attached particle defines the relation of the new sentence to it — に adds information, で marks cause or means, でも concedes. Dictionaries treat all three as single words, which is accurate in practice, but recognizing the components supplies all three meanings at once.

それに — in addition to that — adds a further point of the same kind: moreover, besides. The added information must match the tone of what precedes it: merits are added to merits, complaints to complaints. 安い。それに、おいしい is natural; adding a complaint to a compliment with それに is not.

それで — because of that — makes (A) the reason for (B): so, therefore. It typically opens the second sentence: 熱があった。それで、休んだ. Used alone with rising intonation, それで？ prompts the speaker to continue — and then? so?.

それでも — literally even with that — acknowledges (A) and asserts (B) despite it: even so, nevertheless. (B) is usually unexpected given (A): 何度も失敗した。それでも、あきらめない.

Examplesshow ▶
それに — moreover
この部屋は広いです。それに、駅から近いです。
This room is spacious. Moreover, it's close to the station.
merit stacked on merit — same emotional sign, as それに requires
い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
今日は寒いし、それに風も強い。
It's cold today, and on top of that the wind is strong.
complaint on complaint — the negative pile-up version
い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
それで — therefore
昨日は熱がありました。それで、学校を休みました。
I had a fever yesterday. That's why I stayed home from school.
(A) is the cause, それで hands it to (B) as the reason
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
電車が止まった。それで会議に間に合わなかった。
The train stopped. That's why I didn't make the meeting.

VERB PAST NEGATIVE PLAIN
それでも — even so

The money is poor. Even so, I like this job.

な-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

the defiant それでも — (B) surprises given (A)
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN

7 て-form Constructions
  1. 〜て〜て〜And then, After that — actions in sequence
  2. てBecause ~ · By ~ing · While ~
  3. くて・でAnd ~ — linking adjectives and nouns
  4. なくてNot ~ and · Because not ~
  5. ないでWithout doing ~
  6. てみるTry doing ~ — and see
  7. ておくDo in advance · Leave it done
  8. ても・でもEven if · Even though
  9. ている間に・間にWhile ~ — event within a span
  10. てよかったI'm glad that · It was good that
  11. てすみませんSorry for ~ · Sorry for not ~
N5CH.7 · CR.1
〜て〜て〜
(~te · ~te · ~)
And then, After that — actions in sequence
Verb [て] て-form / repeatable
、
Verb [て] て-form / repeatable
、
Final Verb sets the tense
About

This grammar structure is used to list two or more actions happening in a fixed sequence — equivalent to did X, then Y, then Z in English. Each action in the chain is connected by the て-form (or で for verbs whose て-form ends in で), with a reading pause marked by 、between each.

Only the final verb carries the tense. All preceding て-forms are tense-neutral — they simply chain actions together. If the final verb is past (ました), the entire sequence is interpreted as past. If it is present or future (ます, dictionary form), the whole sequence refers to present or future.

This structure implies strict order — the actions happened one after another. It is not used for listing things that occurred in no particular order; for that, たり〜たりする is used instead.

Examplesshow ▶
毎朝、起きて、顔を洗って、朝ごはんを食べます。
Every morning I get up, wash my face, and eat breakfast.
sequential morning routine; て-form chains without changing the final tense
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
シャワーを浴びて、本を読んで、まだ寝ません。
I'll take a shower and read, but I won't sleep yet.

VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE
電車に乗って、音楽を聞いて、駅に着きました。
I got on the train, listened to music, and arrived at the station.
past sequential transit routine; events described in order
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
ご飯を作って、弟に電話して、食べませんでした。
I made food, called my younger brother, and didn't eat.
ironic chain; cooked and called but then didn't eat
VERB PAST NEGATIVE POLITE
家に帰って、シャワーを浴びて、寝る。
I'll come home, take a shower, and sleep.
end-of-day plain sequence; habitual routine
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
公園に行って、木の下で本を読んで、犬と走った。
I went to the park, read a book under a tree, and ran around with the dog.
casual pleasant outing described step by step in past
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
財布を忘れて、何も買わなかった。
I forgot my wallet and didn't buy anything.
causal chain; forgetting the wallet meant no purchases
VERB PAST NEGATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.7 · CR.2
て
(~te)
Because ~ · By ~ing · While ~
Cause
Verb [て]て-form
+
Result (B)beyond control
Means / Manner
Verb [て]て-form
+
Action (B)how it's done
Contrast
Verb [て]て-form
+
Clause (B)equal weight
About

This grammar structure covers two further readings of the bare て-form link between clauses, beyond the sequence use in card CH.7 · CR.1.

Usage 1 — cause: when clause (B) expresses an emotion, a potential verb, or something otherwise outside the speaker's control, the て-clause reads as its cause — since (A), (B): ニュースを聞いて、安心しました. Because (B) must be uncontrollable, cause-て cannot attach a reason to a command or request — for those, ので or から is used instead. The negative counterpart is なくて, adjectives and nouns get the same causal shade through くて・で (card CH.7 · CR.3), and the apology pattern てすみません (card CH.7 · CR.11) is this usage fossilised into a set phrase.

Usage 2 — means: the て-form can state how an action is carried out — by doing (A): 歩いて駅まで行きます, where walking is the means of getting there. With nouns this job belongs to the instrumental particle で (card CH.1 · CR.5), so the means reading is a verb pattern. It differs from sequence て in that (A) and (B) are not two events in a row — (A) merely describes the manner of (B).

Usage 3 — contrast: with a different subject in each clause, て can simply set two situations side by side — (A), and/while (B): 父は新聞を読んで、母はラジオを聞いています. Both halves carry equal weight; this is what separates て from けど or のに, which single one side out as the important one. The reading often matches the contrastive は that typically marks both subjects.

Cause — since (A), (B)
ニュースを聞いて、安心しました。

(B) is an emotion — the て-clause is its cause

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.7 · CR.3
くて・で
(~kute · ~de)
And ~ — linking adjectives and nouns
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + くて
な-adjective
な-adj + で
Noun
Noun + で
About

This grammar structure extends the linking function of the て-form beyond verbs: it joins adjectives and noun predicates into one flowing sentence — cheap and delicious, a student, and also working part-time. い-adjectives drop the final い and add くて (安い → 安くて; the irregular is いい → よくて). な-adjectives and nouns attach で directly — this で is the conjunctive form of the copula です, not the location particle.

Only the sentence's final predicate carries tense and politeness — the whole chain inherits them, and more than two elements can be strung together (広くて、明るくて、静かだ). Qualities linked this way are felt to belong together, and like the verbal て-form the link often carries a light causal shade (狭くて不便だ — cramped and, for that reason, inconvenient); for contrasting qualities が or けど is used instead. Verbs chain with the て-form itself (card CH.7 · CR.1), and the negative counterpart of this whole paradigm is なくて, covered in card CH.7 · CR.4.

Examplesshow ▶
い-adjective — くて
このラーメン屋は安くて、量も多いです。
This ramen place is cheap, and the portions are big too.
two virtues in one sentence — くて carries no tense of its own

drop い, add くて — the final predicate makes it polite
い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
今日は風が強くて、自転車がつらい。

the causal shade — strong wind is why cycling is rough
い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

い-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
な-adjective — で

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.7 · CR.4
なくて
(~nakute)
Not ~ and · Because not ~
Verb
Verb [ない]negative form
+ くて
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + くなくて
な-adjective
な-adj + ではなくて
Noun
Noun + ではなくて
About

This grammar structure is the negative counterpart of the て-form link: the negative ない takes its conjunctive form なくて and joins two clauses as not (A), and (B). Formation follows the negative form — verbs replace the final い of ない with くて (飲まない → 飲まなくて), い-adjectives become くなくて, and な-adjectives and nouns take ではなくて, with じゃなくて as the everyday spoken equivalent. The irregulars are する → しなくて, くる → こなくて and いい → よくなくて.

Usage 1 — sequence and contrast: with nouns and adjectives, なくて typically corrects or contrasts — it isn't (A), it's (B): 医者ではなくて、看護師です. With these word types the ない involved behaves like an い-adjective, so は can slip in before it for emphasis (甘くはなくて — it's not sweet, mind you); with verbs, ない is an auxiliary and no は can intervene.

Usage 2 — reason: when clause (B) expresses a feeling, a potential verb, or something otherwise beyond the speaker's control, なくて reads as a cause — because (A) doesn't/didn't happen: お金が足りなくて、買えない. This is also why apologies take the pattern 〜なくてすみません — sorry for not… — the negated clause is the reason for the apology.

With verbs, なくて competes with ないで (card CH.7 · CR.5). The rule of thumb: なくて gives a reason, while ないで describes doing (B) without (A). When (B) is a feeling or an inability, only なくて is natural.

Sequence — not (A), and (B)

This area isn't well known, and at night it's a little dark.

VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN

VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.7 · CR.5
ないで
(~naide)
Without doing ~
Verb [ない]negative form
+ で
About

This grammar structure is used to state that one action is performed without doing another — (B) without doing (A). It is the combination of the plain negative ない and the particle で, and it attaches only to verbs: 寝ないで勉強した — studied without sleeping. The final predicate carries the tense and politeness of the whole sentence; ないで itself never changes form.

Because (A) is usually something that would normally be expected to happen, ないで often carries a shade of surprise or reproach — sentence-final questions like 予約しないで来たの？ lean on exactly that broken expectation. The request use — ないでください, please don't — is covered in card CH.11 · CR.2.

ないで vs なくて: both negate a linked clause, but ないで highlights that (B) was done without (A) — one subject, one scene — while なくて presents not-(A) as a reason for (B). 電気を消さないで寝た says you went to bed leaving the light on; 電気が消えなくて困った says the light's refusing to go off is why you were troubled.

Examplesshow ▶
父は電気をつけないで新聞を読みます。
My father reads the newspaper without turning on the light.
attendant circumstance — reading happens minus the expected light
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE
妹は牛乳を入れないでコーヒーを飲みます。
My little sister drinks her coffee without adding milk.

N4CH.7 · CR.6
てみる
(~te miru)
Try doing ~ — and see
Verb [て]て-form
+ みる
About

This grammar structure is used to express trying something to see what happens. It attaches みる — from 見る, but written in hiragana in this use — to the て-form: 食べてみる is not watch while eating but try eating (and see). The nuance is tentative — the action is done once, out of curiosity or as an experiment, typically for the first time. As a helper it conjugates like any regular る-verb, so the pattern moves freely through the module's forms:

てみます,
てみた,
てみたい.

To suggest that someone else try, use てみて or the polite てみてください; in very casual speech even the て of みて drops, leaving てみ — go on, give it a go. The invitation forms てみない？/てみませんか (want to try…?) follow the invitation pattern in card CH.10 · CR.3. One caution: past てみた implies the attempt ran its course and is generally understood as successful unless the speaker says otherwise — 帰ってみたけど、逆に遠かった spells the failure out.

N4CH.7 · CR.7
ておく
(~te oku)
Do in advance · Leave it done
Verb [て]て-form
+ おく
About

This grammar structure is used to describe doing something in advance — for convenience, preparation, or a future need. It combines the て-form with the verb おく — to put · to place: do (A) now and leave it in place until it is needed, as in ビールを冷やしておく — chill the beer now, drink it later. The same "placing" logic gives the structure its second shade of meaning, do (A) and leave it at that — deliberately going no further. In this auxiliary use おく is normally written in hiragana, not as 置く.

The future event being prepared for can also be something unwanted: 毎日歯を磨いておく is brushing daily so that cavities never get their chance — ておく regularly marks preventive measures. In casual speech ておく contracts to とく, and でおく to どく (頼んでおく → 頼んどく); the contraction is everywhere in conversation, drama and manga, but out of place in formal or business contexts. Compare also てある (card CH.8 · CR.8): ておく focuses on the deliberate act of preparing, while てある describes the state left behind afterwards — 窓を開けておく — I'll open the window in advance vs 窓が開けてある — the window has been opened (and stands open).

N4CH.7 · CR.8
ても・でも
(~te mo · ~de mo)
Even if · Even though
Verb
Verb [て]て-form
+ も
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + くても
な-adjective
な-adj + でも
Noun
Noun + でも
All types — negative
Negative て-formなくて / くなくて / じゃなくて
+ も
About

This grammar structure is used to express concession — even if (A), (B) or even though (A), (B): condition (A) may hold, but the outcome (B) stays the same. It attaches も to the て-form: verbs and い-adjectives take ても/くても, while な-adjectives and nouns take でも. Unlike the conditionals たら and ば, which present (A) as leading to (B), ても states that (B) holds regardless of (A). The ても clause itself carries no tense — the final predicate decides it — and the intensifiers いくら and どんなに — no matter how much pair with it naturally.

The negative — even if (A) does not happen — runs through the negative て-form paradigm: なくても for verbs, くなくても for い-adjectives, じゃなくても (formal ではなくても) for な-adjectives and nouns. Two relatives to keep apart: the permission pattern in card CH.12 · CR.1 is this same ても plus いい — it's fine even if you do, and the noun form here shares its shape with the standalone particle でも from the Particles chapter (or something; WH-word + でも).

N4CH.7 · CR.9
ている間に・間に
(~te iru aida ni · ~aida ni)
While ~ — event within a span
Verb
Verb [ている]ている form - ongoing action
+ 間に
Noun
Noun [の] + 間に
Whole span — no に
Same forms + 間
About

This grammar structure is used to say that an event (B) happens within the timeframe of an ongoing action or state (A) — while (A), (B). (A) takes the ている form (or a noun plus の), and (B) must be a short, contained event that completes inside that span: シャワーを浴びている間に、宅配便が来ました. 間 literally means interval, read あいだ, and に points at one moment within it; (B) is very often something outside the speaker's control — but plans also fit, as in while my parents are here, I want to….

Without に, the nuance changes: (A)間(B) means (B) continued throughout the whole of (A) — the two fill the same span: 妹が練習している間、私は本を読んでいた. Choose 間に for a point event inside the span and bare 間 for a parallel activity across it. Compare ながら (card CH.8 · CR.16): ながら joins two simultaneous actions of one subject, while 間・間に typically links different subjects or scenes.

N4CH.7 · CR.10
てよかった
(~te yokatta · ~te yokatta desu)
I'm glad that · It was good that
Verb
Verb [て]て-form
+ よかった
Verb — negative
Verb [なくて / ないで]negative て-form
+ よかった
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + くてよかった
な-adjective
な-adj + でよかった
Noun
Noun + でよかった
About

This grammar structure is used to express relief or gratitude that something happened — I'm glad that… or it was good that…. よかった is the past form of いい, and for verbs it attaches to the て-form: 来てよかった — I'm glad (we) came. The expression always ends in this past form, because the speaker is looking back at something already settled; adding です makes it polite.

To say you are glad something did not happen, attach よかった to the negative て-form: なくてよかった or ないでよかった. Both mean I'm glad that (A) didn't happen, but they differ in register — ないでよかった is by far the more common choice in speech, while なくてよかった leans toward writing and can sound slightly formal or old-fashioned to some speakers.

The pattern extends beyond verbs:

い-adjectives drop the final い and take くてよかった (近い → 近くてよかった),
な-adjectives and nouns attach でよかった directly (元気でよかった — I'm glad you're well), where the で is the conjunctive form of the copula.

Combined with a benefactive, the structure yields the set phrase 〜ていてくれてありがとう — thank you for being… — that combination is covered under Giving & Receiving.

てすみません
(~te sumimasen · ~te sumimasen deshita)
Sorry for ~ · Sorry for not ~
Casual
Present offence
Verb [て]て-form
+ ごめん
Negative
Verb [なくて]negative て-form
+ ごめん
Formal
Present offence
Verb [て]て-form
+ すみません
Past offence
Verb [て]て-form
+ すみませんでした
Negative
Verb [なくて]negative て-form
+ すみません
About

This grammar structure is used to apologise for something — sorry for (A). The て-clause names the offence and すみません carries the apology; grammatically it is the cause reading of て from earlier in this chapter fossilised into a set phrase. すみません comes from the verb 済む — to be settled: the wrong feels unsettled because of (A). For a completed offence, especially in formal contexts, the past すみませんでした closes the matter: 昨日は集合時間を間違えてすみませんでした.

Sorry for not doing (A) uses なくて: 手伝えなくてすみません. In casual speech ごめん or ごめんなさい replaces すみません — 服を汚してごめん. The more formal apology set — 申し訳ありません and its honorific relatives — replaces すみません altogether in business and service settings; those forms belong to honorific language, which sits outside this module.

N5CH.8 · CR.1
〜ている
(~te iru)
Is · Am · Are ~ing — ongoing action
Very casual — contraction
Verb [て]て-form
+ いる
Casual
Verb [て]て-form
+ いる
Formal
Verb [て]て-form
+ います
About

This grammar structure is used to express an action that is currently in progress. It is the closest equivalent to the English present continuous (I am doing), though it is not a perfect match. It is formed by attaching いる to the て-form of any verb; verbs whose て-form ends in で follow the same pattern.

The final meaning depends on the verb, but in this group the action is actively ongoing — something is happening right now and has not stopped.

In casual speech, いる contracts to る — dropping the い entirely. This gives forms like 食べてる, 見てる, 読んでる. The contraction is extremely common in everyday spoken Japanese.

N5CH.8 · CR.2
〜ている
(~te iru)
Has done, Is [result still present] — resulting state
Very casual — contraction
Verb [て]て-form
+ いる
Casual
Verb [て]て-form
+ いる
Formal
Verb [て]て-form
+ います
About

This grammar structure is used to express a resulting state — an action has already been completed, but its effect or condition is still present. The focus is not on the action itself, but on the fact that it happened and the result still holds. Think of it as has done, and it is still that way.

This use is dominated by intransitive verbs — verbs that describe a state change without a direct object. The subject enters a new state, and ている describes that state as currently true. The action occurred; what you are describing is the aftermath.

The key to recognizing this use is the verb type. Intransitive verbs describing a state change — opening, closing, stopping, falling — almost always signal resulting state rather than ongoing action.

(~te iru)

Casual

+ いる

About

This grammar structure is used to express a current condition, status, or state of being — something that is simply true right now, with no active process or completed action behind it. The subject just is that way.

This use applies to a fixed set of stative and mental verbs — verbs like "to know," "to understand," "to live," "to work," "to own," "to be married." These verbs do not describe physical activity or change; they describe how things stand. The set of verbs that carry this meaning is largely fixed — you cannot apply it freely to new verbs the way you can with ongoing action. Almost all verbs in this group are う-verbs.

Quick RecapCH.8 · CR.4
The three faces of ている
ongoing action · resulting state · current state of being
Comparison
Use Typical verbs Function Feels like
Ongoing action 食べる / 読む / 走る — durative action verbs An action in progress at this very moment "Is / Am / Are ~ing"
Resulting state 結婚する / 死ぬ / 開く — change-of-state verbs A change happened earlier and its result still holds now "Has done" / "Is [result still present]"
State of being 住む / 働く / 知る — verbs of life circumstance An ongoing condition of someone's life, not an event "Knows / Lives / Works"
When to use what
The action is unfolding right now, in the middle of happening → 食べている — is eating
Something changed at some point and the result is still true now → 結婚している — is married
A long-term fact about someone — residence, occupation, knowledge → 住んでいる — lives
Same form, three readings — the verb's meaning decides: durative verbs read as ongoing, change-of-state verbs read as result, life-circumstance verbs read as state
N4CH.8 · CR.5
ていた
(~te ita)
Was doing · Was in a state
Verb [て]て-form
+ いた
About

This grammar structure is the past form of ている. Because いる conjugates like any other verb, every use of ている shifts into the past with ていた: an ongoing action (歌っていた — was singing), a resulting state (壊れていた — was broken), and a past habit (通っていた — used to go). The polite form is ていました.

ていた is also used when the action may well still be going on, but the speaker only vouches for the period they observed: 田中さんはさっきまでここに座っていた — Tanaka-san was sitting here until a moment ago does not claim that he has stopped sitting somewhere — only that this is what the speaker saw. This makes ていた a careful, non-committal way to report on situations the speaker has walked away from.

Examplesshow ▶
昨日は一日中、報告書を書いていました。
Yesterday I was writing the report all day.
ongoing action across a past period
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
子供の時、どんなスポーツをしていましたか？

past habit questioned
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
帰ったら、家の戸が開いていた。

resulting state found in the past
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N5CH.8 · CR.6
〜たり〜たりする
(~tari ~tari suru)
Do things like ~ and ~
representative actions — no fixed order
Verb A [た] plain past
+ り +
Verb B [た] plain past
+ り + する
single action — implies "among other things"
Verb [た] plain past
+ り + する
About

This grammar structure is used to list representative actions — things you did or do, without implying that the list is complete or that the actions happened in a specific order. The closest English equivalent is do things like A and B.

Each verb is put into its plain past (た-form) with り added after it. Only the final する is conjugated for tense and polarity — します for present polite, しました for past polite, しません for negative.

〜たり vs 〜て: the て-form connects actions in a strict sequence. 〜たり makes no claim about order and signals the list is not exhaustive. Use て when sequence matters; use たり when giving examples.

Single verb use: たりする can follow a single verb, implying the speaker did that action among other unspecified things.

Note: in sequences where する itself is the last listed verb, する at the end is often omitted in natural speech.

Examplesshow ▶
休みの日は料理したり、買い物したりします。

About

This grammar structure is used to express that you have done something at least once — that there has been a time in your life when X happened. It translates as I have done X before or I have the experience of doing X. The focus is on whether the experience exists, not on when it happened.

Only the verb goes into the plain past (た-form). ある carries all tense and polarity. こと nominalizes the verb phrase. の cannot replace こと in this expression.

Questions and responses: ことがありますか turns the structure into Have you ever...? The natural responses are はい、あります and いいえ、ありません.

N4CH.8 · CR.8
てある
(~te aru)
Has been done — state left on purpose
Verb [て]て-form - transitive only
+ ある
About

This grammar structure is used to describe a present state that is the result of a deliberate past action. The person who acted goes unmentioned, but their intention is implied: 窓が開けてある means the window has been opened by someone, on purpose, and is still open. Only transitive verbs — verbs that take an object with を — can be used, because the structure is built on intentional human action. Since the resulting state still holds, ある stays in the present tense; its past form てあった reports a prepared state that existed at some earlier point.

The contrast with ている is a classic pair: 窓が閉めてある (transitive 閉める) says someone shut the window and it remains shut, while 窓が閉まっている (intransitive 閉まる) simply describes the closed window with no agent implied. The object of てある is usually marked with が, which puts the focus on the state of the thing; を also appears, keeping attention on the unmentioned doer's action — common with preparation words such as 予約 or 準備.

Examplesshow ▶
ホテルはもう予約してありますから、ご安心ください。
The hotel is already booked, so please don't worry.
preparation made earlier — the state still holds
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
教室の電気は消してありました。

てあった — the prepared state in the past
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

someone put it out on purpose — the state remains
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.8 · CR.9
ていく・てくる
(~te iku · ~te kuru)
To go on · To come to — direction of change
ていく
Verb [て]て-form
+ いく
てくる
Verb [て]て-form
+ くる
About

This grammar structure combines the て-form of a verb with the motion verbs いく — to go and くる — to come to mark the direction of an action or a change — away from the speaker with ていく, toward the speaker with てくる. The direction can be through physical space or through time, and the motion verb conjugates as usual, so tense and politeness are carried by いく and くる themselves.

In the physical sense, ていく means doing the action and then moving away: 持っていく is to take (along) and 着ていく is to wear (something) there. てくる is its mirror image — 持ってくる is to bring, and with errand verbs it builds a round trip into the sentence: 買ってくる means going somewhere, buying the thing, and coming back. When the meaning is genuinely physical, the kanji spellings 行く and 来る are often used; in the temporal uses below, hiragana is the norm, though this is a convention rather than a fixed rule.

In the temporal sense, ていく marks a change that starts now and continues into the future, as in 物価が上がっていく — prices will keep rising, while てくる marks a change that began earlier and has arrived at the present, as in 寒くなってきた — it has gotten cold. The past form てきた therefore often translates as has been …ing or has gotten, and with certain verbs it signals the onset of something new: 雨が降ってきた — it has started to rain.

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION

VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.10
ところだ
(~tokoro da)
About to · In the middle of · Just did — stage of an action
About to
Verbdictionary form
+ ところだ
In the middle
Verb [ている]ている form
+ ところだ
Just did
Verb [た]plain past
+ ところだ
About

This grammar structure is used to state what stage an action is at. ところ is a noun meaning place, used here abstractly for the point a situation has reached, and the tense of the verb in front of it sets that point: the dictionary form gives about to (書くところだ — on the verge, nothing has started), ている gives right in the middle of (書いているところだ), and the past form gives just did (書いたところだ — the moment immediately after). だ/です carries politeness, and its past form marks a stage in the past: 出かけるところだった — was just about to leave.

ているところだ often serves as a polite explanation of being busy — 今、資料を作っているところです — I'm right in the middle of preparing the materials. In casual speech ところ is frequently shortened to とこ. The kanji form 所 tends to be read as a physical place, so hiragana is the usual spelling in this grammatical use, although both do appear.

るところだ — about to
これから会議が始まるところです。

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.11
たばかり
(~ta bakari)
Just did — still fresh
Verb [た]plain past
+ ばかり
About

This grammar structure is used to express that something happened only a short time ago — just did. The particle ばかり has several senses built on closeness to a point of reference; after the past form of a verb it marks closeness in time, so the action reads as freshly completed: 起きたばかり — just woke up. With の it modifies a noun directly (習ったばかりの文法 — grammar we just learned), and in casual speech the variants ばっかり and ばっか are common. The kanji form 許り is rare.

The difference from たところ is perspective. たところ pins the objective moment right after the action, while たばかり expresses the speaker's feeling that the event is still recent — so it stretches as far as that feeling does. 先月買ったばかり — I only just bought it last month is natural, but 先月買ったところ is not, because a month is no longer the moment after.

Examplesshow ▶
入社したばかりなので、まだ分からないことが多いです。
I've only just joined the company, so there's still a lot I don't understand.
subjectively recent — weeks can still be "just"
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
習ったばかりの文法をもう忘れてしまいましたか？
Have you already forgotten the grammar we just learned?
たばかりの modifies a noun directly
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
このスマホは先月買ったばかりなのに、もう調子が悪い。
I only bought this phone last month, and it's already acting up.
stretches with the speaker's feeling — たところ could not span a month
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
起きたばかりで、頭がまだ働かない。
I just woke up, so my brain isn't working yet.
immediately after waking
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.12
てしまう
(~te shimau · ~chau · ~jau)
Completely · Unfortunately — completion and regret
Standard
Verb [て]て-form
+ しまう
Contracted — て
Verb [て]
+ ちゃう
Contracted — で
Verb [で]
+ じゃう
About

This grammar structure attaches しまう to the て-form of a verb and carries two main senses, decided entirely by context. The first is completion: the action is done thoroughly, to its natural conclusion — 本を読んでしまいました — I read the book from cover to cover. The second is regret or accident: something happened that was unintended, careless, or unwelcome — かばんを電車に忘れてしまいました — I went and left my bag on the train.

The two senses share one core idea: the action has run its full course and cannot be taken back. ケーキを全部食べてしまった can therefore mean I finished off the cake or I regret eating all the cake — the speaker's tone and the situation decide which reading the listener takes.

In casual speech, てしまう contracts to ちゃう and でしまう (after て-forms ending in で) contracts to じゃう: 食べてしまった → 食べちゃった, 飲んでしまった → 飲んじゃった. The contractions conjugate as godan verbs and are very common in conversation, but are avoided in formal writing.

Examplesshow ▶
Completion — done for good
週末に、借りた小説を全部読んでしまいました。
Over the weekend I read the whole novel I'd borrowed.
completion — read through to the end
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
宿題は今日中にやってしまおう。
Let's get the homework completely out of the way today.
volitional — finish it off for good
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
Regret — it happened
大事な書類を電車に忘れてしまいました。
I went and left important documents on the train.
regret — unintended and irreversible
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
ごめん、君の皿を割ってしまった。
Sorry, I broke your plate.
apology — the damage cannot be undone
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
ちゃう・じゃう — contracted
ダイエット中なのに、ケーキを全部食べちゃった。
I'm on a diet, but I ate the whole cake.
てしまう contracts to ちゃう in speech
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
牛乳、全部飲んじゃったの？
Did you drink all the milk?
でしまう contracts to じゃう after で te forms
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.8 · CR.13
始める・続ける・終わる
(~hajimeru · ~tsuzukeru · ~owaru)
To start · To continue · To finish — aspect of an action
Start
Verb stem + 始める
Continue
Verb stem + 続ける
Finish
Verb stem + 終わる
About

This grammar structure is used to state that an action starts, continues, or ends. The verbs 始める — to begin, 続ける — to continue and 終わる — to end attach to the stem of another verb, and the combination conjugates as an ordinary verb, so tense and politeness fall on the final element:

習い始めます,
走り続けた,
読み終わった.

始める marks a neutral or deliberate start: 来月から習い始める (start learning next month). Whether the kanji or hiragana form is used makes no difference in meaning. For sudden, unplanned beginnings, Japanese prefers 出す, covered in card CH.8 · CR.14.

続ける marks uninterrupted continuation: 走り続ける (to keep running). Linking through the stem makes the two verbs one continuous action — 頑張り続ける is to keep giving one's best, whereas linking with the て-form (頑張って続ける) means doing one thing and then continuing another.

終わる marks completion: 食べ終わる (to finish eating). It often appears with まで clauses to set the boundary of another action — nothing happens until the 終わる point is reached.

Examplesshow ▶
始める — to start
来月からピアノを習い始めます。
I'll start learning the piano next month.
deliberate start of a new habit
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
空が暗くなって、雪が降り始めた。
The sky darkened and it began to snow.
neutral onset — compare 降り出す for suddenness
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
続ける — to continue
足が痛くても、選手たちは走り続けました。
Even with painful legs, the athletes kept running.
continuing despite an obstacle
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

She kept studying for ten years to become a doctor.
uninterrupted effort toward a goal
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
終わる — to finish
やっと卒業論文を書き終わりました。
I finally finished writing my graduation thesis.
the writing reached its end
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
その本、もう読み終わった？
Have you finished reading that book yet?
plain question — rising intonation, no か
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.8 · CR.14
出す
(~dasu)
To burst into · To suddenly start
Verb stem + 出す
About

This grammar structure is used to express that an action begins suddenly — to burst into or to break out. The verb 出す attaches to the stem of another verb: 泣き出す — to burst into tears, 笑い出す — to burst out laughing, 降り出す — to suddenly start raining. The combination conjugates as an ordinary godan verb.

The contrast with 始める is the point of this structure. 始める presents a start neutrally, often as the subject's own intention, while 出す presents it as abrupt and unplanned — frequently something the subject cannot control. 歌い始める suggests a planned start to singing; 歌い出す suggests someone suddenly broke into song. For deliberate, scheduled beginnings, 出す is not used.

Examplesshow ▶
会議の最中に、部長が急に笑い出しました。
In the middle of the meeting, the department head suddenly burst out laughing.
uncontrolled onset — nobody planned it
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
どうして急に走り出したんですか？
Why did you suddenly start running?
asking about an abrupt, unplanned action
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
家を出るとすぐ、雨が降り出した。
Right after I left the house, it suddenly started raining.
sudden natural onset — 降り始める would sound neutral
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
赤ちゃんが夜中に泣き出したから、ほとんど寝られなかった。
The baby started crying in the middle of the night, so I barely slept.
the subject cannot control the action
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.15
直す
(~naosu)
To do over · To redo
Verb stem + 直す
About

This grammar structure is used to express doing something over again — to redo. The verb 直す — to fix attaches to the stem of another verb, and the combination usually implies that the first attempt was unsatisfactory and needs correcting: 書き直す — to rewrite, 作り直す — to remake. The combined verb conjugates as an ordinary godan verb, so tense and politeness attach to 直す itself.

する verbs become し直す: 設定する → 設定し直す — to reconfigure. In casual speech, する is often replaced by やる, giving やり直す — an extremely common word meaning to start over from scratch.

Note that 直す — to fix, to straighten out should not be confused with 治す — to heal, which shares the reading なおす but is used for illness and injury. In this redo construction, only 直す appears.

Examplesshow ▶
名前の漢字が間違っていたので、書き直しました。
The kanji in the name was wrong, so I rewrote it.
redo because the first attempt came out wrong
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
この説明は分かりにくいので、やり直してください。
This explanation is hard to follow, so please redo it.
やり直す — casual やる replaces する for a full restart
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
失敗したから、計画を立て直そう。
It failed, so let's rebuild the plan.
volitional — rebuild from the ground up
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
Wi-Fiのパスワード、設定し直した？
Did you reset the Wi-Fi password?
する verb — する becomes し before 直す
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N4CH.8 · CR.16
ながら
(~nagara)
While doing — two actions, one subject
Verb stem + ながら
About

This grammar structure is used to connect two actions happening at the same time, performed by the same subject. ながら attaches to the stem of the background action, and the clause that follows carries the main action: in 音楽を聞きながら勉強する — to study while listening to music, the studying is the point of the sentence and the music accompanies it. Tense and politeness come from the final verb.

The same-subject requirement is strict — ながら cannot join actions performed by two different people, even if they happen simultaneously. The structure describes one person genuinely doing two things at once, which is also why it appears in warnings about multitasking, such as using a phone while driving. ながら additionally has a separate concessive sense (while in the sense of although), found in set expressions like 残念ながら — unfortunately — that use is treated as its own grammar point at a later level.

Examplesshow ▶
コーヒーを飲みながら、メールをチェックします。
I check my email while drinking coffee.
A is background — checking mail is the main action
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
運転しながらスマホを使わないでください。
Please don't use your phone while driving.
one subject doing both at once — here prohibited
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE
音楽を聞きながら走るのが好きだ。
I like running while listening to music.
the ながら clause sets the accompanying action
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
妹は歌いながらシャワーを浴びている。
My little sister sings while taking a shower.
simultaneous actions by the same person
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.17
〜方・の仕方
(~kata · ~no shikata)
Way of doing · How to
Verb
Verb stem + 方
する verb
Noun + の仕方
About

This grammar structure is used to turn a verb into a noun phrase meaning the way of doing something or how to do it. 方 attaches to the stem of the verb: 読む → 読み方 — how to read. Because the result behaves like an ordinary noun, it can be followed by particles such as は, が and を to build longer sentences.

Particles inside the phrase shift when 方 is attached. An object marked with を becomes possessive の: 漢字を読む → 漢字の読み方 — how to read kanji. With movement verbs, the destination particle に becomes への: 駅に行く → 駅への行き方 — how to get to the station.

する compound verbs use 仕方 instead: drop する and attach の仕方 to the noun part — 予約する → 予約の仕方 — how to book. 仕方 is itself a noun meaning way of doing, so the meaning is identical to the plain 方 form.

When a 方 phrase is made the topic with は, it often describes someone's personal manner or habit rather than instructions — 彼の話し方 — the way he speaks comments on personal style, not on a method to be learned.

〜方 — verb stem + 方
課長の話し方はとても上品です。
The section chief's way of speaking is very refined.
with は — personal manner, not instructions
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
この漢字の読み方が分かりません。
I don't know how to read this kanji.
the verb's を object becomes の before 読み方
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE
美術館への行き方を教えてくれませんか？
Could you tell me how to get to the art museum?
destination に becomes への before 行き方
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION
カメラの正しい持ち方を子供に教えた。
I taught my child the correct way to hold a camera.
the 方 phrase takes を like any noun
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
〜の仕方 — する verbs
ゴミの分別の仕方は市のサイトで確認できます。
You can check how to sort the rubbish on the city's website.
分別する → 分別の仕方; する drops out
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

the 仕方 phrase stands as the topic with は
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.18
やすい・にくい・づらい
(~yasui · ~nikui · ~zurai)
Easy to · Hard to — ease and difficulty of an action
Easy to
Verb stem + やすい
Hard to — obstacle
Verb stem + にくい
Hard to — burden
Verb stem + づらい
About

This grammar structure is used to describe how easy or difficult an action is to perform. All three endings attach to the stem of a verb, and the whole expression becomes an い-adjective that conjugates normally:

past 使いやすかった,
negative 読みにくくない,
polite 飲みにくいです.

やすい means easy to — the action requires little effort or happens readily (使いやすい — easy to use). With verbs of emotion or involuntary reaction, the meaning shifts toward prone to: 怒りやすい is quick to anger and 泣きやすい is prone to crying. It is unrelated to the adjective 安い (cheap), and the construction is normally written in hiragana — the kanji 易い is rarely used.

にくい means hard to because of an obstacle in the task itself — the size of the handwriting, the shape of the tool, the skill required (読みにくい — hard to read). づらい also means hard to, but the difficulty is a burden on the person performing the action, whether psychological or physical: 言いづらい is hard to say because saying it costs the speaker something. It comes from the adjective 辛い (painful). As a rule of thumb, にくい points at the task and づらい points at the doer.

None of the three measures objective difficulty — for that, Japanese uses the ordinary adjective 難しい. 漢字は覚えにくい says that memorizing kanji feels hard to the speaker, while 漢字を覚えるのは難しい states that it is a difficult task in general.

Examplesshow ▶
やすい — easy to
部長は心配しやすいので、早めに報告してください。
The department head worries easily, so report to him early.
with emotion verbs やすい means prone to
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
先生の説明は分かりやすかったです。
The teacher's explanation was easy to understand.
conjugates as an い-adjective — past やすかった
VERB PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
この辞書は例文が多くて使いやすい。
This dictionary has lots of example sentences and is easy to use.
a tool judged by the ease of the action
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
にくい — hard to
雨の日は、この坂は運転しにくいです。
On rainy days, this hill is hard to drive.
external circumstances make the action difficult
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
彼の字は小さくて読みにくい。
His handwriting is small and hard to read.
physical obstacle — the difficulty sits in the task
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
新しいアプリは思ったより使いにくくなかった。
The new app wasn't as hard to use as I expected.
negative い-adjective conjugation — にくくない
VERB PAST NEGATIVE PLAIN
づらい — hard to bear

physical strain on the doer
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

psychological burden — saying it costs the speaker
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.19
〜化する
(~ka suru)
-ization · To turn into
Noun + 化する
About

This grammar structure is used to express that something changes into a new state or form. The suffix 化 means change or transformation, and attached to a noun with する it means to -ize or to -ify: 自動化する — to automate, データ化する — to digitize, 国際化する — to internationalize. The result conjugates exactly like する.

To modify a following noun, the past form 化した or the particle の is used: 劣化した建物 — a deteriorated building. In formal or scientific writing, する and の are often dropped and the noun + 化 stands alone as a noun naming the process itself: 高齢化が進んでいる — the aging of the population is advancing.

紙の書類をデータ化するのに時間がかかります。
It takes time to digitize the paper documents.
turning one form into another — data-ization
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

noun + 化 names the process itself
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
うちの会社は経理の仕事を自動化した。
Our company automated the accounting work.
化する conjugates like する
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

formal style — 化 stands alone as a noun with が
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N4CH.8 · CR.20
〜風
(~fuu)
-style · In the manner of
Style label
Noun + 風
Before a noun
Noun + 風の + Noun
About

This grammar structure is a suffix used to label something as being in the style of or in the fashion of another thing. It attaches to a noun: アメリカ風 — American-style, 九十年代風 — nineties-style. In this use it is always read ふう, never かぜ. Two fixed words built on it are extremely common: 和風 — Japanese-style and 洋風 — Western-style.

To describe a following noun, の is added: メキシコ風の料理 — Mexican-style food. The bare form can also close a sentence as a predicate with だ/です — 彼の話し方は先生風だ — the way he talks is teacher-like — labelling a manner rather than a genuine origin: the food is not actually from Mexico, and he is not actually a teacher; things are merely done in that style.

母の家には昔風の台所が残っています。
My mother's house still has an old-style kitchen.
風の links the style to the following noun

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
母はよくイタリア風のパスタを作ってくれる。

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
9 Preferences, Desire & Intention
  1. が好き · がきらいLike · Dislike — expressing preference
  2. 〜たいWant to do ~
  3. ほしい・てほしいWanting a thing · Wanting someone to act
  4. がる・たがるShowing signs of · Third-person wants
  5. といいI hope · It would be good if
  6. ように祈るPraying that · Fingers crossed
  7. ようと思うI think I'll — intention
  8. つもりだ・予定だI intend to · Scheduled to
  9. ばよかったShould have · I wish I had
N5CH.9 · CR.1
が好き · がきらい
(~ga suki · ~ga kirai)
Like · Dislike — expressing preference
Casual
like
Noun + が好きだ
dislike
Noun + がきらいだ
Formal
like
Noun + が好きです
dislike
Noun + がきらいです
About

This grammar structure is used to express likes and dislikes toward nouns — objects, people, or abstract things. 好き means like and きらい means dislike. Prefixing either with 大 amplifies the intensity: 大好き means love and 大嫌い means hate.

Despite translating like verbs in English, all four are な-adjectives — they describe an emotional state, not an action. Note that きらい ends in い but is still a な-adjective, not an い-adjective. It conjugates exactly like 好き.

The thing you like or dislike is marked with が, not を. This is because が marks it as the subject of the feeling — the thing that triggers the emotion — rather than a direct object being acted upon.

Negation follows standard な-adjective rules: 好きじゃない · 好きじゃないです — don't like, きらいじゃない (don't dislike — roughly fine with it).

Examplesshow ▶
子供の時から、音楽が好きです。
I've liked music since I was a child.
lifelong preference; から marks the starting point of the feeling
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
日本料理が好きですか？
Do you like Japanese food?
simple polite preference question; 好き takes が not を
NOUN PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION

I don't like crowds.
polite negative; じゃありません is more formal than じゃないです
NOUN PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE

unexpected question assuming dislike; slight surprise in the phrasing

I liked maths when I was a student.
past academic preference; 好き in past tense with でした

asking about childhood food preferences
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION

NOUN PAST NEGATIVE POLITE

NOUN PAST NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION

plain assertion about a third party's preference

NOUN PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION

大好き = love (stronger than 好き); plain past
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

casual past preference question
NOUN PAST AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION

NOUN PAST NEGATIVE PLAIN
昔、本当に数学がきらいじゃなかった？

casual check on past attitude toward a subject
NOUN PAST NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
N5CH.9 · CR.2
〜たい
(~tai)
Want to do ~
Casual
want
Verb stem + たい
don't want
Verb stem + たくない
Formal
want
Verb stem + たいです
don't want
Verb stem + たくないです
About

This grammar structure is used to express a desire or aspiration to perform an action — equivalent to want to do ~ in English. たい attaches to the verb stem.

Tense and polarity: たい conjugates exactly like a い-adjective — four forms: たい (present affirmative) → たくない (negative) → たかった (past) → たくなかった (past negative). Adding です to any form makes it polite.

を vs が: verbs that normally take を can also take が when used with たい. を is neutral and marks the action toward the object. が shifts focus onto the object of desire itself, adding an emotional or selective nuance. Both are grammatically correct — を is the safer default.

First-person restriction: たい is for expressing your own desires or directly asking someone about theirs. It cannot be used to guess or assume what a third party wants — for that, たがっている is used instead.

Not for requests or invitations: たい cannot be used to tell someone you want them to do something (use てほしい) or to invite someone to do something together (use ませんか).

Examplesshow ▶

N4CH.9 · CR.3
ほしい・てほしい
(~ga hoshii · ~te hoshii)
Wanting a thing · Wanting someone to act
Thing
Noun + がほしい
Action
Persondoer
+ に +
Verb [て]て-form
+ ほしい
About

Usage 1 — がほしい: this grammar structure is used to say that someone wants a thing — a physical object or something tangible. ほしい is an い-adjective meaning wanted, and the desired thing is marked with が (or は when contrasting: 高いかばんはほしくない). Because it is a regular い-adjective, it conjugates as one — ほしくない, ほしかった, ほしくなかった — and works the same in polite and plain speech with or without です. It refers to things, never actions: wanting to do something is expressed with the auxiliary たい instead. The kanji form 欲しい is common in writing.

Usage 2 — てほしい: when ほしい follows a verb's て-form, it expresses that the speaker wants someone else to do something. The person expected to act is marked with に: 父にたばこをやめてほしい — I want my father to quit smoking. The subject of ほしい is the speaker, not the doer. To want someone not to do something, attach ほしい to the ないで form (話さないでほしい) or negate ほしい itself (てほしくない). In questions the wanting shifts to the listener — 手伝ってほしいの？ asks do you want me to help? For a third party's visible desires, both patterns hand over to 欲しがる and たがる from card CH.9 · CR.4.

An extension combines this with ように: with a potential verb, ようになってほしい expresses wanting someone to reach the point of being able to do something (英語が話せるようになってほしい), and after a noun, のように〜てほしい means wanting someone to act in the manner of that noun (アナウンサーのように話してほしい).

The three "want" patterns divide the ground cleanly: たい — I want to act; がほしい — I want to have; てほしい — I want someone else to act.

PatternAttaches toMeaning
たい Verb stem I want to do
がほしい Noun + が I want a thing
てほしい Person に + Verb て-form I want [person] to do

N4CH.9 · CR.4
がる・たがる
(~garu · ~tagaru)
Showing signs of · Third-person wants
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + がる
な-adjective
な-adj + がる
Verb
Verb stem + たがる
About

This grammar structure is used to describe another person's feelings or desires through their visible behaviour — to show signs of or to act like. In Japanese, emotion words such as 怖い, ほしい, or 嫌 describe inner states that only the person feeling them can report directly, so they are not asserted about third parties as they stand. Attaching がる converts the emotion word into a う-verb of observable behaviour: 怖がる — to show fear, 欲しがる — to show wanting.

Usage 1 — がる with adjectives: attach がる to the stem of an い-adjective (drop the final い: 寒い → 寒がる) or directly to a な-adjective stem without な (嫌 → 嫌がる). Because がる is a regular う-verb, it conjugates normally, and the choice of form matters: plain がる states a habitual, characteristic tendency (うちの犬はいつも寒がる — he always acts cold), while がっている reports signs being shown at a specific moment (あの人は寒がっている — that person seems cold right now). Note also a particle shift: where 欲しい marks the desired thing with が, the verb 欲しがる takes を.

Usage 2 — たがる with verbs: the same suffix applied to the desiderative たい. Attach たい to the verb's stem, then replace its final い with がる: 行きたい → 行きたがる — [someone] wants to go. The habitual/current split works the same way (したがる vs したがっている), and the negative reports visible reluctance: 息子は学校に行きたがらない — my son doesn't want to go to school.

Keep the direction of desire straight: 食べたがる means a third party shows they want to eat, while 食べてほしい means the speaker wants someone else to eat — the latter is covered with ほしい・てほしい in card CH.9 · CR.3. For things rather than actions, 欲しがる is the third-person counterpart of が欲しい.

N4CH.9 · CR.5
といい
(~to ii)
I hope · It would be good if
Verb
Verbplain present
+ といい
い-adjective
い-adjplain present
+ といい
な-adjective
な-adj + だといい
Noun
Noun + だといい
About

This grammar structure is used to express hope that something nice will happen — I hope, it would be good if. It combines the particle と, which presents an outcome as the certain or natural result of a condition, with the い-adjective いい: literally if (A) happens, it is good. The word before と stays in its plain non-past form regardless of how the sentence ends; な-adjectives and nouns insert だ before と. Because と frames the outcome as definite, the hope carries real weight — closer to I'm really hoping than a passing remark.

What follows いい decides who the hope is for. Ending in といいですね or casual といいね wishes good luck to someone else: いい仕事が見つかるといいですね — I hope you find a good job. Ending in といいんですが or といいんだけど voices a hope for your own sake in a modest, tentative way — the trailing が/けど is left hanging on purpose, softening the statement so it does not sound presumptuous.

To hope that something does not happen, put the clause in the ない form: 雨が降らないといいね — I hope it doesn't rain. Combined with てくれる from the giving-and-receiving family, てくれるといいんですが blends hope with an indirect request — hoping that someone will do something for your benefit. The conditional と itself is treated fully with the other conditionals later.

N4CH.9 · CR.6
ように祈る
(~you ni inoru · ~masu you ni)
Praying that · Fingers crossed
Full form
Verbdictionary / negative
+ ように祈る
Sentence-final wish
Verbpolite form
+ ように。
About

This grammar structure is used to say that someone prays or earnestly hopes for an outcome — pray that, hope that, fingers crossed. As in the other よう patterns, ように presents the completion of the action as the wished-for goal; it is followed by the う-verb 祈る — to pray (or 願う — to wish). Despite the literal meaning, it is used far more often for everyday hopes than for actual prayer: 試験に受かるように祈っている — I'm praying he passes the exam. The clause before ように takes the plain non-past form, and ないように covers hoping that something does not happen.

Uniquely among the よう structures, the verb after ように can be dropped entirely, leaving a free-standing wish that ends the sentence: 合格できますように。 — may I pass! This shortened form usually follows the ます form and is the standard formula for shrine wishes, birthday wishes, and well-wishing messages. Because only this pattern ends in bare ように, a sentence-final ように always means I hope / I pray — do not confuse it with ようになる or ようにする, where the following verb is what carries the meaning.

ようと思う
(~ou to omou · ~you to omou)
I think I'll — intention
Decided now
Verb [おう / よう]volitional
+ と思う
Standing plan
Verb [おう / よう]volitional

About

This grammar structure is used to state an intention — I think I'll (A), I'm planning to (A). It pairs the volitional form (card CH.10 · CR.5) with the verb 思う: of the volitional's readings, only the will-expressing one survives here, so 買おうと思う is a statement of intent, close to 〜するつもりだ. Plain と思う/と思います suggests the decision is forming as you speak; と思っている/と思っています presents it as a standing plan you have held for some time.

Keep intent and prediction apart: 日本の会社で働こうと思う states the speaker's own plan, while 日本の会社で働くと思う — with the plain present instead of the volitional — is a prediction, usually about someone else. And since only ている can describe another person's inner state, と思っている is also the form used for third-party intentions.
