N4CH.9 · CR.8
つもりだ・予定だ
(~tsumori da · ~yotei da)
I intend to · Scheduled to
Intention
Verbplain present
+ つもりだ
No intention
Verbplain present
+ つもりはない
Schedule
Verbplain present
+ 予定だ
Noun
Noun + の予定だ
About

Usage 1 — つもりだ: this grammar structure expresses a firm personal intention or plan — I intend to, I plan to. It attaches to the plain present form of a verb: the dictionary form for positive intentions (来年、日本で働くつもりです), and the ない form for intentions not to do something (たばこを吸わないつもりです — I intend not to smoke). The intention lives inside the speaker's head — nothing needs to be arranged yet — but it is settled, not a passing thought. Two refinements are worth knowing. First, negating つもり itself gives a different shade from negating the verb: 行かないつもりだ means I intend not to go — the avoidance is active — while 行くつもりはない means I have no intention of going — there is simply no such plan, which often sounds firmer as a refusal. Second, the past form つもりでした marks a plan that failed or was abandoned: 勉強するつもりでしたが、寝てしまいました — I intended to study, but fell asleep.

Usage 2 — 予定だ: 予定 is a noun meaning schedule, and 予定だ marks something as an arranged plan rather than an inner intention — appointments, trips, deadlines. It follows the dictionary form of a verb (出張する予定です) or attaches to a noun phrase with の (三時からの予定です). One caution: the だ/です must be present for 予定 to work as it is planned that — ending a sentence on bare 予定 makes it merely modify what precedes it, like saying I have an eating-steak plan rather than I plan to eat steak.

Together with ようと思う from card CH.9 · CR.7, these three form a scale of commitment: 行こうと思う — the decision is forming in my mind; 行くつもりだ — my mind is made up; 行く予定だ — it is on the calendar.

N4CH.9 · CR.9
ばよかった
(~ba yokatta)
Should have · I wish I had
Regret — didn't do
Verb [ば]ば-form
+ よかった
Regret — did do
Verb [なければ]negative ば-form
+ よかった
About

This grammar structure is used to express regret over a missed opportunity — I should have, I wish I had, it would have been better to. It pairs the conditional ば with よかった, the past form of the い-adjective いい (which conjugates from its older form よい): literally if (A), it would have been good — and (A) is precisely what the speaker failed to do. The reverse regret — wishing you had not done something — uses the negative: drop the い from the ない form and add ければ: 聞かなければよかった — I wish I hadn't asked.

The ば-form is built from the dictionary form even though the regret is about the past: for う-verbs, shift the final syllable to its え-row sound and add ば (行く → 行けば); for る-verbs, replace る with れば (食べる → 食べれば); the irregulars give すれば and くれば. Unlike English "I wish I had gone," the conditional clause never shifts into the past — all the pastness is carried by よかった. Note the contrast with てよかった from card CH.7 · CR.10: 行ってよかった means I'm glad I went (it happened), while 行けばよかった means I wish I had gone (it did not). The ば conditional in its full generality is treated in card CH.15 · CR.8.

Reference — ば-form

遊ぶ (asobu)遊べば (asobeba)ぶ → べば
取る (toru)取れば (toreba)る → れば
買う (kau)買えば (kaeba)う → えば
食べる (taberu)食べれば (tabereba)る → れば
する (suru)すれば (sureba)する → すれば
くる (kuru)くれば (kureba)くる → くれば

もっと早く予約すればよかったです。

10 Volitional, Suggestions & Invitations
  1. ましょうLet's · Shall we — polite volitional
  2. ましょうかShall we · Shall I — polite volitional question
  3. ないか · ませんかWon't you · Would you like to — invitation
  4. The ましょう familyrecap
  5. う・ようLet's · I shall — casual volitional
  6. たらどうWhy don't you ~? · advice
N5CH.10 · CR.1
ましょう
(~mashou)
Let's · Shall we — polite volitional
Verb stem + ましょう
About

This grammar structure is used to suggest or propose doing something together. It can also serve as a personal declaration of intent rather than a suggestion to another person, expressing strong resolve — similar to "I shall" in English.

It is used exclusively in polite speech and has no casual equivalent.

ましょう attaches directly to the verb stem: 行き + ましょう → 行きましょう. Nothing is dropped or altered — the stem is used exactly as it stands.

Examplesshow ▶
モールに行きましょう！
Let's go to the mall!
energetic shared proposal; ましょう expresses collective will
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
映画を見ましょう。
Let's watch a movie.
softer joint suggestion; less pushy than てください
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
もう帰りましょう。
Let's head home now.
もう adds a sense of 'it's time now'; nudges the group to wrap up
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
はい、行きましょう！
Yes, let's go!
echoing the same verb back when agreeing is natural and enthusiastic
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
５キロ走りましょう！
Let's run five kilometres!
self-directed volitional; used as a personal declaration, not an invitation
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
N5CH.10 · CR.2
ましょうか
(~mashou ka)
Shall we · Shall I — polite volitional question
Verb stem + ましょうか
About

This grammar structure is used to suggest a shared action as an open question, or to offer to do something for someone. Depending on context, it translates as either Shall we...? or Shall I...?.

It is used exclusively in polite speech.

ましょうか is formed by adding the question particle か to ましょう. This turns the assertive volitional into a direct question — softer and more tentative than ましょう alone, and open to the other person's response.

ましょうか attaches directly to the verb stem: 行き + ましょうか → 行きましょうか. Nothing is dropped or altered — the stem is used exactly as it stands.

Examplesshow ▶
レストランまで車で行きましょうか？
Shall we go to the restaurant by car?
offers a specific logistical plan; listener expected to agree or counter
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
今夜走りましょうか？
Shall we run tonight?
lighter joint suggestion; inviting someone to share an activity tonight
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
みんなでイタリアに行きましょうか？
Shall we all go to Italy?
tentative long-range plan; 一緒に flags it as shared
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
手伝いましょうか？
Shall I help you?
offering to do something for someone else; 'shall I' = speaker would perform the action
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
ドアを開けましょうか？
Shall I open the door?
small polite service offer; common in formal or hospitality settings
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
N5CH.10 · CR.3
ないか · ませんか
(~nai ka · ~masen ka)
Won't you · Would you like to — invitation
Casual
Verb [ない]negative form
+ か
Formal
Verb stem + ませんか
About

This grammar structure is used to extend a polite invitation or suggest doing something together. Despite its negative grammatical form, ませんか carries a positive, inviting meaning — closer to Would you like to...? or Why don't we...? in English.

It is used exclusively in polite speech. Unlike ましょうか, which proposes a shared action or offers to do something, ませんか specifically extends an invitation to the other person — making it the more considerate and socially appropriate choice when suggesting plans.

ませんか attaches directly to the verb stem: 行き + ませんか → 行きませんか. Nothing is dropped or altered — the stem is used exactly as it stands.

The casual equivalent is ないか — the "Wanna?" of English. Formed by taking the verb's negative plain form (ない-form (negative form)) and adding か, it carries the same inviting nuance but is used only in informal settings with close friends, family, or peers of equal standing. It would sound out of place or rude with anyone you are not on familiar terms with.

Examplesshow ▶
明日は温泉に行きませんか？
Won't you go to the onsen with me tomorrow?
classic polite invitation; warmer and less presumptuous than ましょうか
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION
みんなでお祭りへ行きませんか？
Won't you come to the festival with us?
framing an outing as an invitation rather than a proposal
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION
いっしょに昼ごはんを食べませんか？
Would you like to eat lunch together?
very common workplace or school phrase for lunch invitations
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION
映画を見ませんか？
Would you like to watch a movie?
minimal invitation; open to whoever is present
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION
今晩うちで晩ごはんを食べませんか？
Would you like to have dinner at my place tonight?
hosting invitation; the most personal variant — come to my place
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE POLITE QUESTION
みんなで公園に行かないか？
Why don't we all go to the park?
casual masculine form; used among close male friends or peers of equal standing
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
何か食べないか？
Wanna grab something to eat?
very casual rhetorical offer; expecting the other person to want food too
VERB PRESENT NEGATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
Quick RecapCH.10 · CR.4
The ましょう family
ましょう · ましょうか · ませんか · ないか
Comparison
Form Register Function Feels like
ましょう POLITE Assert a shared action or personal resolve "Let's!" / "I shall!"
ましょうか POLITE Suggest as an open question; offer to do something for someone "Shall we?" / "Shall I?"
ませんか POLITE Invite the other person to do something "Would you like to?"
ないか PLAIN Same as ませんか, but informal "Wanna?"
When to use what
You're suggesting something and assuming the other person is in → ましょう
You're suggesting something but leaving it open, or offering to do something for someone → ましょうか
You're inviting someone and putting the choice in their hands → ませんか
Any of the above, but with a close friend or family member → ないか
N4CH.10 · CR.5
う・よう
(~ou · ~you)
Let's · I shall — casual volitional
う-verb (godan)
う-verbfinal kana → お-row
+ う
る-verb (ichidan)
る-verb [る] + よう
About

This grammar structure is the plain volitional form — the casual counterpart of ましょう (card CH.10 · CR.1): let's (A) as a suggestion, or I shall (A) as a statement of will. In fact ましょう is simply the polite conjugation of this form. Formation: う-verbs shift the final kana to its お-row equivalent and add う (書く → 書こう, 読む → 読もう); る-verbs replace る with よう (食べる → 食べよう); the irregulars are する → しよう and くる → こよう.

Three everyday uses: a suggestion to others (帰ろうよ — let's head home), a decision addressed to oneself, common in inner monologue (もう寝よう — I'll go to bed), and with か a soft offer or shared question (持とうか？ — shall I carry that?), the casual mirror of ましょうか.

泳ぐ (oyogu)泳ごう (oyogou)ぐ → ごう
死ぬ (shinu)死のう (shinou)ぬ → のう
遊ぶ (asobu)遊ぼう (asobou)ぶ → ぼう

買う (kau)買おう (kaou)う → おう

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

N4CH.10 · CR.6
たらどう
(~tara dou · ~tara dou desu ka)
Why don't you ~? · advice
Casual
Verb [たら]たら-form
+ どう？
Formal
Verb [たら]たら-form
+ どうですか？
About

This grammar structure is used to offer advice or a suggestion — why don't you…?, how about…?. It attaches どう — how to a verb in its たら conditional form — the past form plus ら — so the whole reads literally if you did (A), how (would it be)?: 先生に聞いたらどうですか — why don't you ask the teacher? The polite version ends in どうですか; casual speech uses bare どう, and だ or か may be added (たらどうだ？, たらどうか) to sharpen the question. In very casual conversation the whole tail can drop, leaving a trailing たら？ that carries the same meaning. The たら conditional itself is treated fully with the other conditionals later.

Use this pattern only when giving actual advice — the speaker is implying that the listener should act, so it does not work for invitations, which use ませんか instead. Delivered flatly, or aimed at someone who has failed to act, it can sound critical or sarcastic (たまには自分で調べたらどう？ — why don't you look it up yourself for once?), so tone matters. It combines naturally with てみる: てみたら？ — why not give it a try?

Examplesshow ▶
たらどうですか — Polite
疲れた顔をしていますね。今日は早く帰ったらどうですか？
You look tired. Why don't you go home early today?
gentle advice; literally "if you went home, how would it be?"
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
分からないところは、先生に聞いたらどうですか？
Why don't you ask the teacher about the parts you don't understand?
the speaker believes the listener should act
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
旅行の前に、いらない物を売ったらどうですか？

practical suggestion framed as a question
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
最近よく寝られないんですか。寝る前のコーヒーをやめたらどうですか？
You haven't been sleeping well lately? Why not stop the coffee before bed?
advising against a habit via やめる, still affirmative in form
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION
たらどう・たら — Casual
その服、着てみたらどう？
Why don't you try those clothes on?
てみる + たらどう — a very common pairing
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
二つとも気に入ったんでしょう？両方買ったらどう？
You like both of them, right? Why not buy both?
casual どう; rising intonation, no か
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
頭が痛いの？薬を飲んだら？
Got a headache? Why not take something?
clipped to bare たら — the どう is understood
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN QUESTION
心配ばかりしていないで、本人に確認したら？

11 Requests, Commands & Advice
  1. てくださいPlease do — polite request
  2. ないでくださいPlease don't — polite negative request
  3. たほうがいい ·ないほうがいいYou should · You'd better — advice
  4. てくれない？・てもらえない？Won't you? · Could you? — casual requests
  5. ていただけませんかCould you please ~ — humble request
  6. お〜くださいPlease do ~ — honorific request
  7. 命令形・なさいDo ~ · Do it! — commands
  8. ように言うTo tell someone to · indirect commands
N5CH.11 · CR.1
てください
(~te kudasai)
Please do — polite request
Verb [て]て-form
+ ください
About

This grammar structure is used to politely ask or instruct someone to do something. It is the standard way to make a request in Japanese, equivalent to please do [something] in English.

ください is the imperative form of くださる, the honorific equivalent of くれる — to give. In this construction it functions simply as please do — always attaching to the て-form of a verb, never the dictionary or ます-form.

To use てください, conjugate the verb into its て-form and attach ください directly.

In casual speech, ください can be dropped entirely, leaving just the て-form as a softened request. This is common with close friends and family, and works for both genders.

About て — casual requestN4

In casual speech てください is regularly shortened to the bare て-form: 窓を開けて。 — open the window (please). The result is friendly but firmer than it looks — closer to a soft order than a request — so it is best kept for friends, family and people of lower status, never for superiors. Sentence-final position is what signals the request reading; softeners like ね and よ round it off.

A sentence-final て does not always ask for anything. Mid-thought, a drawn-out て (駅まで走っていって…) simply means the speaker has not finished the sentence. て also closes apology phrases — 遅れてすみません, sorry for being late — where the て-clause is the reason being apologised for, not a request.

Examplesshow ▶
ちょっと待ってください。

ubiquitous polite request; ちょっと softens the imposition

ドアを開けてください。
Please open the door.
direct instruction phrased politely; typical in service or guidance contexts
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE

Please write your name.

VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
もう一度言ってください。
Please say it again.
asking for repetition; essential phrase in language learning contexts
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
ここに座ってください。
Please sit here.
directing someone to a specific seat; hospitality or classroom context
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE
ちょっと待って。
Wait a sec.
casual te-form request; works as an informal imperative between close people
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
テレビを消して。
Turn off the TV.
domestic plain request; te-form alone between close family or friends
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
て — casual requestN4
悪いけど、この荷物を二階に運んで。
Sorry, but carry this luggage up to the second floor, will you?
ください dropped — friendly but firm; 悪いけど cushions it
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

Close the windows before you go out.
bare て at sentence end — the request reading
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

ね softens the shortened request
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
ちょっとこのスープの味を見て。
Taste this soup for me a second.
ちょっと + て — the everyday small favour
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN
N5CH.11 · CR.2
ないでください
(~naide kudasai)
Please don't — polite negative request
Verb [ない]negative form
+ でください
About

This grammar structure is used to politely ask someone not to do something. It is the negative equivalent of てください.

Despite the visual similarity to てください, the で here does not come from the て-form. It attaches to the negative plain form (ない-form (negative form)) of a verb, making it a structurally distinct construction.

To use ないでください, take the verb's ない-form (negative form) (negative plain form) and attach でください directly.

In casual speech, ください can be dropped, leaving just ないで as a softened negative request. Used with close friends and family.

About ないで — casual requestN4

In casual speech ないでください loses its ください the same way てください does: a bare sentence-final ないで。 means don't (A) — friendly in tone but firm in substance, typical of parents, teachers and close friends: 廊下では走らないで。 Softeners ね and よ take the edge off.

The shape is identical to the without doing use of ないで (て-form Constructions chapter) — what signals the request reading is that the sentence simply ends there, with nothing following.

たほうがいい ·
ないほうがいい
(~ta hou ga ii · ~nai hou ga ii)
You should · You'd better — advice

About

This grammar structure is used to give direct advice or make a strong suggestion — implying that not following it may lead to negative consequences.

The verb form is fixed and determined by polarity, not by tense. Affirmative advice always takes the た-form (past form); negative advice always takes the present ない-form (negative form) — never the past negative なかった. This is one of the most common mistakes with this structure.

方 (ほう) literally means way or direction — the phrase suggests that one specific course of action is simply the better way. Using the dictionary form instead of the た-form (past form) is possible but shifts the meaning from direct advice to general opinion.

To use ほうがいい, attach the verb's た-form (past form) + ほうがいい(です) for affirmative advice, or the verb's ない-form (negative form) + ほうがいい(です) for negative advice.

N4CH.11 · CR.4
てくれない？・てもらえない？
(~te kurenai? · ~te moraenai?)
Won't you? · Could you? — casual requests
Won't you
Verb [て]て-form
+
くれない(か)？(か) optional
Could you
Verb [て]て-form
+
もらえない(か)？(か) optional
About

This grammar structure is used to make casual requests through a negative question, spoken with rising intonation. てくれない？ comes from てくれる — would you not do (A) for me? — and てもらえない？ from てもらえる, the potential form of てもらう — could I not have you do (A) for me?. The direction of the favour mirrors the benefactive trio: with くれる the other person is the giver, with もらう the speaker is the receiver. Asking in the negative leaves the listener more room to refuse, which is what makes these softer than a direct request.

The question particle か may be added (貸してくれないか？) — the request sounds slightly more polite, and a touch firmer, with it. To ask someone not to do something, the ないで form slots in before either verb: 言わないでくれない？ — could you not tell anyone?. On the politeness ladder these two sit at the casual end — the polite counterparts てくれませんか, てもらえませんか and above are gathered in the reference table of card CH.11 · CR.5. The bare command てくれ below them is considered rather rude and is best avoided.

N4CH.11 · CR.5
ていただけませんか
(~te itadakemasen ka)
Could you please ~ — humble request
Formal / neutral
Verb [て]て-form
+ もらえませんか
Most formal
Verb [て]て-form
+ いただけませんか
About

This grammar structure is used to politely ask someone to do something for you — the most formal and respectful of the request forms. ていただけませんか is the humble-speech version of てもらえませんか: いただく is the humble equivalent of もらう, put into its potential form and asked in the polite negative — literally could I not humbly receive (A)?. The indirectness is the politeness: it softens the request and implies deference and gratitude, which makes it the right form toward people of higher status, strangers, hosts, and anyone outside your circle. It is also the correct pattern for requests that benefit the speaker, where お〜ください would be wrong: 塩を取っていただけませんか — would you kindly pass me the salt?.

One step down, てもらえませんか and てくれませんか stay courteous but suit everyday, semi-formal situations — store clerks, host-family members, colleagues; てくださいませんか, built on くださる, sits between them and the top. The casual floor of the ladder lives in card CH.11 · CR.4. いただく is regularly written with its kanji 頂く — literally to be topped with (雪を頂いた山 — a snow-capped mountain), an acknowledgement that the favour comes from above.

てくれませんかくれるSemi-politeClose acquaintances, informal tone

てくれない？くれるCasualClose relationships; often male, commanding tone

N4CH.11 · CR.6
お〜ください
(o~kudasai)
Please do ~ — honorific request
Standard
お + Verb stem + ください
する verb
ご + Noun (する) + ください
About

This grammar structure is an honorific request — please do (A). ください is the imperative form of くださる, itself the honorific equivalent of くれる, so the pattern politely conveys please do (A) for me. It works much like なさい in role, but it is far more polite and may be used toward almost anybody, regardless of whether they stand above or below the speaker. It is the standard voice of public announcements, written notices, and customer service — train stations, stores, airports — where it gives respectful instructions or encouragement intended for the listener's own benefit: 切符をお取りください — please take a ticket.

Formation: お + the stem + ください (お書きください, お並びください); する-verbs take ご before the noun instead (ご注意ください, ご利用ください). Where a dedicated honorific verb exists, it replaces the stem entirely: ご覧ください for 見る, お召し上がりください for 食べる, お休みください for 寝る. The set phrase お気をつけください is also common and accepted, treating 気をつける as one unit.

One important restriction: this form is for the listener's benefit, never the speaker's. 塩をお取りください sounds like please graciously take some salt — it does not mean pass me the salt. A request that benefits the speaker takes ていただけませんか instead: 塩を取っていただけませんか.

N4CH.11 · CR.7
命令形・なさい
(meireikei · ~nasai)
Do ~ · Do it! — commands
Very casual — 命令形
う-verb (godan)
う-verbfinal kana → え-row
る-verb (ichidan)
る-verb [る] + ろ
Authority — なさい
Verb stem + なさい
About

This card covers the two direct command forms. 命令形 — the imperative: the bluntest form in the language. う-verbs shift the final kana to its え-row equivalent (行く → 行け); る-verbs replace る with ろ (食べる → 食べろ); irregulars are する → しろ, くる → こい, and くれる → くれ (as in 手を貸してくれ). Abrasive in conversation, it belongs to emergencies (逃げろ！), road signs (止まれ), cheering (頑張れ！) and rough masculine speech, where a final よ softens it slightly.

なさい: the verb stem plus なさい gives an authoritative but not rude instruction — 早く寝なさい. It flows from parent to child, teacher to student, and through exam papers (答えなさい); the tone is you should obey, because I know better, which is why it is rarely used between equals or toward strangers.

For ordinary requests the ladder runs — bluntest first:

命令形 — blunt; emergencies, signs and rough speech
なさい — authority speaking downward: parent, teacher
て — casual request between equals
てください — the standard polite request

N4CH.11 · CR.8
ように言う
(~you ni iu)
To tell someone to · indirect commands
Sentence structure
Personlistener
+ に +
Verbplain present
+ ように言う
About

This grammar structure is used to report telling, asking, or ordering someone to do something — an indirect command. ように is the adverbial form of the auxiliary ようだ, meaning in such a way that (A), and 言う supplies the act of speaking: 子供に水をこぼさないように言う — to tell the child not to spill the water, literally to speak in such a way that the water is not spilled. The instructed action stands before ように as a verb in the plain non-past form — very often the ない form, since instructions are frequently about what not to do — and the person receiving the instruction is marked with に. This is the same ように that expresses purpose and appears in ように祈る; here the outcome is brought about by someone's words rather than by effort or prayer.

The speech verb can be swapped to fit the speech act: 言う is the most versatile — depending on tone and context it covers telling, requesting, or ordering. 頼む makes it explicitly a request (破らないように頼む — to ask someone not to rip it), while 命じる makes it a formal order from a position of authority. Note the contrast with direct quotation: ように言う reports the substance of an instruction, whereas quoting someone's actual words uses the quotation particle と, treated in card CH.16 · CR.2.

てもいい
(~te mo ii · ~te mo ii desu)
It's okay to, May · Can — permission

+ もいいですか

Noun

About

This grammar structure is used to give or ask for permission to do something — equivalent to you may, it's okay to, or can I? in English. Adding か turns it into a permission request: てもいいですか (Is it okay if I...? · May I...?).

For verbs, attach もいい to the て-form. Some verbs use で instead of て in the て-form — this follows normal て-form conjugation rules and carries through into this construction.

For い-adjectives, drop the final い, add く, then attach てもいい: for example, 遅い → 遅く → 遅くてもいい. For な-adjectives and nouns, attach でもいい directly to the stem — the で here is the conjunctive form of the copula, not the て-form.

In casual speech, も is sometimes dropped — ていい or でいい — carrying the same meaning but sounding more direct. Keep the も unless you know the listener well.

N5CH.12 · CR.2
なければいけない ·
なければいけません
(~nakereba ikenai · ~nakereba ikemasen)
Must · Have to — obligation
Very casual
Verb
Verb [ない]negative form
+ きゃ
Casual
Verb
Verb [ない]negative form
+ ければいけない
Formal
Verb
Verb [ない]negative form
+ ければいけません
About

This grammar structure is used to express obligation — that something must or has to be done. It implies that not doing it would cause trouble, inconvenience, or be wrong.

Despite its negative grammatical form, this structure carries a positive meaning — must do, not must not do. Both forms are built from the verb's ない-form (negative form): drop the final い, then attach ければいけない (casual) or ければいけません (polite).

To use なければいけない · なければいけません, take the verb's ない-form (negative form), drop the final い, and attach ければいけない or ければいけません directly.

The very casual contraction なきゃ carries the same meaning and is extremely common in spoken Japanese — the equivalent of gotta in English. It is formed the same way, replacing ければいけない entirely with きゃ.

N5CH.12 · CR.3
てはいけない ·
てはいけません
(~te wa ikenai · ~te wa ikemasen)
Must not · May not — prohibition
Very casual
Verb — て-form
Verb [て] + ちゃだめ
Verb — で-form
Verb [で] + じゃだめ
Casual — contracted
Verb — て-form
Verb [て] + ちゃいけない
Verb — で-form

Casual
Verb — て-form
Verb [て] + はいけない
Verb — で-form
Verb [で] + はいけない
Formal
Verb — て-form
Verb [て] + はいけません
Verb — で-form
Verb [で] + はいけません
About

This grammar structure is used to prohibit or strongly forbid an action — expressing that something must not or is not allowed to be done. The は in this construction is the topic particle, pronounced wa, not ha.

Both forms attach to the て-form of a verb. は is the topic particle, and いけない · いけません means it won't do · it's not acceptable. Together they convey: doing X is not acceptable. There is no double negative — the construction is negative in form but singular in meaning.

To use てはいけません · てはいけない, conjugate the verb into its て-form and attach はいけません or はいけない directly. Note that if the verb's て-form ends in で rather than て, the construction becomes ではいけません · ではいけない accordingly.

In casual speech, ては and では both contract by dropping は: ては becomes ちゃ, and では becomes じゃ. Which form appears depends purely on the verb's て-form — if it ends in て, use ちゃいけない; if it ends in で, use じゃいけない. The word だめ goes one step further, dropping いけない entirely and expressing the same prohibition in the most casual register.

Examplesshow ▶
ここでタバコを吸ってはいけません。
You must not smoke here.
public prohibition announcement; rule enforcement register

About

This grammar structure is used to state that something is not necessary — you don't have to (A) or it's okay not to (A). It is the mirror image of the permission pattern in card CH.12 · CR.1: where てもいい allows doing, なくてもいい allows not doing — literally even if (A) is not done, it's fine, the concessive ても run through the negative. Verbs take なくてもいい, い-adjectives くなくてもいい, and な-adjectives and nouns じゃなくてもいい (formal ではなくてもいい). It softens an obligation rather than forbidding anything — contrast なければいけない — must and てはいけない — must not from cards CH.12 · CR.2 and CH.12 · CR.3.

In casual speech the も can drop — なくていい — with no change of meaning, only a friendlier tone: 今日はもう戻らなくていいよ. As a question, なくてもいいですか asks for confirmation that skipping the action is acceptable.

N4CH.12 · CR.5
ないと
(~nai to)
Must · Have to — contracted obligation
Verb
Verb [ない]negative form
+
と(いけない)(いけない) optional
About

This grammar structure is used to express obligation in casual speech — must, have to. It is built from the negative form of a verb plus the particle と in its if meaning: ないといけない reads literally if (A) is not done, it cannot go, and the double negative resolves into a positive obligation — (A) must be done. Because と presents its outcome as automatic and inevitable, ないと carries real force: it is the natural choice for things that simply must happen — obeying the law, meeting a deadline, common sense. The conditional と itself is treated fully with the other conditionals later.

In conversation ないといけない is regularly clipped to bare ないと, left trailing at the end of the sentence with the rest understood: もう行かないと。 — I've got to go. だめ can replace いけない for an even more casual ないとだめ. Note that ならない is generally not used after ないと — ないとならない is best avoided. The full-length obligation forms なければいけない and なければならない say the same thing in a fuller, more formal shape and are covered in card CH.12 · CR.2; the opposite meaning — don't have to — is なくてもいい, covered in card CH.12 · CR.4.

N4CH.12 · CR.6
が必要・必要がある
(~ga hitsuyou · hitsuyou ga aru)
Need · It is necessary to
Noun
Noun + が必要
Verb (nominalized)
Verbplain present
+ が必要
Verb
Verbplain present
+ 必要がある
About

This grammar structure is used to state that something is needed or necessary — need, it is necessary to. Both constructions are built on 必要, necessity, and differ only in what they attach to.

Usage 1 — が必要: a noun takes が必要 directly, with だ or です closing the sentence as usual: 海外旅行にはパスポートが必要です — you need a passport for overseas travel. Because this shape accepts only nouns, a verb must first be nominalized with こと: 鍵をかけることが必要だ — it is necessary to lock up. In casual speech both が and だ are sometimes dropped (眼鏡が必要), but keeping が makes it clear what is needed.

Usage 2 — 必要がある: a verb in its plain form takes 必要がある whole, with no nominalization: 勉強をする必要がある — it is necessary to study. The mechanism is transparent — the verb modifies the noun 必要, and がある states that this need exists, so the whole literally reads the need of doing (A) exists. It leans slightly formal, and is the natural choice when the necessary thing is an action rather than an object.

The negative uses ない in place of ある: 必要がない / 必要がありません — there is no need to, a plain statement that something can be skipped. Contrast this with なくてもいい, which grants a waiver more softly — you don't have to.

Quick RecapCH.12 · CR.7
Obligation, necessity & permission
てもいい · なければいけない · てはいけない · なくてもいい · が必要 · ないと
Comparison
Form Register Function Feels like
〜てもいい POLITE Seek or grant permission "May I?" / "You can"
〜なければいけない POLITE Express obligation — no real choice "Have to / Must"
〜てはいけない POLITE Express prohibition — not allowed "Must not / Can't"
〜なくてもいいN4 POLITE Waive an obligation — the duty does not apply "You don't have to"
〜が必要 · 必要があるN4 POLITE State that a thing or an action is required "~ is necessary / You need to"
〜ないとN4 PLAIN Same obligation, clipped for conversation "I've got to…"
When to use what
Asking if something is okay, or telling someone they can → 〜てもいい
Something is obligatory — external pressure, duty, or rule → 〜なければいけない
Something is forbidden — a rule or social norm prohibits it → 〜てはいけない
The duty simply does not apply — permission not to bother → 〜なくてもいいN4
Naming the requirement itself, often on forms and notices → 〜が必要 · 必要があるN4
Saying it quickly in conversation, trailing off before いけない → 〜ないとN4
The classic confusion: 〜なければいけない is "must", while 〜てはいけない is "must not" — a prohibition, not the opposite of "must"
The true opposite of "must" is 〜なくてもいい — it lifts the duty rather than forbidding the actN4
13 Giving & Receiving
  1. あげるTo give — away from speaker
  2. くれるTo give — toward speaker
  3. もらうTo receive — from someone
  4. てあげる・てくれる・てもらうTo do for · To do for me · To have done — favours
  5. てくれてありがとうThank you for ~ing
  6. Which way does it go?recap
N5CH.13 · CR.1
あげる
(ageru)
To give — away from speaker
Casual
Giver は · が
+
Recipient に
+
Object を
+ あげる
Formal
Giver は · が
+
Recipient に
+
Object を
+ あげます
About

This grammar structure is used to express giving when the transfer goes away from the speaker — either the speaker gives something to someone else, or one third party gives to another third party. The critical constraint: あげる is never used when the recipient is the speaker or someone psychologically close to the speaker. That direction uses a different verb.

Three participants, three particles: the giver takes は or が, the recipient takes に, and the object takes を. Word order is flexible — the particles carry the meaning, not the position. All three arrangements in the examples below express the same thing.

The kanji form 上げる exists but in the giving sense あげる is written in hiragana in everyday contexts.

Examplesshow ▶
私は田中さんにこのカメラをあげます。
I'll give this camera to Tanaka-san.
standard giving; speaker gives outward to a third party; あげる flows away from speaker

田中さんにお土産をあげますか？
Are you going to give Tanaka-san a souvenir?
asking if someone will give a souvenir to a specific person
VERB PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE POLITE QUESTION

I'm not giving him any more presents.
withholding future gifts; は emphasizes the contrast

N5CH.13 · CR.2
くれる
(kureru)
To give — toward speaker
Casual
Giver は · が
+
Recipient に
+
Object を
+ くれる
Formal
Giver は · が
+
Recipient に
+
Object を
+ くれます
About

This grammar structure is used to express giving when the transfer goes toward the speaker — someone gives something to the speaker, or to someone emotionally close to the speaker such as a family member or close friend. The critical constraint: くれる is never used when both the giver and recipient are outside the speaker's psychological in-group — people the speaker has no personal connection to. That direction uses あげる.

The particle structure is the same as あげる: the giver takes は or が, the recipient takes に, and the object takes を. In practice, the recipient (私に) is almost always dropped — it is obvious from context that the speaker is the one receiving. The giver can also be omitted when clear from context, leaving just the object and くれる.

N5CH.13 · CR.3
もらう
(morau)
To receive — from someone
Casual
Recipient は · が
+
Giver に · から
+
Object を
+ もらう
Formal
Recipient は · が
+
Giver に · から
+
Object を
+ もらいます
About

This grammar structure is used to express receiving something from someone. The focus is on the recipient, not the giver. Unlike あげる and くれる where に marks the recipient, in もらう the particles flip: は or が marks the recipient (the one performing the act of receiving), and に or から marks the giver.

Both に and から can mark the giver. に feels more personal and is used when there is a direct human relationship involved. から emphasises the source or origin — from in the sense of a point of departure — and can be used with institutions or less personal sources.

As with くれる, the recipient is often omitted when it is the speaker and obvious from context. The giver can also be dropped when clear or irrelevant to the point being made.

Examplesshow ▶
毎年、会社からカレンダーをもらいます。
I receive a calendar from the company every year.

N4CH.13 · CR.4
てあげる・てくれる・てもらう
(~te ageru · ~te kureru · ~te morau)
To do for · To do for me · To have done — favours
てあげる — I do for others
GiverI / my side
+ は +
Receiversomeone else
+ に +
Verb [て]て-form
+ あげる
てくれる — someone does for me
Giversomeone else
+ が +
Receiverme / my side
+ に +
Verb [て]て-form
+ くれる
てもらう — I get someone to do
Receiverme / my side
+ は +
Giversomeone else
+ に +
Verb [て]て-form
+ もらう
About

This grammar structure family expresses doing a favour or receiving one: the て-form combines with the giving-and-receiving verbs あげる, くれる and もらう, and the choice between them is decided entirely by who does the favour and whose perspective the sentence takes. A sentence without them states a bare fact — 妹にお金を貸しました — I lent my sister money — while 貸してあげました adds that it was done for her.

てあげる — outward: the speaker (or their side) does the favour; the receiver is marked with に. Caution: because it openly labels one's own act as a favour, てあげる easily sounds patronising — never use it about things done for superiors.
てくれる — inward: someone else does the favour for the speaker or their circle; the giver takes が, and gratitude is built in. As a casual request it becomes てくれる？ — will you… for me? or the very casual てくれ.
てもらう — received: the receiver is the subject and the doer takes に — I got/had (person) do (A). It is the natural choice for services (医者に見てもらう) and slightly more direct than くれる.

When the verb has no built-in recipient, のために supplies one: 姉が私のためにケーキを焼いてくれた. The polite equivalents くださる, いただく and 差し上げる belong to honorific speech, which sits outside this module; the humble request ていただけませんか, built on いただく, is covered in card CH.11 · CR.5.

Reference
FormBeneficiaryDoerFeels like
てあげる someone else I · my side "I did them a favour"
てくれる me · my circle someone else "they did me a favour"
てもらう me · my circle someone else "I got them to do it"

N4CH.13 · CR.5
てくれてありがとう
(~te kurete arigatou · ~te kudasatte arigatou gozaimasu)
Thank you for ~ing
Casual
Verb [て]て-form
+ くれてありがとう
Formal / honorific
Verb [て]て-form
+ くださってありがとうございます
About

This grammar structure is used to thank someone for a specific action done for the speaker's benefit — thank you for ~ing. It builds directly on てくれる from the giving-and-receiving family: the favour is named by a verb in its て-form, くれる marks it as done for the speaker and itself takes the て-form, and ありがとう closes with the thanks: 手伝ってくれてありがとう — literally you helped me, and (I'm) grateful. Because the pattern asserts a personal favour, it is reserved for actions that clearly benefit the speaker or their circle — thanking a clerk this way for simply doing their job sounds odd; plain ありがとうございます covers ordinary etiquette.

Register is set by the giving verb. くれてありがとう is the casual-to-standard version, used with friends, family, and equals. Speaking to someone of higher status — a professor, a boss, a stranger — くれる is replaced by its honorific counterpart くださる: てくださってありがとうございます, or ありがとうございました once the favour is fully in the past. くださる itself belongs to honorific speech, which sits outside this module. The verb before くれて can also be a continuing ている state: 覚えていてくれてありがとう — thank you for remembering me — thanking someone for an ongoing kindness rather than a single act.

Comparison
Form Who gives Who benefits Feels like

When to use what
The top three hand over a thing; the bottom three hand over an action — same three directions, attached to the て-form
Handing something to somebody outside your circle → あげる
Anything coming toward you or your family → くれる, never あげる — direction decides this, not politeness
The same event told with yourself as the subject → もらう: 姉がくれた and 姉にもらった describe one gift from two angles
Somebody did you a kindness — the everyday workhorse of the six → 〜てくれるN4
You arranged for it to be done, often paying or asking → 〜てもらうN4
Announcing your own good deed with 〜てあげる can sound patronising — Japanese usually leaves it unsaidN4
Thanking somebody for the favour itself → 〜てくれてありがとうN4
14 Potential & Ability
  1. のが上手 · のが下手Good at · Bad at — expressing skill level
  2. れる・られるCan · Be able to — potential form
  3. ことができるCan · Be able to — formal potential
  4. 見える・聞こえるCan see · Can hear — visible and audible
N5CH.14 · CR.1
のが上手 · のが下手
(~no ga jouzu · ~no ga heta)
Good at · Bad at — expressing skill level
Casual
good at
Verb dictionary form
+ のが上手だ
bad at
Verb dictionary form
+ のが下手だ
Formal
good at
Verb dictionary form
+ のが上手です
bad at
Verb dictionary form
+ のが下手です
About

This grammar structure is used to express how skilled or unskilled someone is at performing an action. 上手 means good at and 下手 means bad at. Both are な-adjectives and conjugate normally.

の nominalizes the verb phrase — it turns the action into a noun-like concept that can be the subject of the predicate. が then marks that noun as the subject of the feeling of skill or lack of it. The verb always stays in the dictionary form, regardless of tense. Tense is expressed by conjugating 上手 or 下手 instead.

One social note: saying 上手ですね directly to someone about their own ability can come across as condescending — as if you're surprised or judging from above. It is safer when talking about a third person or when asked for an opinion.

N4CH.14 · CR.2
れる・られる
(~reru · ~rareru)
Can · Be able to — potential form
う-verb (godan)
う-verbfinal kana → え-row
+ る
る-verb (ichidan)
る-verb [る] + られる
About

This grammar structure is the potential form — can (A), be able to (A), whether by skill, circumstance, or permission. う-verbs shift the final kana to its え-row equivalent and add る (読む → 読める); る-verbs replace る with られる (食べる → 食べられる); する has no potential form of its own and uses できる instead, while くる becomes こられる. Every potential form then behaves as a regular る-verb, conjugating through all the usual tenses.

First, the object of a transitive verb usually switches from を to が: 漢字が読める; both particles are possible, but が is the natural choice, and できる takes only が. Other particles are untouched (山に登れる).

Second, dropping the ら — 食べれる, 見れる — is common in casual speech but nonstandard; as noted in card CH.19 · CR.2, such ら抜き forms can only be potential, never passive.

Third, ability in Japanese is felt as something beyond one's control, which is why the potential pairs so naturally with reason-なくて (買えなくて残念だ). For ambient perception, 見える・聞こえる (card CH.14 · CR.4) replace the potential; the formal alternative ことができる is card CH.14 · CR.3.

N4CH.14 · CR.3
ことができる
(~koto ga dekiru)
Can · Be able to — formal potential
Verb
Verbdictionary form
+ ことができる
Noun
Noun + ができる
About

This grammar structure is the second way to say can (A): the nominaliser こと turns the dictionary-form verb into a noun phrase, and ができる states that this thing is possible — literally (A)-ing is doable. The meaning is identical to the conjugated potential form (card CH.14 · CR.2), but ことができる reads as slightly more formal and polite, which makes it the preferred choice in writing, rules, signs and announcements. It also spares する verbs the awkward double する: 利用することができる, never 利用しできる.

When (A) is already a noun, こと is unnecessary and ができる attaches directly: 運転ができる — can drive. できる takes only が, never を. The shape parallels the experience pattern in card CH.8 · CR.7 — same こと, different closer.

N4CH.14 · CR.4
見える・聞こえる
(mieru · kikoeru)
Can see · Can hear — visible and audible
Noun + が + 見える / 聞こえる
About

This pair of intransitive verbs describes what is visible and audible: 見える — to be visible · can see, 聞こえる — to be audible · can hear. The thing seen or heard — the source — is marked with が: 海が見える, 音が聞こえる. Historically they are old potential conjugations of 見る and 聞く, but today they behave as independent verbs.

The contrast with the true potentials 見られる and 聞ける is about effort: 見える・聞こえる mean the sight or sound simply reaches you, no concentration required (a mountain from the window, a neighbour's piano), while the potential forms describe a deliberate ability or opportunity (being able to watch a film, getting to hear a lecture). The pair also covers appearance — looks/sounds (like) — with the manner marked adverbially: い-adjectives take their く form (若く見える — looks young), な-adjectives and nouns take に.

  17. かどうか・〜かWhether or not · embedded questions
  18. し〜しAnd · listing reasons
  19. ようにSo that · In order to
  20. くはNot exactly ~ · contrastive く
N5CH.15 · CR.1
〜前に
(~mae ni)
Before ~
before doing — temporal
Verb dictionary form
+ 前に
About

This grammar structure is used to express that one action happens before another. The verb directly before 前に is always in the dictionary form, even when the main verb of the sentence is in the past. The subordinate action described by 前に has not yet happened at the time of reference — so past tense is not used there regardless of the overall sentence tense.

N5CH.15 · CR.2
〜てから
(~te kara)
After doing ~ · Once ~ is done
Verb [て] て-form
+ から + Main clause
About

This grammar structure is used to express that one action is fully completed before another begins — equivalent to after doing A, B or once A is done, B. The emphasis is on A enabling or unlocking B.

It can also describe a state that has continued since A happened — 猫が死んでから、さびしいです.

Critical distinction: 食べてから = after eating; 食べるから = because I will eat; 食べたから = because I ate. Only the て-form + から gives after.

N5CH.15 · CR.3
から
(kara)
From ~ · Because ~
Spatial / Temporal
starting point Noun
+ から
Reason — Because
Verb / い-adjective
plain form Verb
/
い-adjplain form
+ から
な-adjective / Noun
な-adj / Noun + だ + から
About

This grammar structure is used to mark a starting point in space or time, or to express a reason. The underlying meaning is always from — from a location, from a time, or from a reason (because).

From (spatial · temporal): attaches directly to a place or time noun. No だ is added — doing so would shift the meaning to because. Often paired with まで to mark a full range: 9時から5時まで — from 9 to 5.

Because (reason): the reason clause comes first, followed by から and then the result clause. Verbs and い-adjectives attach directly in plain form. Nouns and な-adjectives require だ before から in the present affirmative only.

The reason clause before から can also use polite form in formal speech. から is softer and more subjective than ので, which carries a more formal and objective tone.

N5CH.15 · CR.4
まで
(made)
Until ~ · Up to ~ · As far as ~
endpoint — time / location / quantity
Noun + まで
range — from ~ to ~
Noun A + から + Noun B + まで
About

This grammar structure is used to mark the endpoint of time, location, or quantity. It is the natural counterpart to から, and the two are frequently paired: から marks the starting point, まで marks the end.

The noun before まで determines the type of endpoint: a time word gives until that time, a location noun gives as far as that place, and a number or quantity gives up to that amount.

About まで — "even" & "up to"N4

The "until" you already know is only half of まで. Its core is always (A) まで (B) — A is a limit or extent, B the noteworthy part. When A is something surprising or extreme, まで reads as even: 弟は私のケーキまで食べた — my brother even ate my cake — the cake marks how far things went.

With quantities, the same limit-idea becomes up to: 百まで数える — count up to 100, 2時間まで無料 — free for up to two hours. One particle, one meaning — a boundary — read three ways in English.

This grammar structure is used to express that Clause B continues until the event described in Clause A occurs. The verb before まで is always dictionary form regardless of the overall sentence tense. Tense is expressed in the predicate of Clause B.

Quick RecapCH.15 · CR.6
Time boundaries
前に · てから · から · まで
Comparison
Form Attaches to Function Feels like
〜前に Verb (dictionary form) / Noun + の One action happens before another "Before ~"
〜てから Verb (て form) One action happens only after another is completed "After ~ / Once ~ is done"
から Noun (time / place) Starting point of an action or span "From ~"
まで Noun (time / place / quantity) / Verb (dictionary form) Endpoint — the action continues up to that limit "Until ~ / Up to ~"
When to use what
Doing something before another action or event → 〜前に
Doing something after — and only once — another action is finished → 〜てから
Marking where or when something starts → から
Marking where or when something stops — or until an event happens (verb + まで) → まで
Full span in one breath — from A to B → から〜まで
前に / てから order two actions; から / まで mark the boundaries of a single one
N4CH.15 · CR.7
時
(~toki)
When · at the time of
Verb
Verbplain form
+ 時
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ 時
な-adjective
な-adj + な時
Noun
Noun + の時
About

This grammar structure is used to say when something happens or happened — when (A), (B). 時 (とき) is a noun meaning time, so the clause before it simply modifies it the way any clause modifies a noun: verbs attach in the plain form, い-adjectives attach directly, な-adjectives keep their な, and nouns take の (子供の時 — when I was a child). Adding に — 時に — pins the timing more precisely to a specific occasion.

The tense inside the 時 clause is relative to the main clause, not to now — the key rule of this pattern. Use the present if, at the moment of (B), (A) has not yet happened or is still in progress: 日本に行く時、ビザを取りました — I got the visa when (= before) going to Japan; the trip had not happened yet at visa time, so 行く stays present even though the sentence is past. Use the past if (A) was already complete: 日本に行った時、着物を買いました — the buying happened after arrival. For an action ongoing while (B) occurs, use ている: テレビを見ている時、電話がありました. Beware verbs of movement here: 行っている時 means while being there, not while on the way.

One further caution: the 時 clause should describe an event, interval, or condition — not a static identification. Something like 帰った時に火曜日だった — the time I went home was Tuesday sounds unnatural, because 時 frames one thing happening in the span of another rather than simply labelling a moment.

Reference — tense in the 時 clause
Situation at (B)時-clause formExample
(A) has not happened yetVerb [る] + 時行く時、ビザを取る
(A) already completedVerb [た] + 時着いた時、連絡した
(A) ongoing during (B)Verb [ている] + 時見ている時、電話が来た
(A) is a stateAdj / Noun + 時寒い時・子供の時

I'll buy a new suitcase when I go to Japan.
the buying comes before the trip — 行く stays present

If A then B — hypothetical conditional

About

This grammar structure expresses a hypothetical conditional — if (A), then (B). ば presents (B) as the guaranteed or natural consequence of (A) being met, which gives it a distinctive flavor among the conditionals: it is at home in general truths, logical relationships, and advice, and it leans toward favourable outcomes — 早く寝れば、元気になります — if you sleep early, you'll feel better.

う-verbs shift the final syllable to its え-row sound before ば (書く → 書けば),
る-verbs replace る with れば; the irregulars give すれば and くれば,
い-adjectives replace the final い with ければ (安ければ),
every ない — the verb negative and the adjective negative alike — conjugates the same way: 行かなければ, 高くなければ,
な-adjectives and nouns take なら (optionally ならば) or the formal であれば.

Because ば implies a desirable or logical result, sentences pairing it with bad outcomes sound unnatural even when technically correct — other conditionals cover that ground. Its advice use often ends in reassurance: 先生に聞けばいいんですよ — all you have to do is ask the teacher. Two relatives are already covered: ばよかった builds regret from this same form, and ないと handles obligation where なければ-style conditionals meet いけない. The neighbouring conditionals たら, と, and the broader uses of なら are treated in cards CH.15 · CR.9, CH.15 · CR.10 and CH.15 · CR.11.

(~tara)
If · When — completed-trigger conditional
Verb
Verb [た]plain past
+ ら
い-adjective
い-adj [かった]plain past
+ ら
な-adjective

Noun

About

This grammar structure is the most flexible of the Japanese conditionals — a halfway point between "if" and "when". It is formed on the past form plus ら, and its core meaning follows from that: once (A) is completed, (B) follows.

Usage 1 — condition: if (A), then (B) for possible situations: 時間があったら、手伝ってください — if you have time, please help. Unlike と, clause (B) is free to be a request, suggestion, or intention.

Usage 2 — sequence: when / as soon as (A) for events the speaker expects to happen: 家に帰ったら、連絡します — I'll get in touch when I get home.

Usage 3 — hypothetical: unreal or contrary-to-fact conditions and their speculative results: お金があったら、世界中を旅行するんだけど — if I had money, I'd travel the world.

One restriction holds across all three uses: (B) must occur after — or at the same time as — (A). A sentence like "if you have an exam next week, you should study this weekend" cannot use たら, because the studying comes first. Compared with its siblings: ば leans toward general truths and favourable logic, と states automatic consequences, while たら handles one-time events and mixed outcomes freely — which is why the advice pattern たらどう is built on it, and why もし most often pairs with it.

(~to)
Whenever — natural-consequence conditional
Verb/い-adjplain present
+ と
Noun/な-adj + だと
About

This grammar structure is used for results that always follow their trigger — whenever (A), (B), if (A), (B) without fail. As a conjunction particle, と states that (B) is the automatic, natural consequence of (A): 春になると、桜が咲く — when spring comes, the cherries bloom. Clause (A) always stands in the plain present form — never the past — and nouns and な-adjectives insert だ: 地下鉄だと、早く着く. Clause (A) must happen before (B); the relation reads closer to "and" than to a real "if", which is why it is far stronger than the hypothetical conditionals.

The automatic-consequence core imposes two restrictions. First, (B) must be definite — something that merely might happen cannot follow と. Second, (B) cannot carry intention, planning, or control: no requests, suggestions, or statements of will — those belong to たら. The main clause may be past when describing what used to happen habitually: 子供の時、冬になるとよくかぜをひきました — whenever winter came, I caught colds. This is the conditional と promised in cards CH.9 · CR.5 and CH.12 · CR.5 — both are built directly on this "guaranteed outcome" reading.

If it's ~ · topic conditional
Noun/な-adj + なら
Verb/い-adjplain form
+
(の)optional
+ なら
About

This grammar structure singles out one item or situation and makes a statement that applies only to it — if we're talking about (A)…, if it's the case that (A), as for (A). Historically it abbreviates ならば, the hypothetical form of the classical auxiliary なり — to be, which is why it pairs directly with nouns and な-adjectives (無理なら、いいよ) — the roles だ serves today. Verbs and い-adjectives attach in the plain form, with or without a nominalizing の: 田舎に住む（の）なら、車が要る.

What separates なら from the other conditionals is that (A) is not a trigger event but a frame — a topic taken up from context, often from what someone just said. This makes it the tool for limiting scope (ひらがななら分かります — hiragana I can read, implying the rest is another story), for contrast and correction (チリなら行ったことがありますが、ブラジルはありません), and for advice about a plan that has not happened yet — which is why, unlike たら, it tolerates reversed time order: 行くなら、傘を持って行って — if you're going, take an umbrella (the taking comes before the going). It is used for judgments and guesses about a case, not for results that follow automatically from an event.

(~baai wa)

Verb / い-adjective
Phraseplain form
+ 場合は

Noun

About

This grammar structure is used to frame a hypothetical case and state what applies within it — in the event of (A), in the case of (A). 場合 is a noun meaning case or situation, so attachment follows noun-modification rules, exactly as with 時: verbs and い-adjectives in the plain form, な-adjectives with な, nouns with の. The register leans formal and instructional — signage, announcements, manuals: 火事の場合は、エレベーターを使わないでください — in the event of fire, do not use the elevator. Where 時 frames an actual time at which something happens, 場合 frames a contingency that may or may not arise.

A second use highlights one person's situation against the current topic: 私の場合は — in my case — introduces the speaker's own circumstances as a contrast to what has just been said, carried by the contrastive force of は: 私の場合は、朝のほうが集中できます — in my case, mornings work better.

Quick RecapCH.15 · CR.13
The four conditionalsN4
たら · ば · と · なら · 場合は
Comparison
Form What A is What B may be Feels like
〜たら Something that finishes first Anything — requests, suggestions, even past facts "Once A happens…"
〜ば The condition that guarantees B Avoid commands; leans to favourable outcomes "If A, then B follows"
〜と Something always true or always done Automatic results only — no will, no requests "Whenever A, B"
〜なら A topic somebody just raised Your reaction to that topic "If it's A you mean…"
〜場合は A contingency being planned for Instructions, rules, procedures "In the event of A"
When to use what
A has to be over before B starts, and B can be an order or a request → 〜たら
You are stating the condition under which B reliably follows → 〜ば
The result is automatic — nature, machines, directions, habits → 〜と
You are responding to what somebody just said or brought up → 〜なら
Written procedures, notices and rules — the formal one → 〜場合は
Quick test: if B is "please do it" or "let's do it", と is wrong — reach for たら
Quick test: if A is something the other person just mentioned, なら beats all three others
N4CH.15 · CR.14
のに
(~noni)
Despite · Although · Even though
Verb
Verbplain form
+ のに
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ のに
な-adjective
な-adj + なのに
Noun
Noun + なのに
About

This grammar structure is used to connect two factual clauses where (B) happens despite the expectation raised by (A) — although, even though, despite. Because both halves must be facts, のに carries surprise, disappointment, or contradiction: 薬を飲んだのに、熱が下がらない — even though I took medicine, the fever won't go down. Though it looks like の plus に, it functions as a conjunction particle in its own right. Verbs and い-adjectives attach in the plain form; な-adjectives and nouns insert な — 元気なのに, 学生なのに. The variant だのに exists in some dialects but is considered incorrect by most speakers. Negatives slot in as usual: じゃないのに, 行かないのに.

Because のに asserts two facts, clause (B) cannot be a command, suggestion, request, or statement of intent — for those, use が or けど, whose contrast is also simply milder. The hypothetical counterpart is ても — even if (A) concedes something that may not have happened, while のに — even though (A) — insists that it did. And where ので presents (B) as the natural outcome of (A), のに presents it as exactly what (A) should have prevented.

N4CH.15 · CR.15
だが・ですが
(daga · desuga)
But · However — formal contrast
Casual
Clause A + だが、 + Clause B
Formal
Clause A + ですが、 + Clause B
About

This grammar structure is used to state a contrast in a formal register — but, however, nevertheless. Though dictionaries list だが as a word of its own, it is transparently だ (or polite です) plus the contrastive が: the だ settles that statement (A) is true, and が signals that something qualifying it follows. It works in two positions — linking two clauses inside one sentence (この方法は簡単だが、時間がかかる — this method is simple, but it takes time), or standing at the head of a new sentence as a connector: だが、当たらなかった — however, I didn't win.

Register behaves predictably: だが belongs to plain, formal, often written Japanese, while ですが commits the rest of the sentence to polite speech. An added ね — だがね — softens it, though this is now mostly heard from older speakers. The everyday softening preface んですが・んだけど is a separate pattern, treated in card CH.15 · CR.16.

A typhoon was approaching. However, the tournament was held as scheduled.

N4CH.15 · CR.16
んだけど・んですが
(~n da kedo · ~n desu ga)
But… · softening preface
Casual
Phrase + んだけど、 +
…often unsaid
Formal
Phrase + んですが、 +
…often unsaid
About

This grammar structure is used to open a request, question, or piece of news gently — usually translated as a plain but…, though the real sense is closer to with (A) as the background…. It combines the explanatory んだ, which presents (A) as context or cause, with the contrastive けど or が: ちょっと相談したいんだけど — there's something I'd like to ask you about… What follows is often left entirely unsaid, out of politeness or awkwardness — the listener is invited to pick up the thread: 荷物が届いていないんですが… — my package hasn't arrived (so… could you look into it?).

The forms run a ladder from casual to formal. Least formal first:

んだけど — casual
んだけども — casual, a shade softer
んだけれども — neutral to polite
んだが — formal; bluntest of the set and reads as quite masculine, so it wants a softened tone
んですが — most formal; the safe default in polite speech

Replacing ん with の makes any of them one step more formal. The preface works with any word type through the usual んだ attachment (な after nouns and な-adjectives: 明日引っ越しなんだけど).

N4CH.15 · CR.17
かどうか・〜か
(~ka dou ka · ~ka)
Whether or not · embedded questions
Yes / No question
Phraseplain form - noun / な-adj drop だ
+ かどうか +
分かる / 決めるmain verb
With a question word
何 / どこ / 誰 … +
Phraseplain form
+ か +
分かる / 知るmain verb
About

This grammar structure embeds a question inside a larger sentence — I don't know whether…, do you know where…, let's decide if…. A yes/no question takes かどうか, which combines the or sense of か with どう — how — literally whether (A) or however it is: 彼が来るかどうか、分かりません — I don't know whether he's coming. The embedded clause stays in the plain form, and nouns and な-adjectives drop their だ: 彼が医者かどうか知りません. The typical main verbs are 分かる, 知る, 決める, 覚えている, 確認する.

When the embedded question contains a question word — 何, どこ, 誰, いつ — plain か alone does the job: 山下先生が何を食べたか、覚えていません — I don't remember what he ate. Inside the embedded clause, subjects take が rather than は, and an explanatory んですか question converts to のか: どうして来なかったのか分かりません. This mid-sentence か marks uncertainty rather than asking anything itself, so the sentence needs no final か — though one can follow when the whole sentence is itself a question: どこに住んでいるか知っていますか.

N4CH.15 · CR.18
し〜し
(~shi ~shi)
And · listing reasons
Pattern
Reason A + し、 + Reason B + し、 + Result
Attachment
Phraseplain form
+
(だ)for noun / な-adj
+ し
About

This grammar structure lists reasons, explanations, or justifications for a conclusion — …and also…, not only… but also. The conjunction particle し follows each listed reason in its plain form, with だ inserted after nouns and な-adjectives (学生だし, 好きだし): 安いし、おいしいし、駅から近いんです — it's cheap, it's tasty, and it's close to the station. A single し clause also works, implying among other reasons: 物価が安いし、この町の生活は楽です. The final し before the result may be replaced with から or ので.

What し adds over plain listing is the hint that the stated reasons are not the only ones — there is more where these came from. The listed reasons also read as roughly equal in weight, which makes し wrong when one reason clearly dominates: adding a trivial complaint alongside a serious one with し sounds off. For stacking same-sign points across sentence boundaries, それに covers the same ground from card CH.6 · CR.20.

N4CH.15 · CR.19
ように
(~you ni)
So that · In order to
Purpose
Verb [できる / ない]potential / negative / plain
+ ように +
Main clauseaction taken
About

This grammar structure is used to state the purpose behind an action — so that, in order to. The adverbial ように marks the clause before it as an aimed-for outcome, and the main clause as what the speaker does to bring that outcome closer. The key nuance separating it from other purpose expressions is control: the outcome before ように is something the speaker cannot simply decide to achieve — which is why the verb there is typically a potential form (話せるように — so that I can speak), a ない form (遅れないように — so as not to be late), or a non-volitional verb, all in the non-past.

Since する has no potential form of its own, できる steps in: 勉強ができるように、机の上を片付けた — I tidied my desk so that I could study. This is the same goal-marking よう seen in ようにする — deliberate effort and ように祈る — wishing from cards CH.2 · CR.8 and CH.9 · CR.6 — here the sentence simply supplies a concrete action taken toward the goal instead.

I go to the pool every week so that I can swim faster.

N4CH.15 · CR.20
くは
(~ku wa)
Not exactly ~ · contrastive く
Negative
い-adj [い] + くはない
Affirmative
い-adj [い] + くはある
About

This grammar structure inserts the contrastive は into an い-adjective's continuative く form — a small change with a precise effect. Plain 広くない flatly denies spaciousness; 広くはない — not exactly spacious — denies it while implying that something else holds instead: it may not be big, but it is enough, or cosy, or cheap. Because は is doing its contrastive work, the contrast is often spelled out in the following clause (優しくはないけど、背が高い — not exactly kind, but tall), though it can equally be left hanging: 仕事は楽しくはないけど….

The pattern lives mostly in negatives, but the affirmative くはある exists for conceding a property while pushing against its usual implication: 古くはあるけど、気に入っている — old it certainly is, but I like it. The construction belongs to い-adjectives; the same contrastive job for other word types falls to は in its ordinary positions.

16 Quotation & Reported Speech
  1. と思うI think ~
  2. と聞いた・と言っていたI heard that · They said
  3. そうだI hear that ~ · hearsay report
  4. ってCasual quotation · They say
  5. と言ってもいいYou could say · You might say
N4CH.16 · CR.1
と思う
(~to omou)
I think ~
Verb
Verbplain form
+ と思う
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ と思う
な-adjective
な-adj + だと思う
Noun
Noun + だと思う
About

This grammar structure is used to state what the speaker thinks or believes — I think that (A). It combines the quotation particle と, which frames the preceding clause as content, with the う-verb 思う. The thought itself always stays in the plain form regardless of how polite the sentence is — politeness is carried by 思います at the end: 明日は雨が降ると思います — I think it will rain tomorrow. な-adjectives and nouns insert だ before と (親切だと思う, フランス語だと思う); dropping this だ is common in casual speech but not technically correct. Since the thinker is normally the speaker, 私は is usually left unsaid.

To report what somebody else thinks, と思っている is used instead — 彼は自分が正しいと思っている — he thinks he is right. Plain と思う expresses a judgment only its owner can make, so it is reserved for the speaker; と思っている describes a held, ongoing opinion and therefore works for third parties, as well as for the speaker's own standing convictions. The related pattern ようと思う — volitional + と思う for intentions, and the 働こうと思う／働くと思う intent-versus-prediction split — is covered in card CH.9 · CR.7.

N4CH.16 · CR.2
と聞いた・と言っていた
(~to kiita · ~to itte ita)
I heard that · They said
I heard that
Phraseplain form
+
(だ)for noun / な-adj
+ と聞いた
They said
Phraseplain form
+
(だ)for noun / な-adj
+ と言っていた
About

This grammar structure is used to pass on information received from someone else. The quotation particle と partners with verbs of hearing and saying to form two set patterns. と聞いた — I heard that (A) — centres on the hearer: word reached the speaker, without necessarily naming who said it, though a source can be added with から (友達から聞いた — I heard from a friend). と言っていた — (X) said that (A) — reports a specific person's utterance; the ている form is standard here because a past act of speaking is being relayed as still-relevant content.

The reported clause stays in the plain form; nouns and な-adjectives take だ before と — 大学生だと聞いた. As with と思う, this だ is often dropped in casual conversation (下手と聞いたけど); it sounds perfectly normal, but is technically not correct Japanese. Both patterns are inherently retrospective — the hearing or saying has already happened — so the final verb appears in the past:

聞いた・聞きました,
言っていた・言っていました.

N4CH.16 · CR.3
そうだ
(~sou da · ~sou desu)
I hear that ~ · hearsay report
Verb
Verbplain form
+ そうだ
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ そうだ
な-adjective
な-adj + だそうだ
Noun
Noun + だそうだ
About

This grammar structure is used to report something the speaker has heard or been told — second-hand information learned from another person, a broadcast, or some other outside source. It is the difference between stating a fact and passing one on: 台風が来ます asserts that a typhoon is coming, while 台風が来るそうです reports that this is what the speaker was told.

Attachment: そうだ follows the plain form. Verbs and い-adjectives attach as they are (話すそうだ, 楽しいそうだ — the です is dropped), while な-adjectives and nouns require だ before it (親切だそうだ, 学生だそうだ). The critical rule is that tense and polarity live inside the reported clause, never on そうだ itself: what was originally said in the past negative stays that way — 授業がなかったそうです — I heard there was no class — while そうだ remains in the present. There is no そうでした and no negative form of そうだ in this use.

Naming the source: to make explicit where the information came from, the sentence opens with によると — 天気予報によると、台風が来るそうです — according to the weather forecast, a typhoon is coming. The pattern is standard in news and in careful reporting, and it distinguishes そうだ from the vaguer evidential structures: this one implies a definite source, even when that source is left unnamed.

Reference — formation
TypeOriginal (plain)Hearsay form
VERB話す話すそうです
い-ADJさびしいさびしいそうです
な-ADJ好きだ好きだそうです
NOUN学生だ学生だそうです
PASTNEGATIVEなかったなかったそうです
そうだ and its neighbours

Two structures share this shape but do different work. The appearance そう attaches to verb stems and adjective stems and guesses from what can be seen (雨が降りそうだ — it looks like rain); the hearsay そうだ attaches to plain forms and reports what was said (雨が降るそうだ — I hear it's going to rain). The single syllable る is the whole difference, so the attachment form must be read carefully.

Among the reporting structures, そうだ is the neutral one: it passes information along without commenting on its reliability. らしい adds distance and a shade of inference, と聞いた foregrounds the act of hearing and its source, and the casual って does the same job as そうだ in relaxed speech. Because そうだ merely relays, it is unsuited to information the speaker witnessed personally.

N4CH.16 · CR.4
って
(~tte)
Casual quotation · They say
Quoting
Quote + って +
言う / 聞く / 思うoften omitted
Hearsay
Phraseplain form - sentence-final
+ って。
About

This grammar structure is the casual variant of the quotation particle と. In its quoting use it stands after the quoted content and before a verb of communication — 言う, 聞く, 思う: 「すぐ戻る」って母が言った — Mom said she'd be right back. Just as with と, the following verb is very often omitted, and even more so with って given how much casual speech leaves out: 田中さん、「先に行く」って。 — Tanaka said he's going ahead.

Standing at the end of a sentence, って reports what the speaker heard — they say (A), apparently (A) — replacing the formal hearsay and reported-speech patterns of polite registers, frequently as んだって: 田中さん、来月結婚するんだって — I hear Tanaka is getting married next month. Because it is thoroughly casual, って sits badly in sentences built on です／ます politeness — in those contexts use と言っていました — though between people who are formal but friendly it passes. The same clipped spirit gives ってこと for ということ (card CH.17 · CR.3) and the wrap-up って感じ, covered in card CH.18 · CR.14.

(~to itte mo ii)

(だ)for な-adj

About

This grammar structure is used to assert that a characterization is fair — you could say (A), you might say (A). It is assembled from parts already covered: the quotation と frames the claim, 言って is the て-form of 言う, and もいい is the permission pattern from card CH.12 · CR.1 — literally even if you say (A), it is fine. The result hedges the form while keeping the content confident: the speaker believes the statement, but presents it as one acceptable way of putting things. Nouns and な-adjectives can take だ before と, though it is often dropped here.

Adding でしょう — と言ってもいいでしょう — softens the claim one step further, common in writing and careful speech. As with most grammar patterns built on 言う, the kana spelling といってもいい is frequent — kanji-free spelling marks it as a grammatical pattern rather than the ordinary verb to say.

17 Nominalisation & Noun Conversion
  1. こと・のは・のがConverting verbs into nouns — nominalizers
  2. Clause + NounDescribing a noun with a clause

N4CH.17 · CR.1
こと・のは・のが
(~koto · ~no wa · ~no ga)
Converting verbs into nouns — nominalizers
こと
Verbplain form
+ こと
の
Verbplain form
+ のは / のが
About

This grammar structure is used for nominalization — treating a whole phrase as if it were a single noun: the act of (A), that which (A), the one who (A). Japanese has two workhorses for this job, こと and の, and both attach directly to the plain forms of verbs — any standard form, including past and ない negatives, but never the polite ます・ません.

こと is a noun in its own right (事 in kanji, though the nominalizer is almost never written that way), often translated as thing — so 泳ぐこと is literally the thing that is swimming. It tends to describe intrinsic, describable things that are not necessarily observable — feelings, events, conditions — where もの covers tangible things. A related use closes short sentences: a statement ending in こと。 reads as a rule or command (廊下では走らないこと。); in that role こと behaves like a sentence-ending particle rather than a noun.

の is a particle doing the same job, behaving very much like English "that" or "which": お菓子を全部食べたのは、妹だ — the one who ate all the sweets is my little sister. Followed by は or が, the nominalized phrase slots into the sentence exactly as a single noun would.

The two are not freely interchangeable. の cannot replace こと in set expressions such as ことができる or ことがある, and a の-phrase may not be followed by だ, である or です — that combination would be read as the explanatory 〜んです・のです instead. For clause-sized content built on quotation, see card CH.17 · CR.3.

N4CH.17 · CR.2
Clause + Noun
(plain clause + noun)
Describing a noun with a clause
Verb
Verbplain form
+ Noun
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ Noun
な-adjective
な-adj + な + Noun
About

This grammar structure is used to describe a noun by placing a clause — a mini-sentence — directly in front of it. It replaces the English relative pronouns "who", "that" and "which", and it is fundamental to natural Japanese: 本を読む人 — a person who reads books, 昨日会った人 — the person I met yesterday. There is no pronoun, no comma, and no added particle — the clause simply comes first and the noun last, the reverse of English order.

The clause must end in a plain form: dictionary form, た past, ない negative, or ている — never ます or です inside the clause. When the clause contains its own subject, that subject is marked with が: 私が書いた本 — the book I wrote, 犬が好きな人 — a person who likes dogs. い-adjectives stand before the noun as they are (高いビル), and な-adjectives take な (静かな町).

Once built, the whole unit behaves as one noun and takes は, が or を in the main sentence as usual. This is the same mechanism behind 時-clauses and 場合は, where the modified noun happens to be time or case, and it pairs with the nominalizers こと・の, which turn a clause into a noun instead of hanging one on it.

N4CH.17 · CR.3
ということ
(~to iu koto)
The fact that ~ · clause nominalization
Casual
Phrase + ってこと
Formal
Phrase + ということ
About

This grammar structure is used to turn a whole phrase into a noun — one of the main ways of performing nominalization in Japanese. It combines the quotation particle と, the verb 言う, and the noun こと: literally the thing that (A) is said to be, though in practice it sounds far less formal than that. It attaches to the end of any phrase without です or ます, and is almost always written in hiragana — と言う事 is possible but not the norm, kana being the regular choice for grammaticalized patterns.

Its most common job is drawing a conclusion or asking for confirmation of one: ということですか — does that mean…? — checks the speaker's understanding of what was just said, and ということだ states the takeaway: 要するに、計画は中止になったということだ — in short, it means the plan was cancelled. In conversation the という part is regularly clipped to って (card CH.16 · CR.4), giving ってこと: これ、全部無料ってこと？ — you mean this is all free?

N4CH.17 · CR.4
さ
(~sa)
Adjective → noun — ‑ness
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + さ
な-adjective
な-adj + さ
About

This grammar structure is used to convert an adjective into a noun expressing the amount or degree of that quality — English "-ness". さ is a suffix that attaches to the stem of both い-adjectives and な-adjectives: 長い → 長さ — length, 大切 → 大切さ — importance. For い-adjectives the final い is dropped before さ; な-adjectives attach it to the bare stem.

The resulting word is a full noun and takes particles like any other: 道の長さを測る — measure the length of the road. Measurable qualities are the most common conversions — 高さ, 重さ, 速さ, 深さ — but abstract ones work the same way:

大切さ,
便利さ,
丁寧さ.

The suffix is thought to stem originally from the kanji 差 (distinction). In classical usage さ could also follow the dictionary form of verbs to mark the point in time of an action (帰るさ — at the point of returning); this survives only as poetic language and is rarely met in modern Japanese.

N5CH.18 · CR.1
だろう
(~darou)
Probably · I think — casual supposition
Verb
Verbplain form
+ だろう
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ だろう
な-adjective
な-adj (no な) + だろう
Noun
Noun + だろう
About

This grammar structure is used to express probability or supposition in casual speech — the plain/casual equivalent of でしょう. It translates as probably, I think, or right? in English.

だろう is the presumptive form of だ, the plain copula. For verbs and い-adjectives, it follows the plain form directly — any tense or polarity. For な-adjectives, attach だろう to the adjective stem — do not add な before it. For nouns, attach だろう directly.

Because だ is more casual than です, だろう carries a more casual or masculine tone than でしょう. It is often used by men or in contexts where a more assertive tone is intended.

With a rising intonation, だろう can contract to だろ, functioning as a rhetorical confirmation — seeking agreement from the listener, like "right?" in English.

N5CH.18 · CR.2
でしょう
(~deshou)
Probably · I suppose — polite supposition
Verb
Verbplain form
+ でしょう
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ でしょう
な-adjective

Noun
Noun (no だ) + でしょう
About

This grammar structure is used to express a guess, prediction, or inference about something — equivalent to probably, I suppose, or I think in English. It can also be used to soften an assertion or hedge an opinion politely.

でしょう is the presumptive form of です — its plain/casual equivalent is だろう. For verbs and い-adjectives, attach でしょう to the plain form directly — any tense or polarity. For な-adjectives, attach to the adjective stem — do not add な or だ before it. For nouns, attach directly — do not add だ.

Adding か gives でしょうか — a polite way to ask for someone's guess or opinion, softer than ですか.

In casual speech, でしょ with a rising intonation works as a rhetorical confirmation — like "right?" in English.

N4CH.18 · CR.3
かもしれない
(~kamo shirenai)
Might · Maybe
Verb
Verbplain form
+ かもしれない
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ かもしれない
な-adjective
な-adj + かもしれない
Noun
Noun + かもしれない
About

This grammar structure is used to express uncertainty or mere possibility — might, maybe, possibly. Though treated as a single word, it is a combination of the particle かも with 知れない, the negated potential of the う-verb 知る: literally one cannot know even (A). It attaches to the plain form of any word class, in any tense or polarity; with nouns and な-adjectives in the present tense, the だ that plain speech would use is dropped, because かもしれない takes its place (教会かもしれない, never 教会だかもしれない).

The polite form conjugates 知れない itself: かもしれません. Because the pattern is so frequent in daily speech, clipped colloquial forms are common — bare かも at the end of a casual sentence (ドライブするかも), and the rougher かもしれん/かもしらん. Distinguish it from でしょう: でしょう asserts probability — the speaker thinks it is likely — while かもしれない claims only possibility, hedging a guess without committing to it. It sits at the low end of the confidence scale, below the whole そう/みたい/ようだ appearance family, because it needs no evidence at all.
