N4CH.18 · CR.4
そう・そうに・そうな
(~sou · ~sou ni · ~sou na)
Looks like · About to
Verb
Verb stem + そうだ
い-adjective
い-adj [い] + そうだ
な-adjective
な-adj + そうだ
About

This grammar structure is used to describe how something appears — it looks like, it seems, or, with verbs, it's about to happen. そう is an auxiliary that attaches to stems:

the stem of a verb: 雨が降りそうだ — it looks like it's about to rain,
an い-adjective with the final い dropped: おいしそう,
a bare な-adjective stem: 元気そう.

The one exception is いい, which becomes よさそう. The judgment is a visual, low-confidence guess made on the spot without confirming anything as fact — when the evidence is stronger or the thing is obvious, みたい from card CH.18 · CR.5 is the better choice: 雨が降りそうだ — I'd guess so, from the sky versus 雨が降るみたいだ — the forecast says so.

Negatives split by word class:

For adjectives, the ない is itself an い-adjective, so a さ is inserted: 難しくない → 難しくなさそう, 上手じゃない → じゃなさそう (the alternative そうじゃない — 上手そうじゃない — also exists and is a little less formal),
For verbs, the ない is an auxiliary, not an adjective, so no さ is added — just drop its い: 帰らない → 帰らなそうだ.

Like the みたい family, そう behaves as a な-adjective when modifying: そうな before a noun (暖かそうなセーター — a warm-looking sweater) and そうに before a verb (おいしそうに食べる — eat with apparent relish).

One caution: this stem-based そう covers appearance only — the hearsay そうだ that attaches to plain forms (I heard that…) is a separate structure, covered in card CH.16 · CR.3.

N4CH.18 · CR.5
みたい・みたいに・みたいな
(~mitai · ~mitai ni · ~mitai na)
Like · Seems like — casual
Inference
Verbplain form
+ みたいだ
Resemblance
Noun + みたいだ
Modifying a noun
Noun + みたいな + Noun
Modifying an action
Noun + みたいに + Verb
About

This grammar structure is used to say that something is like something else, or that something seems to be the case — the everyday, conversational member of the appearance family. みたい behaves like a な-adjective and attaches directly to what precedes it: a noun with no connector at all (忍者みたいだ — unlike のような, there is never a の), or the plain form of a verb or adjective. Sentence-finally it is followed by だ/です, though the だ is frequently dropped in speech.

Usage 1 — resemblance: after a noun, みたい states that (B) resembles (A): あの雲は綿菓子みたいだ — that cloud looks like cotton candy.

Usage 2 — inference: after a plain verb or adjective, it draws a conclusion from evidence at hand — it looks like, apparently: 雨が降ったみたいだ — looks like it rained. The clause before みたい carries its own tense and polarity (来ないみたい, 寝なかったみたい), and it even works about yourself when you are not certain: 財布を忘れたみたいです.

As a な-adjective, みたい takes な when describing a noun (夢みたいな話 — a story like a dream) and に when describing how an action is done (魚みたいに泳ぐ — swim like a fish). These are interchangeable with のような/のように but casual and more common in spoken Japanese. Two placement notes: みたい is based on direct, reliable information — more confident than a visual そう guess, less formal than ようだ (both covered next). And despite the sound, it has no connection to 見たい — want to see — みたい has no kanji form.

N4CH.18 · CR.6
ようだ・のような・のように
(~you da · ~no you na · ~no you ni)
It seems · Like — formal
Verb
Verbplain form
+ ようだ
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ ようだ
な-adjective
な-adj + なようだ
Noun
Noun + のようだ
About

This grammar structure is the formal counterpart of みたい — the auxiliary よう (kanji 様, manner) states that something is in the manner of, or appears to be, something else. It attaches to plain verb and い-adjective forms directly, to な-adjectives with な, and to nouns with の — exactly the connectors that みたい does without.

Usage 1 — inference: sentence-final ようだ/ようです draws a conclusion — it seems that, it appears that: あそこのプールは深いようだ. Because よう is usually grounded in the speaker's direct information or experience, it signals notably higher confidence than そう and sounds firmer than みたい; the price is formality — in casual conversation it can come across as stiff, which is why みたい dominates speech.

Usage 2 — simile: with の after a noun, のような modifies a following noun (鎌倉のような町 — a town like Kamakura) and のように modifies a verb or adjective (魚のように泳ぐ — swim like a fish; 鬼のように怖い — scary as a demon). These are interchangeable with casual みたいな/みたいに. Beyond nouns, ように/ような also follow full clauses to mean as if — the comparison is to a whole imagined situation: バケツをひっくり返したように雨が降っている — it's raining as if a bucket had been tipped over; 何でも知っているような顔 — a face as if he knows everything.

The appearance family — least formal first:

そう — a visual, on-the-spot guess
みたい — a casual conclusion from direct information
ようだ — the same conclusion in its formal dress

N4CH.18 · CR.7
らしい
(~rashii)
Apparently · Typical of
Hearsay / inference
Verbplain form
+ らしい
Typical of
Noun + らしい
About

Usage 1 — hearsay and inference: as an auxiliary, らしい expresses that the speaker believes something is true on reasonable grounds — they heard it, read it, or saw signs of it — without being fully certain: apparently, it seems, I heard. It attaches to the plain form of verbs and い-adjectives, and to bare な-adjective and noun stems (フランス人らしい). Within the appearance family it sits close to ようだ in meaning, but sounds noticeably less confident — the information is usually second-hand, which gives it its gossip-and-news flavour.

Usage 2 — typical of: attached to a noun, らしい works as an auxiliary adjective meaning that something has the qualities expected of that noun — -ish, befitting: 春らしい天気 — properly spring-like weather; 自分らしい生き方 — a way of life true to oneself. In this use it conjugates as an い-adjective: adverbial らしく (キャプテンらしくしなさい — act like a captain), and negative らしくない for something uncharacteristic (田中さんらしくない — that's not like Tanaka-san). Note that a sentence like 彼は学生らしい is ambiguous between the two readings — apparently he's a student or he's properly student-like — and only context decides.

N4CH.18 · CR.8
はずだ・はずがない
(~hazu da · ~hazu ga nai)
Bound to be · Can't possibly be
Verb
Verbplain form
+ はずだ
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ はずだ
な-adjective
な-adj + なはずだ
Noun
Noun + のはずだ
Impossibility
Verbplain form
+ はずがない
About

Usage 1 — はずだ: はず (kanji 筈) is a noun expressing that the speaker is quite sure of something through reasoning, but cannot confirm it — bound to, should be, supposed to. Because it is a noun, な-adjectives connect with な and nouns with の, and it is usually followed by だ/です. One caution on the English gloss should: はず only ever means should be true by my reckoning — it cannot give advice or make suggestions, so bound to is the safer translation to keep in mind. The past form はずだった marks an expectation that reality contradicted: 九時に出るはずだったが、遅れている — it was supposed to leave at nine. Dropping the だ and trailing off on bare はず softens the certainty toward probably.

Usage 2 — はずがない: adding が and ない negates the very possibility — can't possibly be, hardly possible: literally, (A) being true is not among the possibilities. Keep it distinct from ないはずだ, where the negation sits inside the claim: 高くないはずだ reasons its way to it's bound to not be expensive, while 高いはずがない rejects the idea outright — there's no way it's expensive. The first is a confident negative conclusion; the second dismisses someone else's premise.

Quick RecapCH.18 · CR.9
The conjecture ladder
かもしれない · だろう · でしょう · そう · みたい · ようだ · らしい · はずだ
How sure, and on what basis
Form Certainty Based on Feels like
〜かもしれないN4 Lowest Nothing firm — the possibility simply exists "Might · Maybe"
〜だろう Moderate Your own guess, stated plainly "Probably"
〜でしょう Moderate Your own guess, stated politely "Probably · I suppose"
〜そうN4 Moderate What you can see in front of you, right now "Looks about to · Looks ~"
〜みたいN4 Moderate Your overall impression — casual register "Seems like"
〜ようだN4 Moderate–high The same impression — formal or written register "It appears that"
〜らしいN4 Moderate What you picked up from elsewhere — you keep your distance "Apparently"
〜はずだN4 Highest Reasoning from facts you trust — it ought to follow "Bound to be · Should be"
When to use what
Guessing out loud among friends → だろう
Guessing politely, or softening a claim that would sound too blunt → でしょう
You have no evidence, only the possibility → かもしれないN4
You are reading the situation in front of you — clouds, a face, a wobbling shelf → そうN4
Same judgement, casual conversation → みたい · formal or written → ようだN4
The information came from somebody else and you would rather not own it → らしいN4
You can argue it from something you know for a fact → はずだN4
Watch the attachment, not the word: そう on a stem is what something looks like, but そうだ on a plain form is what you were told — that one belongs with the reporting formsN4
N4CH.18 · CR.10
に見える・と見える
(~ni mieru · ~to mieru)
Looks like · Can be deduced
Appearance — nouns
Noun + に見える
Appearance — い-adjectives
い-adj [い] + く + 見える
Deduction
Clauseplain form
+
(だ)for noun / な-adj
+ と見える
About

Usage 1 — に見える: the particle に plus 見える — to be visible states that something looks or appears to be (A). Nouns attach directly (アイスクリームに見える — looks like ice cream), and い-adjectives take their adverbial く form (年より若く見える — looks younger than their age, building on the 見える appearance use from card CH.14 · CR.4). The appearance family slots in freely to add guesswork: 寒そうに見える, 溺れているように見える, 太ったみたいに見える — each keeps its own confidence flavour. As with most grammar constructions, hiragana みえる is common — kanji tends to push the reading toward literal sight.

Usage 2 — と見える: with the result-marking と, the meaning shifts from looks to logic: from the appearance, one can conclude that (A). It follows a plain clause — nouns and な-adjectives keep their だ (嫌いだと見える) — and typically comes after stating the evidence: 彼は上着を脱いだ。暑いと見える — he took off his jacket; he must be hot. Because it implies the speaker has reasoned from evidence, it sounds fairly confident, closer to a deduction than a guess.

N4CH.18 · CR.11
が見られる
(~ga mirareru)
Can be seen · Observable
Noun + が + 見られる
About

This grammar structure uses 見られる, the potential form of 見る, to say that something can be seen or observed. The contrast with 見える from card CH.14 · CR.4 is the effort involved: 見える reports what enters the eyes on its own, while 見られる covers sights that need conditions, luck, or deliberate looking — この部屋からは富士山が見られる implies a clear day and a look in the right direction. This is why it attaches naturally to chances, changes, and trends.

In formal writing and reports the same pattern means can be observed or is evident: データには改善が見られる — an improvement can be seen in the data. Grammatically 見られる is both the potential and the passive of 見る, so context decides the reading; the clipped ら抜き form 見れる, covered in cards CH.14 · CR.2 and CH.19 · CR.2, can only ever be the potential.

N4CH.18 · CR.12
がする
(~ga suru)
To give off — smell · sound · taste · feeling
Sense noun + がする
About

This grammar structure is used to describe things experienced through the senses — smell, sound, taste, or a bodily feeling (sight is excluded; that territory belongs to 見える). Where English uses dedicated verbs — smells like, tastes like, feels like — Japanese makes the sensory experience itself the subject of the sentence: a sense noun such as 匂い, 音, 味, 声 or 感じ is marked with が, and する states that this sensation occurs, or is being given off.

The sense noun is described by whatever precedes it — a noun with の (カレーの匂い), an adjective (変な味), or a full modifying clause in the Clause + Noun pattern (誰かが呼んでいる声). The source of the sensation stands as the topic, and the person perceiving it is left unstated. Note the contrast with the conjecture family: がする reports a direct sensation, while ようだ and みたい draw an inference from evidence.

Japanese also treats 気 — one's spirit or attention — as something perceivable by the senses, which produces the very common 気がする: I have a feeling that… (忘れた気がする). It voices a hunch with no hard evidence behind it, softer than any of the conjecture structures, and it runs on the same 気 as に気が付く.

N4CH.18 · CR.13
に気が付く
(~ni ki ga tsuku)
To notice · To realise
Noun
Noun + に気が付く
Clause
Verbplain form
+ こと / の + に気が付く
About

This grammar structure is used when someone notices or realises something. 気 here is best understood as attention or presence of mind, and 付く is the intransitive partner of 付ける — to attach — so the phrase literally describes attention attaching itself to something, an event that happens to you rather than something you perform. That intransitive character (card CH.19 · CR.1) is why noticing feels sudden and unplanned. The particle に marks where the attention lands: a noun directly (間違いに気が付く), or a clause nominalised with こと or の (忘れたことに気が付いた).

The compressed single-word form 気づく is common and interchangeable (間違いに気づいた). The negative 気が付かない covers things that escape notice entirely — often the more revealing half of the pattern: メッセージに気が付かなかった — I didn't notice your message.

N4CH.18 · CR.14
って感じ
(~tte kanji)
Kind of · That vibe
Phraseany word or clause
+ って感じ
About

This grammar structure is a casual spoken phrase used to say that something feels like or has the vibe of (A). It combines the casual quotation marker って with the noun 感じ — feeling — literally the feeling of: (A). Because the quotation marker can quote anything, it follows any word or phrase unchanged: 昭和って感じ — very Shouwa-era vibes. Like ending an English sentence with "…kind of thing," it softens a statement and makes it deliberately indirect.

A second common role is wrapping up a loose train of thought: after describing a situation at length, a speaker closes with って感じ to summarise the overall gist or atmosphere — …and it was just, the worst, basically. One register caution: this is casual speech through and through. In writing or formal contexts it sounds vague, as though the speaker's thoughts are not fully formed — reach for のような or a plain statement instead.

19 Voice & Valency
  1. 他動詞・自動詞Transitive vs intransitive — done to something · happens on its own
  2. れる・られるPassive — an action done to the subject, often to their dismay
  3. せる・させるCausative — make, let, or have somebody do something
  4. させられるCausative-passive — to be made to do something against one's will
  5. と言われている・と考えられている・とされているIt is said · thought · considered — impersonal passive of public opinion
N4CH.19 · CR.1
他動詞・自動詞
(tadoushi · jidoushi)
Transitive vs intransitive — done to something · happens on its own
Transitive 他動詞
Agentは / が — does the action
+
Objectthing acted on
+ を +
Verbtransitive
Intransitive 自動詞
Subjectundergoes the change
+ が +
Verbintransitive
About

This grammar structure covers the two fundamental types of Japanese verb. Transitive verbs (他動詞) describe an action that somebody does to something — an agent acts on a direct object, and that object is marked with を. Intransitive verbs (自動詞) describe an event or change that happens on its own — the subject itself undergoes the change, and it is marked with が. The kanji spell the difference out: 他 means other, so the action moves onto something else, while 自 means self, so the movement stays with the subject.

The pairs: most Japanese verbs stand alone, but many common verbs of change come in pairs built on the same root — one transitive, one intransitive: 開ける — to open something against 開く — to open by itself. The pairs follow no reliable formation rule and must be memorized individually; the reference table below lists the ones every N4 learner is expected to know. The particle is the signal to watch. 電気をつけました means somebody turned the light on; 電気がつきました reports that the light came on. Choosing the wrong member of a pair, as in ドアを開きました, is one of the most common errors at this level, precisely because English uses the same verb for both directions.

With ている: the two types behave differently when combined with ている.

A transitive verb with ている describes an action in progress: ドアを閉めています — somebody is closing the door right now,
An intransitive verb with ている describes the state that remains after the change: ドアが閉まっています — the door is closed.

Japanese cares not only about what happened but about what condition things are in now, and intransitive + ている is the standard way to report such conditions. The ている forms themselves are covered in cards CH.8 · CR.1 to CH.8 · CR.3.

する and なる: on the broadest view, する and なる can be understood as the most fundamental transitive–intransitive pair of the language — doing something versus becoming something — and the pairs in this card repeat that same division verb by verb.

Reference — common pairs
Transitive を meaning Intransitive が meaning
開ける open sth 開く open
閉める close sth 閉まる close
入れる put in 入る go in
出す take out 出る go out
つける turn on つく come on
消す turn off 消える go off
壊す break sth 壊れる break
汚す make dirty 汚れる get dirty
落とす drop sth 落ちる fall
沸かす boil sth 沸く come to a boil

Irregular
する → される · くる → こられる
About

This grammar structure is used to express that an action was done to the subject by somebody else — the passive voice. The affected person or thing becomes the subject of the sentence, marked with は or が, and the agent who performs the action is marked with に. For う-verbs, the final う-sound changes to its あ-row equivalent before れる (読む → 読まれる); for る-verbs, る is replaced by られる (食べる → 食べられる); する becomes される and くる becomes こられる. Whatever the original verb type, the resulting passive verb conjugates as a regular る-verb — the tables below follow 読む through the full pattern.

Usage 1 — the suffering passive (discomfort · annoyance): the most characteristic use at this level frames the action as an inconvenience or annoyance to the subject: 兄に日記を読まれた does not merely state that the diary was read — it complains about it. In this use the affected person takes は, the agent takes に, and a direct object keeps its を. Japanese even allows intransitive verbs into this pattern to express pure adversity: 雨に降られる — to be rained on and 友達に来られる — to have a friend turn up on you have no direct English passive equivalent at all.

Usage 2 — the neutral passive (objective reporting): the passive is also used with no emotional coloring for objective statements and formal reporting: この雑誌は若い女性によく読まれている simply describes a fact. Neutral passives take が for new information, or は when the subject is already the topic. In formal and academic writing, the agent of creation or discovery is marked with によって rather than に (紫式部によって書かれた), and から can replace に when the agent is a source rather than a direct actor (先生から頼まれた).

Cautions: two neighbouring forms need to be kept apart from the passive. First, てもらう presents the same event as a favor the subject wanted — 手紙を読まれた resents the reading, while 読んでもらった is grateful for it; the benefactive forms belong to the Giving & Receiving group. Second, られる itself is four-ways ambiguous: the same shape also serves as the potential form (can read), the spontaneous (comes to mind by itself), and the respectful form used in polite speech — context decides which reading applies. The colloquial ら抜き shortening (見れる for 見られる) is only ever the potential meaning; a passive can never drop its ら. The potential form is treated as its own grammar point.

Causative — make, let, or have somebody do something

Causerholds authority
+ は / が +

+ に +
Objectif any
+ を +
Verbcausative form
Formation
う-verb (godan)
Verb [あ]あ-row stem
+ せる
る-verb (ichidan)
Verb [る]
+ させる
Irregular
する → させる · くる → こさせる
About

This grammar structure is used to express that somebody makes, lets, or has another person do something — the causative. The causer, who holds the authority or grants the permission, becomes the subject and is marked with は or が; the person who actually performs the action — the doer — is marked with に; and a direct object keeps its を. For う-verbs, the final う-sound changes to its あ-row equivalent before せる (読む → 読ませる); for る-verbs, る is replaced by させる (食べる → 食べさせる); する becomes させる and くる becomes こさせる. Like the passive, every causative conjugates as a regular る-verb — the tables below run 読む through the same pattern as the passive card, so the two forms can be compared line by line.

Usage 1 — coercion (make): on its own the causative defaults to coercion: 母は妹に野菜を食べさせた reads as made her eat them. This is the natural reading wherever the causer holds authority — parents, teachers, bosses — and it stays "make" even where the English translation would soften it.

Usage 2 — permission (let): combined with the benefactive てあげる, てくれる, or てもらう, the same form flips to willing permission: 食べさせてくれた — let her eat them, as a favour. Only these helping verbs license the "let" reading; without one, assume "make".

Usage 3 — させてください: this set phrase politely asks for permission to do something oneself: 私に説明させてください — please let me explain. In this pattern the reading is always "let", never "make", and no helping verb is needed. Among friends the bare て-form does the same job: 休ませて — let me rest.

Caution — the doer's particle: when the caused action has its own direct object marked を, the doer must take に — Japanese does not allow two を in one clause (息子に野菜を食べさせる). When the verb is intransitive, the doer itself may take を or に, and the choice colours the meaning: に suggests the doer was willing or permitted (子どもに遊ばせる — let), while を suggests the causer's one-sided decision (子どもを遊ばせる — make). The causative attaches to transitive and intransitive verbs alike.

Victimforced person

+ に +
Objectif any
+ を +
Verbcausative-passive form
Formation
う-verb (godan)
Verb [あ]あ-row stem
+ される
う-verb ending in す
Verb [あ]あ-row stem
+ せられる
る-verb (ichidan)
Verb [る]
+ させられる
Irregular

About

This grammar structure is used to express that somebody was made to do something against their will — the causative-passive, which stacks the passive onto the causative. The victim, the person forced to act, becomes the subject and is marked with は or が; the forcer is marked with に; a direct object keeps its を. The full ending is させられる (causative させる + passive られる); for う-verbs not ending in す, everyday Japanese fuses it into the shorter される — 読まされる rather than 読ませられる, both correct, the shorter one standard in speech; う-verbs ending in す avoid the fusion and take only させられる (話させられる). Whatever the base verb, the result conjugates as a regular る-verb, and the tables below run 読む through the same pattern as the passive and causative cards.

Usage — being forced: the causative-passive is always coercive. The subject did not want to perform the action but was pressured or obligated into it, typically inside hierarchies — parent and child, teacher and student, boss and employee. 毎週長い会議に出させられる complains about the meetings in a way the plain causative never could, and the form works with transitive and intransitive verbs alike, since what matters is the unpleasant imposition, not the presence of an object.

Causative vs causative-passive — who is the subject: the same event flips depending on the form. 兄は私に宿題を手伝わせた — the brother is the subject, he made me help. 私は兄に宿題を手伝わされた — now I am the subject, and I was made to help. In the causative the causer is the subject; in the causative-passive the victim is. Note the が trap: in 姉が皿洗いをさせられていた, が marks the forced person — the sister suffered. The moment the forcer appears in the sentence, they take に instead, and the victim reading shifts to the speaker. Misreading who forced whom is the classic error with this form.

Cautions: the ら抜き shortening is impossible here — させられる never drops its ら, because dropping ら is licensed only for the potential meaning of られる, which the causative-passive never carries. Also keep the fused shape apart from the plain passive of する: 掃除される means to be cleaned, while 掃除させられる means to be made to clean.

It is said
Phrase +
(だ)for noun / な-adj
+ と言われている
It is considered

(だ)for noun / な-adj
+ と考えられている
It is thought / assumed
Phrase +
(だ)for noun / な-adj
+ と思われている

Phrase +
(だ)optional
+ とされている
About

This grammar structure covers a family of impersonal statements built on one skeleton: a phrase, the quotative particle と, and the passive form of a verb of saying or thinking in its ている form. と言われている — it is said, と考えられている — it is considered, と思われている — it is thought, and とされている — it is regarded as all report an opinion held by people in general rather than by any named person — the passive removes the opinion-holder exactly the way English "it is said that…" does, and ている presents the opinion as currently held. Phrases ending in a noun or な-adjective take だ before と: ストレスは病気の原因だと考えられている.

Choosing between them: 言われている reports what people actually say — reputations, sayings, folklore. 考えられている reports a reasoned consensus — researchers, experts, informed opinion. 思われている reports a felt impression — the image people carry, including stereotypes. とされている reports what is accepted as established — rules, official positions, textbook facts; its と leans on する in the sense of to regard · decide as, so it carries the nuance of a settled result rather than a quoted voice. The kanji in 言う is optional here — と言われている and といわれている are the same expression.

Cautions: these forms can smuggle in the speaker's own view — presenting a personal opinion as what "everyone knows" is a common rhetorical use, so treat the claimed consensus with appropriate suspicion. In the past tense (と考えられていた) the family reports beliefs that have since been abandoned — a standard pattern in science and history writing.

N5CH.20 · CR.1
か
(ka)
Question marker · Or
or — choice
Noun A + か + Noun B +
(か)optional
yes/no question
Statement + か
About

か is a particle that functions as a verbal question mark. Placed at the end of a statement, it turns that statement into a yes/no question without changing word order.

Or — choice questions: placed between two or more nouns, か means or. The options are listed with か after each one; the final か is optional in spoken Japanese.

Uncertainty: か is also used embedded mid-sentence to express that something is unknown: 美味しいか分からない.

Register: か regularly follows です and ます. In casual speech, bare か can sound blunt or demanding: 大丈夫ですか (standard) vs 大丈夫か (very casual).

もう食べましたか。

plain + か is blunt; used among close peers or by seniors to juniors
な-ADJ PRESENT AFFIRMATIVE PLAIN

N5CH.20 · CR.2
よ · ね
(yo · ne)
Sentence-final particles — assertion · agreement
assertion / emphasis
Sentence + よ
agreement / softening
Sentence + ね
softened assertion
Sentence + よね
About

よ and ね are conversational particles placed at the end of a sentence. They don't change the core meaning but signal how the speaker wants to engage the listener. They are not interchangeable — each serves a distinct communicative purpose.

よ — assertion & emphasis: よ is used to assert or emphasize information that the speaker believes the listener does not know or needs to hear. It adds a sense of just so you know or I'm telling you. Used when giving new information or being emphatic. Can sound stronger or more confident than plain statements.

ね — seeking agreement & softening: ね is used when the speaker is looking for agreement, wants confirmation, or wishes to soften a statement. It functions like "right?", "isn't it?", or "you know?" in English. It indicates the speaker expects the listener shares the same view. It may also be pronounced ねえ for added softness.

よね — softened assertion: used together (usually as よね), the two particles combine the assertiveness of よ with the shared-understanding quality of ね. The speaker asserts something but still invites agreement — closer to right?! than either particle alone.

N5CH.20 · CR.3
んです · のです
(~n desu · ~no desu)
The fact is, You see, It's because — explanatory · emphatic
Casual

+ んだ

+ んだ

+ んです

+ んです

Formal / Written
Verb
Verbplain form
+ のです
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ のです
な-adjective
な-adj + なのです
Noun
Noun + なのです
About

This grammar structure is used to explain, justify, or provide background context — implying the reason is, you see, or the fact is. Rather than simply reporting information, it signals that the statement is connected to something the listener has observed, asked about, or reacted to. In questions, んですか prompts the listener to explain themselves.

んです never conjugates itself. Tense and polarity come from the word before it — attach んです to any plain form, present, past, or negative. For verbs and い-adjectives, attach directly to the plain form. For な-adjectives and nouns, add な before んです.

ん is a contraction of の. The original form is のです — technically more correct, and used in formal or written Japanese, but can sound stiff in speech. んです is the standard spoken form. In casual speech it contracts further to んだ.

Do not use んです for every sentence — only when there is context, emotion, or justification involved. Overuse sounds unnatural and comes across as over-explaining.

N4CH.20 · CR.4
かな・かしら
(~kana · ~kashira)
I wonder — self-directed question
Neutral
Sentenceplain form - だ / です dropped
+ かな
Feminine
Sentenceplain form - だ / です dropped
+ かしら
About

This grammar structure is used to ask a question of oneself — I wonder if…. かな originated as a combination of the sentence-ending particles か and な: か presents a question, while な marks a statement as belonging purely to the speaker's own thoughts. Combined, they turn the question inward — the speaker questions their own statement rather than asking a listener, which is why these sentences are normally written with 。 rather than ？.

かな can be added to the end of almost any sentence in its plain form. With な-adjectives and nouns, both だ and です are usually omitted, and かな follows the word stem directly: 学生かな, never 学生だかな.

かしら is the feminine counterpart. It began as an abbreviation of か知らぬ — whether it is (A), I don't know — and now works as a standalone sentence-ending particle expressing the same self-directed doubt, much as かも does for clipped uncertainty. Although the original long forms were once used by everybody, modern かしら is felt to be distinctly feminine and is rarely used by men; かな is neutral and available to any speaker.

Both particles voice a soft, passing wondering. When the question is weightier — brooding over something rather than idly voicing it — Japanese reaches for のだろうか, covered in card CH.20 · CR.5.

N4CH.20 · CR.5
のだろうか
(~no darou ka)
I wonder… — pondering question
Verb
Verbplain form
+ のだろうか
い-adjective
い-adjplain form
+ のだろうか
な-adjective
な-adj + なのだろうか
Noun
Noun + なのだろうか
About

This grammar structure is used to wonder about something in a pondering, deliberative way — I wonder if (A). だろう, the plain conjectural form of the copula, is grouped with the question particle か, presenting the statement before it as something the speaker is unsure about and cannot settle. It is the weightier counterpart of かな: where かな voices a passing thought, のだろうか broods over a real question.

The statement before だろうか must first be nominalized — turned into a noun-phrase — with の, or なの in the case of な-adjectives and nouns. Verbs and い-adjectives attach directly to the plain form. In speech this の regularly contracts to ん (なん), exactly as のです becomes んです. Versions that omit the の・なの altogether (来るだろうか, 店だろうか) are also acceptable, but they carry a somewhat old-fashioned ring.

だろうか sounds quite masculine. To sound more polite or more ladylike, でしょう replaces だろう: のでしょうか works for any speaker, and doubles as a soft, polite way of putting a question to someone else rather than to oneself.

N4CH.20 · CR.6
じゃないか
(~ja nai ka)
Isn't it? — confirmation tag
Casual
Phraseplain form - verbs usually add ん
+ じゃないか
Formal
Phraseplain form
+ ではないか
About

This grammar structure is used to seek the listener's agreement or confirmation — the Japanese counterpart of finishing an English sentence with "isn't it?". It combines the negative copula じゃない with the question particle か. Although it contains ない, the sentence is not a negation: the speaker asserts the statement and invites the listener to agree with it.

As plain negations, じゃない and ではない attach only to nouns and な-adjectives. As a confirmation tag, however, じゃないか can follow almost any phrase in its plain form — verbs and い-adjectives included; です never appears before it. With verbs, the explanatory ん is very commonly inserted before it (来るんじゃないか) — the same ん as in んだけど・んですが.

When じゃないか feels too casual, ではないか is used instead. It is more formal, but it can sound somewhat stiff, so it is best reserved for situations where politeness is genuinely expected.

Casual question marker — masculine

About

This grammar structure is used to mark a question in very casual speech. かい is commonly thought of as one word, but it is actually the question particle か plus い, a sentence-ending particle used almost exclusively by men, in the same family as ね and よ. The result is a strongly masculine, familiar question marker.

かい usually follows the word or phrase it highlights directly. Verbs and い-adjectives may insert の before it, while な-adjectives and nouns take なの. Because かい is so casual, the の・なの is frequently omitted — and when it is kept, it often shortens to ん (なん), just as のです becomes んです. With few exceptions, かい asks simple yes-no questions; question-word questions take だい instead.

Because かい is very casual and quite direct, it can easily sound like an accusation, so care should be taken with tone of voice. The particle い itself is felt to be fairly rough, which means かい belongs strictly to conversations with close, familiar people — never with someone above you.

か · よ · ね · んです · かな · かしら · のだろうか · じゃないか · かい
Comparison
Form Register Typically used by Function
か POLITE Anyone Turn a sentence into a question
よ · ね NEUTRAL Anyone Assert something new · invite agreement
んです / のです POLITE Anyone Explain the background, or ask for it
かなN4 PLAIN Anyone Wonder to yourself — question turned inward
かしらN4 PLAIN Women The same wondering, distinctly feminine
のだろうかN4 PLAIN Anyone — だろうか leans masculine Brood over a question you cannot settle
じゃないかN4 PLAIN Anyone Push for agreement — "isn't it?"
かいN4 PLAIN Men, to people they know well Ask a simple yes-no question
When to use what
Asking anybody anything, politely → か
Telling someone something they did not know → よ · checking they agree → ね
Giving or asking for the reason behind a situation → んです
Thinking aloud rather than asking anyone — note these end in 。, not ？ → かな · かしらN4
The same wondering, but weightier — something genuinely troubling you → のだろうかN4
You have made up your mind and want the other person to say yes → じゃないかN4
Rough, familiar, and easily mistaken for an accusation — use with care and only with close company → かいN4
